                                                              Inside a Textile Elastic Factory: Machines, Process and Quality Checks

                                                              A look inside an elastic factory, from raw yarn and rubber thread to weaving, knitting, finishing and final inspection, with the quality checks that keep every roll consistent.

                                                              By SNEH Editorial•16 November 2026•6 min read•1,229 words

                                                              In this article

                                                              1. The overall flow
                                                              2. Raw materials and incoming inspection
                                                              3. Yarn preparation
                                                              4. The main machines
                                                              5. Finishing: setting, dyeing and softening
                                                              6. Quality checks along the line
                                                              7. Cutting, packing and dispatch
                                                              8. People, safety and the working environment
                                                              9. Efficiency and continuous improvement
                                                              10. Final thoughts

                                                              Most people only meet elastic as a small strip inside a waistband or a loop on a mask. Behind that strip is a factory with many machines, a careful flow of materials and a strict set of checks. A textile elastic factory turns yarn, rubber thread and spandex into tapes, cords and bands that must stretch, recover and last in thousands of garments. This article walks through a typical factory floor, following the material from the store room to the packed carton.

                                                              The overall flow

                                                              Factories differ, but most follow the same broad path:

                                                              1. Incoming material is received and checked.
                                                              2. Yarns are prepared for the machines.
                                                              3. Elastic is woven, knitted or braided.
                                                              4. The tape is finished, dyed or heat set.
                                                              5. The product is inspected, cut and packed.

                                                              Each stage has its own machines, people and quality points. Mistakes found early are cheap to fix, while mistakes found at the end can mean scrapping whole lots, so good factories check at every step.

                                                              Raw materials and incoming inspection

                                                              Everything begins at the store. Typical raw materials include:

                                                              • Polyester and nylon yarns for the body of the tape.
                                                              • Cotton or other yarns for specific products.
                                                              • Natural rubber thread or spandex for the stretch.
                                                              • Dyes and finishing chemicals for colouring and softening.
                                                              • Packing materials such as cores, bags and cartons.

                                                              Incoming lots are usually checked against supplier documents and sampled for things such as yarn count, strength, colour and cleanliness. Rubber thread may be checked for thickness and elasticity. Material that fails is held back, since a poor input cannot be fixed later.

                                                              Yarn preparation

                                                              Before a loom or knitting machine can run, yarn must be wound and arranged properly.

                                                              • Winding transfers yarn from large supply packages to bobbins or cones that suit the machine, while removing weak spots and knots.
                                                              • Warping arranges many yarns in parallel on a beam at even tension.
                                                              • Covering is the process of wrapping a rubber or spandex core with another yarn to produce covered elastic, often used in knitting and in some narrow fabrics.
                                                              • Creeling places the prepared packages onto the machine in the correct order.

                                                              Operators follow a production sheet that lists yarn types, number of ends, widths and settings. A small mistake in this stage can spoil an entire run.

                                                              The main machines

                                                              The core of the factory is its set of tape-making machines.

                                                              • Narrow fabric looms weave tapes with several elastic threads inside a woven structure. They make firm, stable elastic with neat edges and are common for waistbands and straps.
                                                              • Knitting machines, often warp knitting or crochet-type, build tape from interlooped yarns. Knitted elastic is usually softer and more flexible and is common in underwear and soft trims.
                                                              • Braiding machines interlace yarns diagonally to produce round or flat braided elastic and cords, widely used for drawcords and lighter products.
                                                              • Covering machines wrap a core with yarn at high speed.
                                                              • Rewinding machines transfer finished tape onto rolls or spools of the required length.

                                                              Machines run for long hours, so maintenance is vital. Regular cleaning, lubrication and replacement of worn parts prevent breakdowns and keep the output consistent.

                                                              Finishing: setting, dyeing and softening

                                                              Tape leaving the loom is not always ready for use. Finishing steps improve its look and stability.

                                                              1. Scouring or washing removes oils and sizing from the yarn.
                                                              2. Dyeing adds colour, either by dyeing the finished tape or by using pre-coloured yarn. Dyeing must be done with care, because heat and chemicals can affect the elastic.
                                                              3. Heat setting uses controlled heat to stabilise width and shape, so the tape does not shrink unpredictably later.
                                                              4. Softening or special finishes can improve feel or add properties such as grip.
                                                              5. Drying and conditioning bring the tape to a stable moisture level.

                                                              Controlling temperature and time is essential, since too much heat can weaken the elastic and too little leaves the tape unstable.

                                                              Quality checks along the line

                                                              Quality control is not a single step at the end. It is a series of checks, and a good factory records the results.

                                                              • In-process checks. Operators measure width, check pick density and watch for faults such as broken ends or wavy edges. Samples are often taken at the start of each run and at regular intervals.
                                                              • Stretch and recovery tests. A sample is stretched to a set level and released, and the tape is checked for how well it returns to its original length.
                                                              • Width and thickness. Measured against the specification and agreed tolerance.
                                                              • Strength tests. Checking how much force the tape withstands before breaking.
                                                              • Colour matching. Comparing the tape with an approved sample under standard lighting. Colour fastness to washing, rubbing and light can also be tested, depending on the customer's needs.
                                                              • Shrinkage tests. Checking how the tape changes after washing or heat.
                                                              • Visual inspection. Trained inspectors check rolls for stains, knots, uneven stripes and other defects.

                                                              Customers may also ask for tests against their own requirements or against recognised standards, and factories keep records so that any lot can be traced back to its materials and machines.

                                                              Cutting, packing and dispatch

                                                              Once approved, the elastic is measured, rolled and packed according to the order.

                                                              • Length counting. Rolls are measured with counters to ensure correct length.
                                                              • Labelling. Each roll or carton carries information such as product code, colour, width, length and batch number.
                                                              • Packing. Tapes are wrapped or bagged to protect against dust, moisture and sunlight, then placed in cartons.
                                                              • Storage and dispatch. Stock is kept in a clean, cool, dry area away from direct sunlight and strong chemicals, because heat and light can age elastic.

                                                              Batch numbers matter. If a customer reports a problem, the factory can trace the batch, check its records and find the cause.

                                                              People, safety and the working environment

                                                              Machines do not run themselves. A factory depends on skilled operators who understand tension, thread paths and the sound of a healthy machine. Supervisors, technicians, quality staff and planners complete the team. Good factories invest in training and safety, including guarding on moving parts, dust control, safe handling of chemicals and clear walkways.

                                                              Cleanliness also matters. Lint and dust can contaminate yarn and tape, so many plants keep floors clean and control airflow near sensitive machines.

                                                              Efficiency and continuous improvement

                                                              Modern factories track more than output. They watch downtime, waste, rework and delivery times. Common practices include:

                                                              • planning production to reduce changeovers between products;
                                                              • recycling or reusing yarn waste where possible;
                                                              • saving energy in dyeing and heat setting;
                                                              • keeping spare parts and maintenance schedules in order;
                                                              • collecting customer feedback to improve products.

                                                              Small improvements, repeated over thousands of metres, make a real difference to cost, quality and reliability.

                                                              Final thoughts

                                                              A textile elastic factory is a chain of connected steps, and the strength of the chain depends on every link. Good yarn, careful preparation, well-maintained machines, controlled finishing and honest testing together produce elastic that performs the same way from the first roll to the last. For buyers, knowing how the factory works makes it easier to ask useful questions about process, tolerance and testing, and to choose a partner who treats quality as a daily habit and not only a final inspection.

                                                              Frequently asked questions

                                                              What are the main stages in an elastic factory?

                                                              Typical stages include yarn preparation, warping, weaving or knitting, dyeing and finishing, inspection and packing.

                                                              Why is tension control so important?

                                                              It sets the stretch and recovery of the elastic, so poor control produces uneven or unreliable bands.

                                                              How do factories check elastic quality?

                                                              They test stretch, recovery, width, shrinkage and colour fastness on samples from each production lot.

                                                              Why are lot numbers important?

                                                              They let manufacturers trace colour and quality back to a batch and keep consistent shades within an order.

                                                                Colour Elastic: How Elastic Is Dyed

                                                                Why dyeing elastic is harder than dyeing ordinary fabric, and how disperse, acid and reactive dyes bring bright colour to stretch bands.

                                                                By SNEH Editorial•16 November 2026•6 min read•1,347 words

                                                                In this article

                                                                1. Why dyeing elastic is special
                                                                2. Which fibre takes which dye?
                                                                3. Dyeing before or after forming the band
                                                                4. The dyeing process, step by step
                                                                5. Shade matching and consistency
                                                                6. Metamerism and light
                                                                7. Special effects
                                                                8. Environmental considerations
                                                                9. Common dyeing defects
                                                                10. Tips for buyers
                                                                11. Final thoughts

                                                                Open a drawer of sewing supplies or a rack of fashion trims and you will find elastic in every colour imaginable: bright neon, deep navy, soft pastel, black and white. Behind that rainbow lies a difficult piece of textile chemistry. Elastic is a composite of different fibres, it is under internal tension, and it must stay bright through washing and wear. This article explains how colour elastic is dyed, which dyes are used and why colour consistency is such a challenge.

                                                                Why dyeing elastic is special

                                                                Dyeing an ordinary cotton fabric is relatively straightforward. Dyeing elastic is more complicated for several reasons.

                                                                • Mixed fibres. A single band may contain polyester, nylon, cotton, rubber and spandex, each of which takes dye differently.
                                                                • Heat sensitivity. Rubber and spandex can be damaged by high temperatures and long dye cycles.
                                                                • Tension. Elastic must be dyed in a relaxed state so that it does not shrink or distort afterwards.
                                                                • Narrow width. Elastic is narrow and often wound in large quantities, which makes even liquor flow and uniform penetration difficult.
                                                                • Colour fastness. The colour must stay on the elastic through washing, sweat and rubbing without staining adjoining fabric.

                                                                For these reasons, elastic dyeing needs a high level of experience and process control.

                                                                Which fibre takes which dye?

                                                                The first rule of dyeing is matching dye class to fibre type.

                                                                Polyester is usually dyed with disperse dyes. These are non-ionic dyes with low water solubility, applied at high temperature, typically around one hundred and thirty degrees Celsius in pressurised equipment, so the dye can enter the tight polyester structure.

                                                                Nylon is dyed with acid dyes or metal-complex dyes, which bond to amino groups in the fibre. Nylon dyes well at about ninety to one hundred degrees Celsius with a mildly acidic bath.

                                                                Cotton is dyed with reactive dyes, which form covalent bonds with the cellulose, or sometimes direct or vat dyes, giving bright and relatively washfast colours.

                                                                Spandex can take disperse dyes or acid dyes, depending on its chemistry, but is usually dyed at lower temperatures to avoid damage. In many elastics, the spandex is hidden inside a covering and takes little colour, so only the cover is dyed.

                                                                Natural rubber usually remains its natural cream colour or is pigmented at the latex stage. The rubber inside the elastic is often hidden by the covering.

                                                                Dyeing before or after forming the band

                                                                Producers can colour elastic at different stages.

                                                                Yarn dyeing

                                                                The covering yarns are dyed before they are wrapped and woven or knitted into elastic. Dyed yarn is wound onto cones, dyed in packages, then dried and used. Advantages include deep, uniform colour, the ability to create stripes and patterns using different colours, and good penetration. This method suits large orders in standard colours.

                                                                Piece dyeing of finished elastic

                                                                The elastic band is formed first, usually in white or natural, and then dyed in a machine, which may be a hank dyeing machine, jet dyeing machine or a beam dyeing machine. This gives flexibility, since a producer can make a neutral stock and dye it quickly for different customers. Piece dyeing is common for small batches and fast fashion orders.

                                                                Spin or solution dyeing

                                                                In solution dyeing, pigment is added to the polymer before the fibre is spun, giving a colour that runs through the whole fibre. It offers very good colour fastness and uses much less water than traditional dyeing, but colour choices are fixed at the fibre stage, so it is practical mainly for large volumes of popular colours such as black.

                                                                The dyeing process, step by step

                                                                1. Preparation. The elastic is scoured, meaning washed with mild detergents to remove oils, waxes and sizing agents so dye can enter evenly.
                                                                2. Relaxation. The elastic is allowed to shrink and relax, often in warm water or steam, so it will not change dimensions later.
                                                                3. Dye bath. The elastic is placed in a bath with dye, water and auxiliaries that control pH, levelling and temperature. Heat is raised slowly to give even dye uptake.
                                                                4. Holding at temperature. The bath is kept at the right temperature for a set time while dye migrates into the fibre.
                                                                5. Cooling and rinsing. After dyeing, the elastic is cooled gradually and rinsed to remove loose dye.
                                                                6. Soaping or reduction clearing. For polyester dyed with disperse dyes, a clearing step removes surface dye, which improves wash fastness.
                                                                7. Fixing and softening. Finishing agents may be applied to set the dye and improve softness.
                                                                8. Drying and heat setting. The elastic is dried under controlled conditions, then heat set to stabilise width and shape.

                                                                Shade matching and consistency

                                                                One of the biggest challenges is producing the same colour batch after batch. Several factors influence shade.

                                                                • Dye concentration and recipe. Tiny changes in dye quantity change depth of colour.
                                                                • Water quality. Minerals and pH affect dye uptake.
                                                                • Temperature profile. Heating rate and holding time determine levelness and depth.
                                                                • Substrate variation. Different lots of yarn or elastic may take dye differently.
                                                                • Machine conditions. Liquor ratio, circulation and loading influence results.

                                                                Producers use laboratory dyeing trials, spectrophotometers and colour standards to match shades. A colour measured numerically is compared against a standard, and tolerances are set. Buyers should specify acceptable tolerances and check approval samples, often called lab dips, before bulk production.

                                                                Metamerism and light

                                                                A phenomenon called metamerism occurs when two colours match under one light source but differ under another. Elastic and garment fabric may match in the shop but look different under daylight. To avoid problems, colour matching should be checked under several light sources, such as daylight, store lighting and indoor lamps.

                                                                Special effects

                                                                Dyed elastics can have special visual styles.

                                                                • Space-dyed or melange effects created by dyeing sections of yarn with different colours.
                                                                • Printed elastic, where patterns or logos are printed on the surface, often using heat transfer or screen printing.
                                                                • Jacquard woven elastic, where coloured yarns create patterns during weaving, often used for branded waistbands.
                                                                • Fluorescent colours that use special dyes, which can be less lightfast.
                                                                • Reflective or glow effects that use coating or special yarns.

                                                                Environmental considerations

                                                                Dyeing is one of the most resource-intensive stages in textile production, using large amounts of water, energy and chemicals. Responsible producers take several measures.

                                                                • Wastewater treatment to remove colour and chemical residues before discharge.
                                                                • Low-liquor-ratio machines that use less water.
                                                                • Restricted substance lists that ban hazardous dyes and chemicals.
                                                                • Closed-loop systems that recover and reuse water and heat.
                                                                • Safer dyes and auxiliaries with certification, such as bluesign or OEKO-TEX approved products.
                                                                • Spin-dyeing to reduce water use in suitable products.

                                                                Buyers can ask suppliers about their environmental management and certifications.

                                                                Common dyeing defects

                                                                • Uneven dyeing or streaks from poor levelling or contamination.
                                                                • Shade variation between batches from inconsistent process control.
                                                                • Poor colour fastness with colour bleeding in washing.
                                                                • Loss of elasticity from excessive heat or harsh chemicals.
                                                                • Staining of the rubber or core that shows through.
                                                                • Shrinkage differences between dyed and undyed parts.

                                                                Testing and quality control help prevent these problems.

                                                                Tips for buyers

                                                                1. Request lab dips for colour approval before bulk production.
                                                                2. Specify colour fastness requirements for washing, rubbing, perspiration and light.
                                                                3. Check shade under multiple light sources.
                                                                4. Order enough from one dye lot to complete the project.
                                                                5. Ask about dye types and certifications if safety or sustainability is important.
                                                                6. Test washing with white fabric to check for bleeding.

                                                                Final thoughts

                                                                Colour elastic looks simple, but achieving bright, consistent and durable colour on a stretchy, multi-fibre band is a complex technical achievement. It requires the right dyes for each fibre, careful temperature control, relaxed handling and rigorous testing. When you choose a coloured elastic, you are enjoying the result of skilled chemistry and craft. Understanding how it is done helps you ask better questions and choose elastic that stays vibrant for as long as the garment lasts.

                                                                Frequently asked questions

                                                                How is elastic dyed?

                                                                Elastic is dyed in a hot dye bath or dye machine, where the dye is absorbed by the fibres and then fixed.

                                                                Why is dyeing elastic harder than dyeing fabric?

                                                                The rubber or spandex core and the cover yarn can take dye differently, and heat can affect stretch.

                                                                Can colours be matched exactly?

                                                                Close matches are possible with lab dips and shade cards, but exact matches depend on the fibre and the dye.

                                                                Does dyeing weaken the elastic?

                                                                Poor control of temperature and chemicals can, so good manufacturers keep the process carefully managed.

                                                                  Colour Fastness in Elastic: Tests, Ratings and Standards

                                                                  Will the colour run in the wash, rub off on a shirt or fade in the sun? Learn how colour fastness is tested and rated.

                                                                  By SNEH Editorial

                                                                  ← Elastic Basics

                                                                  How Elastic Is Made: From Raw Material to Finished Roll

                                                                  Follow the journey of elastic through yarn preparation, covering, weaving or knitting, dyeing and finishing before it reaches your sewing table.

                                                                  By SNEH Editorial•16 November 2026•7 min read•1,402 words

                                                                  In this article

                                                                  1. Step one: choosing the raw materials
                                                                  2. Step two: preparing the yarns
                                                                  3. Step three: covering the elastic core
                                                                  4. Step four: forming the band
                                                                  5. Step five: relaxing the elastic
                                                                  6. Step six: dyeing and colouring
                                                                  7. Step seven: finishing treatments
                                                                  8. Step eight: testing and inspection
                                                                  9. Step nine: cutting, winding and packing
                                                                  10. Why two elastics of the same width can differ so much
                                                                  11. Quality starts with consistency
                                                                  12. Looking ahead

                                                                  A roll of elastic on a shelf looks simple, but it is the result of a surprisingly long chain of processes. Raw materials are converted into threads, threads are wrapped and combined, machines interlace them at high speed, and the resulting band is dyed, finished and tested. This article walks through that journey step by step so you can understand why elastics differ in price, feel and performance.

                                                                  Step one: choosing the raw materials

                                                                  Everything begins with the choice of the elastic core and the textile yarns that surround it. The core is usually natural rubber thread, synthetic rubber thread or spandex filament. The surrounding yarns are normally polyester, nylon, cotton or a blend. The decision depends on the end use. A soft waistband for children's wear might use fine nylon and spandex, while a heavy-duty strap might use thick polyester and rubber.

                                                                  Quality control starts here. Rubber thread is checked for diameter, tensile strength and elongation. Spandex is checked for linear density, usually measured in denier or decitex. Textile yarns are checked for evenness, strength and colour consistency. A weakness in any of these inputs is very hard to fix later, so careful manufacturers inspect incoming materials before using them.

                                                                  Step two: preparing the yarns

                                                                  Yarns arrive on cones, bobbins or spools. Before they can be used they must be prepared for the machine. This includes rewinding onto suitable packages, checking tension and sometimes applying a light lubricant or wax so the yarn runs smoothly through guides and needles. For woven elastic, long parallel sets of yarn are arranged on a warp beam, which is a large spool carrying many threads side by side. For knitted elastic, similar beams feed the warp-knitting machine. For braided elastic, individual bobbins are loaded onto a braiding machine.

                                                                  Rubber thread needs special attention. It is usually kept stretched at a controlled level while it feeds into the machine, because the amount of pre-stretch decides how much the finished elastic will gather and how it will recover.

                                                                  Step three: covering the elastic core

                                                                  Many elastics use a covered core. This means the rubber or spandex thread is wrapped with another yarn before the band is formed. A covering machine spins a fine yarn around the stretched core in a spiral. Single covering uses one wrap, and double covering uses two wraps wound in opposite directions so that the thread does not twist or curl.

                                                                  Covering has several benefits. It protects the elastic core from friction and light. It limits the maximum stretch, which prevents overstretching. It makes the thread easier to handle, and it gives a smoother surface for knitting or weaving. A separate article on this blog explains rubber covered elastic and covered yarns in depth, because the technique is central to the industry.

                                                                  Step four: forming the band

                                                                  This is the stage that gives elastic its final shape. The method depends on the type.

                                                                  Weaving. On a narrow-fabric loom, warp threads run lengthwise and weft threads cross them. The elastic core threads are usually placed in the warp direction while the weft yarn locks everything together. Many narrow bands are woven side by side on the same machine and are later separated. Woven elastic comes out dense and stable.

                                                                  Warp knitting. On a crochet or raschel type machine, needles form loops of yarn that connect with neighbouring loops, creating a flexible structure. Elastic threads are laid in between the loops. Knitted elastic is softer and more drapey than woven elastic and can include decorative patterns, picots and scalloped edges.

                                                                  Braiding. On a braiding machine, bobbins travel in interlacing paths around a central core. This creates a flat or round cord in which yarns cross over and under one another. Braided elastic is quick to produce and often cheaper.

                                                                  During this stage the machine speed, tension settings and stitch density are adjusted carefully. A small error in tension can change the stretch of the whole roll.

                                                                  Step five: relaxing the elastic

                                                                  Freshly formed elastic is under internal stress because its core has been held stretched during production. It needs to be allowed to relax so it reaches its natural state. This can be done by passing the elastic through a controlled heat or steam process, or by resting it in a loose state for a period of time. If this step is skipped, the elastic may shrink unpredictably after it is cut or sewn, which causes problems such as puckering and uneven garments.

                                                                  Step six: dyeing and colouring

                                                                  Most elastic is dyed to match garments. The choice of dye depends on the yarn. Polyester is typically dyed with disperse dyes at high temperature. Nylon uses acid dyes. Cotton uses reactive dyes. Because an elastic may contain several fibres, the dyeing process needs to be carefully balanced so every component takes colour properly and the result does not stain or fade.

                                                                  Dyeing can be done on yarn before the band is formed or on the finished band afterwards. Yarn dyeing gives more consistent depth and allows stripes and patterns. Piece dyeing of the finished band is more flexible for small orders. Colour elastic and the standards that govern it will be explored in other articles here.

                                                                  Step seven: finishing treatments

                                                                  After dyeing, the elastic usually goes through finishing. This may include washing to remove leftover chemicals and spinning oils, softening to improve comfort, heat setting to stabilise width and shape, and drying under controlled tension. Some products receive additional treatments such as silicone dots for grip, anti-slip coatings, antimicrobial finishes or a brushed surface for extra softness.

                                                                  Heat setting is particularly important. It locks the structure of synthetic yarns in a stable form so the finished elastic holds its width and does not shrink excessively when washed by the end user.

                                                                  Step eight: testing and inspection

                                                                  Responsible producers test the elastic before it is shipped. Typical checks include width and thickness measurement, stretch and recovery tests, strength tests, colour fastness to washing, rubbing and perspiration, and dimensional stability after washing. Visual inspection looks for broken threads, uneven edges, stains and weaving faults.

                                                                  Testing is not just a formality. A roll that looks perfect can still fail in use if its recovery is weak or its colour bleeds. Test results also allow buyers to compare suppliers on facts instead of promises.

                                                                  Step nine: cutting, winding and packing

                                                                  Finally the elastic is wound onto rolls, spools or cartons in the lengths required by customers. Some is cut into short pieces for products such as masks or hair ties. Labels are attached with details such as width, composition and batch number. The batch number is valuable because it allows any later problem to be traced back to its production conditions.

                                                                  Why two elastics of the same width can differ so much

                                                                  Because of all these stages, the price and performance of elastic reflect many hidden decisions. A cheaper elastic may use thinner rubber thread, fewer covering turns, lower-grade dyes or less thorough finishing. It may look identical on day one and behave very differently after ten washes. A premium elastic often costs more because its core is better, its tension is more carefully controlled and its dye and finish are more durable.

                                                                  Understanding the process helps buyers ask the right questions: What is the core? How many ends of rubber are used? How is it dyed? Has it been heat set? What is the stretch and recovery? These questions separate informed purchasing from guesswork.

                                                                  Quality starts with consistency

                                                                  The most important quality in elastic manufacturing is not any single feature but consistency. Roll after roll must give the same width, the same stretch and the same colour. Achieving this requires well-maintained machines, trained operators, controlled environments and rigorous testing. A factory that has mastered consistency is a factory that its customers can rely on when they scale up production.

                                                                  Looking ahead

                                                                  New technologies are changing the process. Computer-controlled looms give more precise tension. Spandex filaments are becoming finer and stronger. Dyeing processes are being improved to use less water and fewer chemicals. Recycled and bio-based yarns are entering the market. Yet the basic journey remains the same: choose the materials, cover the core, form the band, dye, finish and test. When you next hold a roll of elastic, you are holding the product of all these steps working together, and now you know how to judge it.

                                                                  Frequently asked questions

                                                                  What are the main steps in making elastic?

                                                                  Stretch yarn and cover yarn are prepared, then woven, knitted or braided into a narrow fabric. The elastic is then finished, dyed if needed, tested and wound onto rolls.

                                                                  Why is elastic stretched during production?

                                                                  Tension control matters because it decides how the elastic relaxes later. Uneven tension can cause waves, shrinkage or different widths on the same roll.

                                                                  Why does finished elastic sometimes shrink after washing?

                                                                  Elastic is made under tension, and heat or moisture can let the yarns relax. Good manufacturers pre-relax or heat-set it to reduce this.

                                                                  Is elastic tested before it is sold?

                                                                  Quality-focused makers check width, stretch, recovery, strength and colour fastness before dispatch.

                                                                    How Elastic Tape Is Woven: Narrow Fabric Looms Explained

                                                                    Woven elastic is made on narrow fabric looms that interlace warp, weft and rubber or spandex threads. Learn the machine, the steps and what shapes the final tape.

                                                                    By SNEH Editorial•16 November 2026•7 min read•1,396 words

                                                                    In this article

                                                                    1. What makes a narrow fabric loom different
                                                                    2. The three sets of yarn
                                                                    3. Preparing the yarn before weaving
                                                                    4. The weaving cycle step by step
                                                                    5. Why the elastic stays inside the tape
                                                                    6. Weave patterns and what they do
                                                                    7. Weaving compared with other methods
                                                                    8. What affects the final tape
                                                                    9. Common weaving faults to watch for
                                                                    10. Final thoughts

                                                                    Pick up a strip of woven elastic and look closely. You will see tiny interlaced threads forming a firm, flat tape with a clean edge on each side. This is not cut from a wide cloth. It is woven at its final width on a special machine called a narrow fabric loom. Understanding how this loom works explains why woven elastic behaves the way it does: why it is firm, why it holds its width, and why it is trusted for waistbands, straps and medical supports. This article walks through the loom, the yarns and the steps that turn thread into tape.

                                                                    What makes a narrow fabric loom different

                                                                    A normal cloth loom weaves a wide sheet, often more than a metre across, and the fabric is later cut into shapes. A narrow fabric loom weaves many narrow tapes side by side, each with its own finished edges, called selvedges. A single machine may produce a dozen or more tapes at once, each only a few millimetres to a few centimetres wide.

                                                                    The key difference is the edge. In wide cloth the edge is a by-product. In a narrow tape the edge is part of the design, and the weft thread turns back at each side to lock the tape together. Because each tape has its own finished edge, it does not fray when used, and it can be sewn directly into garments.

                                                                    The three sets of yarn

                                                                    Woven elastic is built from three kinds of yarn, and each has a clear job.

                                                                    • Warp yarns run along the length of the tape. They are wound onto beams or fed from bobbins and form the main structure.
                                                                    • Weft yarns run across the width. A single weft thread travels back and forth, interlacing with the warp yarns and turning at the edges.
                                                                    • Elastic yarns are the rubber threads or spandex that give the tape its stretch. They are placed in the warp direction and are held under controlled tension.

                                                                    The warp and weft are usually polyester or nylon, and sometimes cotton. They form the visible face of the tape. The elastic yarns sit inside the structure, held between the interlacing threads, which is why many woven elastics look like ordinary tape until you pull them.

                                                                    Preparing the yarn before weaving

                                                                    A loom can only run well if the yarn is ready for it. Preparation is quiet, unglamorous work, but it decides much of the quality.

                                                                    1. Yarn selection. The yarn type, thickness and colour are chosen to match the order and the required strength.
                                                                    2. Warping. Hundreds of warp ends are wound in parallel onto a beam, all at the same tension. Uneven tension here shows up later as wavy or tight lines in the tape.
                                                                    3. Elastic placement. Rubber or spandex threads are mounted on their own supply so they feed at a steady, measured rate.
                                                                    4. Creeling and threading. Each yarn is guided through the correct guides and eyes so that it reaches the weaving zone in its proper position.

                                                                    Operators check the loom set-up against the specification before starting, because a mistake in threading can ruin a whole beam of yarn.

                                                                    The weaving cycle step by step

                                                                    The weaving action repeats many times every minute. Although machines differ, the basic movements are the same.

                                                                    1. Shedding. The warp yarns are divided into two groups. One group lifts and the other lowers, creating a gap called the shed. The pattern of lifting decides the weave, such as plain or twill.
                                                                    2. Weft insertion. A weft thread is carried through the shed. On many modern narrow looms a needle carries the thread across and leaves a loop at the edge.
                                                                    3. Beating up. A comb-like part called the reed pushes the new weft thread firmly against the fabric already woven. How hard and how often this is done affects the density of the tape.
                                                                    4. Take-up. The finished tape is pulled forward at a steady speed and wound onto a roll or package, while fresh warp is let off the beam.

                                                                    Then the two groups of warp yarns swap positions and the cycle begins again. Each cycle adds one weft pick, and the number of picks per centimetre is a key measure of how tight or open the tape is.

                                                                    Why the elastic stays inside the tape

                                                                    During weaving, the elastic threads are kept under tension, which stretches them to a certain degree. This is called the draft. When the finished tape leaves the loom and the tension is released, the elastic pulls back, and the warp and weft yarns bunch together into a compact, slightly crinkled structure.

                                                                    This is why a relaxed woven elastic is narrower and thicker than it appears while being woven. It also explains why the same machine can produce tapes of different stretch levels. A higher draft usually gives a tape with more available stretch, while a lower draft gives a firmer one. The draft must be controlled carefully, because uneven draft between threads causes puckering and uneven pull.

                                                                    Weave patterns and what they do

                                                                    The pattern of interlacing changes how the tape feels and performs.

                                                                    • Plain weave is the simplest pattern. It gives a flat, stable tape that is good for general use.
                                                                    • Twill weave produces fine diagonal lines. It is often softer and smoother, and is used for comfortable waistbands and visible trims.
                                                                    • Ribbed or corded effects are made by changing thread thickness, giving the tape more texture and grip.
                                                                    • Patterned or jacquard effects use special mechanisms to lift individual yarns, which allows names, logos or repeating designs to be woven into the tape.

                                                                    Pattern is not only decoration. A tight weave gives a firmer tape with less width change, while a looser one gives softness and a little more flexibility.

                                                                    Weaving compared with other methods

                                                                    Elastic tape can also be made by knitting or braiding, and each method suits different needs.

                                                                    • Woven elastic is firm, holds its width and resists curling, so it works well where a stable strap is needed.
                                                                    • Knitted elastic is softer and more flexible and tends to stretch more easily, which suits lingerie and comfort waistbands.
                                                                    • Braided elastic is round or flat and is made by interlacing threads diagonally. It is common for cords and lighter uses.

                                                                    Neither is better in every case. The choice depends on how the product will be worn, how much stretch is wanted and how stable the tape must remain when pulled.

                                                                    What affects the final tape

                                                                    Even on the same loom, several choices change the outcome.

                                                                    • Yarn count and quality. Finer yarns make lighter tapes, coarser yarns make heavier and stronger ones.
                                                                    • Number of elastic ends. More elastic threads usually give more recovery power.
                                                                    • Picks per centimetre. A denser weave gives a firmer tape.
                                                                    • Tension and draft. These decide the stretch level and how smooth the tape looks.
                                                                    • Reed and loom setting. These decide the width and the neatness of the edge.

                                                                    After weaving, tapes often go through finishing steps such as heat setting, washing or dyeing, which stabilise the width and clean the surface. Colour can also be added by using pre-dyed yarn, which helps shade consistency across large orders.

                                                                    Common weaving faults to watch for

                                                                    A good buyer or maker knows what poor weaving looks like. Typical faults include:

                                                                    • Wavy edges, caused by uneven weft tension or poor take-up.
                                                                    • Broken or missing elastic ends, which leave a weak, uneven stripe.
                                                                    • Uneven width, often from tension changes during the run.
                                                                    • Slubs or knots in the yarn that show as bumps.
                                                                    • Puckering, caused by uneven draft between elastic threads.

                                                                    Good factories check samples at the start of every run and at regular intervals, comparing width, stretch and appearance against an approved standard.

                                                                    Final thoughts

                                                                    Woven elastic looks simple, but every metre is the result of careful yarn preparation, controlled tension and a loom that repeats its cycle thousands of times with precision. Knowing how the warp, weft and elastic yarns work together helps you read a specification more confidently, ask better questions of a supplier and choose a tape that suits your product. The next time you hold a strip of woven elastic, remember that its firm edges, its width and its snap all began on a narrow loom.

                                                                    Frequently asked questions

                                                                    What is a narrow fabric loom?

                                                                    A loom that weaves many narrow bands side by side, so elastic tape comes off ready to use without cutting from wide cloth.

                                                                    What are warp and weft in elastic tape?

                                                                    Warp threads run along the length, including the rubber or spandex core, while weft threads cross them to bind the band together.

                                                                    Why is elastic woven with the core under tension?

                                                                    Controlled tension sets the stretch and recovery of the finished band, so uneven tension causes uneven elastic.

                                                                    How is woven elastic different from knitted elastic?

                                                                    Woven elastic is firmer and more stable with less width change, while knitted elastic is softer and stretches more in width.

                                                                      How Spandex Fibre Is Produced: Dry Spinning Explained

                                                                      From liquid polymer to filament: a clear, step-by-step explanation of how spandex is made, with a focus on the dry spinning process.

                                                                      By SNEH Editorial•16 November 2026•7 min read•1,428 words

                                                                      In this article

                                                                      1. The chemistry in a nutshell
                                                                      2. Stage one: making the prepolymer
                                                                      3. Stage two: chain extension
                                                                      4. Stage three: spinning methods
                                                                      5. Dry spinning in more detail
                                                                      6. Stage four: finishing oil and winding
                                                                      7. Stage five: heat setting and ageing
                                                                      8. Quality control
                                                                      9. Thread sizes
                                                                      10. Environmental and safety considerations
                                                                      11. Why production quality matters to buyers
                                                                      12. From fibre to fabric
                                                                      13. Key points to remember
                                                                      14. Final thoughts

                                                                      Spandex looks like an ordinary white or transparent thread, but making it involves sophisticated chemistry and engineering. The fibre begins as liquid chemicals, becomes a thick polymer solution and then emerges from a spinning machine as a bundle of fine filaments that can stretch many times their length. This article explains the main stages of spandex production, with special attention to dry spinning, the method used for most of the world's spandex.

                                                                      The chemistry in a nutshell

                                                                      Spandex is a segmented polyurethane, a polymer made of two kinds of building blocks that alternate along each long chain. One kind is soft and flexible, usually derived from a long-chain polyol such as a polyether or polyester glycol. The other kind is hard and rigid, created by reacting a diisocyanate with a short-chain molecule called a chain extender.

                                                                      The soft segments are coiled and stretchy. The hard segments cluster together and form tiny stable regions that act like anchors or physical cross-links. When the fibre is stretched, the soft segments uncoil, while the hard segments hold the structure together. When the force is released, the soft segments snap back to their coiled state. This molecular design is what gives spandex its remarkable stretch and recovery.

                                                                      Stage one: making the prepolymer

                                                                      Production usually starts with a reaction between the polyol and an excess of diisocyanate. The result is a prepolymer, a medium-sized molecule with reactive isocyanate groups at both ends. This prepolymer is a thick liquid that carries the potential for building the final long polymer chains.

                                                                      The exact choice of polyol, diisocyanate and ratio determines many fibre properties. For example, polyether-based soft segments tend to give better resistance to hydrolysis and microbes, while polyester-based ones may offer other mechanical properties. Chemists adjust the formula to create fibres for different applications, such as swimwear, hosiery or medical products.

                                                                      Stage two: chain extension

                                                                      The prepolymer is then dissolved in a solvent and reacted with a chain extender, typically a diamine. This reaction links the prepolymer molecules together into very long polymer chains, creating the segmented polyurethane. At this stage, the mixture becomes a viscous solution known as the spinning dope, ready to be formed into fibre.

                                                                      Additives are mixed into the spinning dope to improve performance. These may include antioxidants, stabilisers against light and chlorine, pigments or delusterants such as titanium dioxide to control brightness, and other functional agents. Each additive must be carefully dispersed so that the fibre remains uniform.

                                                                      Stage three: spinning methods

                                                                      There are several ways to turn spandex solution or melt into fibre.

                                                                      Dry spinning is the dominant process for spandex worldwide. The polymer solution is extruded through tiny holes in a spinneret into a tall, heated chamber. Hot gas, usually nitrogen or air, flows through the chamber and evaporates the solvent from the thin streams of solution. As the solvent leaves, the polymer solidifies into filaments.

                                                                      Wet spinning extrudes the solution into a liquid bath that causes the polymer to coagulate. It is used for some fibres but is less common for spandex.

                                                                      Melt spinning heats the polymer until it melts, extrudes it, and cools it into filaments. It avoids solvents but requires polymers that can be melted without damage, and it is used for some special spandex types.

                                                                      Reaction spinning extrudes the prepolymer into a bath where chain extension occurs, forming the fibre at the same time as the final polymerisation.

                                                                      Each method has advantages and trade-offs in cost, fibre quality and environmental footprint, but dry spinning remains the standard for high-quality, fine-denier spandex.

                                                                      Dry spinning in more detail

                                                                      In a dry spinning plant, the spinning dope is pumped at precise pressure through a filter that removes any particles, and then through a spinneret. A spinneret is a metal plate with many small holes, each smaller than a human hair. The number of holes determines how many filaments are in the finished yarn.

                                                                      Below the spinneret, the thin streams fall through a vertical shaft called a spinning cell. Heated gas flows through the cell, taking away solvent. The solvent is recovered from the gas stream and recycled, because it is valuable and must not be released into the environment. As the filaments dry, they become solid enough to be handled.

                                                                      At the bottom of the cell, the individual filaments are brought together and passed through a device that twists or coalesces them into a single multifilament thread. Because spandex filaments are slightly tacky, they stick together lightly, forming a bundle that behaves like one thread but still has the surface area to bond with other fibres.

                                                                      Stage four: finishing oil and winding

                                                                      After spinning, a finishing oil is applied, usually based on silicone or mineral oil. The finish reduces friction, prevents sticking on the package and helps the thread run smoothly through knitting and weaving machines. The thread is then wound onto cylindrical packages at a controlled speed. Winding tension must be steady so that the package is uniform and the thread does not stretch unevenly.

                                                                      Stage five: heat setting and ageing

                                                                      Some freshly spun fibre benefits from a rest period or a heat treatment to stabilise its properties. Textile processors later apply heat setting to fabrics, which fixes the fabric's shape and sets the stretch characteristics. The spandex must be able to tolerate this heat without losing power, so producers design fibres with suitable thermal behaviour.

                                                                      Quality control

                                                                      Throughout production, laboratories test the fibre and the process. Typical measurements include the linear density, measured in denier or decitex, which shows how thick the thread is. Other tests examine tensile strength, elongation at break, modulus, recovery, and uniformity along the length. Visual inspection checks the package for defects. Consistent quality is critical because even a tiny variation can affect fabric appearance in high-speed knitting.

                                                                      Thread sizes

                                                                      Spandex is available in a wide range of sizes, from extremely fine threads of around ten denier up to several hundred denier. Fine sizes are used in sheer hosiery and delicate fabrics, medium sizes in everyday knitwear and sportswear, and heavier sizes in bands, medical products and technical uses. The number of filaments in a thread and the way they are bundled also vary with application.

                                                                      Environmental and safety considerations

                                                                      Spandex production involves chemicals that must be handled carefully, including diisocyanates and solvents. Modern plants use closed systems, solvent recovery units, air treatment and wastewater controls to reduce emissions. Responsible producers follow safety regulations and often seek independent certification for their processes and products.

                                                                      Efforts to reduce the environmental footprint include solvent-free methods, bio-based raw materials, recycled content and energy savings. The industry is also exploring ways to improve the recyclability of blended fabrics. These are active research areas, and progress continues.

                                                                      Why production quality matters to buyers

                                                                      You may never see the spinning machine, but its quality shows up in the products you use. A well-made spandex has even thickness, consistent strength and reliable recovery, which means fabrics look uniform and garments last. Poorly spun fibre can show thick and thin places, produce streaks in fabric, snap during knitting or lose power quickly after washing. Choosing suppliers with transparent processes and testing is a practical way to avoid problems.

                                                                      From fibre to fabric

                                                                      Once produced, spandex is rarely used alone. It may be covered with nylon or polyester to make covered yarn, or fed bare into a knitting machine together with other yarns, a method called plating. It can also be core-spun, with staple fibres wrapped around a spandex core. In woven fabric, it is often used as a core-spun weft yarn for stretch denim. Each route needs careful control of tension and draft, because spandex is stretched during processing and relaxes later.

                                                                      Key points to remember

                                                                      1. Spandex is a segmented polyurethane with soft and hard segments.
                                                                      2. Production begins with a prepolymer, followed by chain extension and spinning.
                                                                      3. Dry spinning, where solvent evaporates in a heated cell, is the most widely used method.
                                                                      4. Finishing oil and careful winding prepare the thread for textile machinery.
                                                                      5. Quality control ensures uniform size, strength and recovery.
                                                                      6. Environmental management and innovation are central concerns in modern production.

                                                                      Final thoughts

                                                                      Behind every stretchy garment is a precise chain of chemistry and engineering. Dry spinning transforms a thick solution into delicate threads, each one capable of stretching several times its length. Understanding this process gives new appreciation for a fibre that most people never see. It also shows why quality, control and responsibility matter so much in the stretch materials that shape the clothes we wear.

                                                                      Frequently asked questions

                                                                      What is dry spinning?

                                                                      In dry spinning, a polymer solution is pushed through tiny holes into hot air, where the solvent evaporates and leaves solid fibres.

                                                                      What is spandex made of?

                                                                      It is a polyurethane-based polymer made of soft, stretchy segments and hard, strong segments.

                                                                      Why is spandex so stretchy?

                                                                      Its long molecules can uncoil when stretched and coil back when released, which gives high stretch and recovery.

                                                                      Is spandex made in different thicknesses?

                                                                      Yes. It is made in a range of deniers, from very fine for hosiery to thicker for heavy stretch uses.
