                                                                                                  Organic Cotton and Natural Rubber Elastic for Baby Clothing

                                                                                                  Soft, gentle and safe: how to choose elastic for newborn and baby garments, from skin comfort to safety and testing.

                                                                                                  By SNEH Editorial•16 November 2026•6 min read•1,310 words

                                                                                                  In this article

                                                                                                  1. Why baby clothing needs special elastic
                                                                                                  2. Softness first
                                                                                                  3. Organic cotton covers
                                                                                                  4. The rubber or spandex core
                                                                                                  5. Safe dyes and finishes
                                                                                                  6. Colour fastness for babies
                                                                                                  7. Washing and hygiene
                                                                                                  8. Safety design: avoid hazards
                                                                                                  9. Choosing elastic for specific baby items
                                                                                                  10. Tips for sewing baby clothes
                                                                                                  11. For brands and manufacturers
                                                                                                  12. Balancing comfort, safety and sustainability
                                                                                                  13. Questions to ask before buying
                                                                                                  14. Final thoughts

                                                                                                  Few garments deserve more care than those worn by babies. An infant's skin is thinner and more delicate than an adult's, and babies spend long hours in clothing that is washed again and again. Elastic in waistbands, cuffs and leg openings touches the body constantly, so poor elastic can cause red marks, irritation and discomfort. This article explains what to look for when choosing elastic for baby and children's clothing, with a focus on soft organic cotton covers, natural rubber and safe finishing.

                                                                                                  Why baby clothing needs special elastic

                                                                                                  Sensitive skin. Babies have a thinner outer skin layer that loses moisture quickly and absorbs substances more readily. Rough edges, harsh dyes or irritating chemicals can cause redness or rashes.

                                                                                                  Constant contact. Bodysuits, sleepers and nappy covers sit directly on the skin for many hours.

                                                                                                  Frequent washing. Baby clothes are washed often, sometimes at higher temperatures to ensure hygiene, so elastic must survive laundering.

                                                                                                  Safety. Small parts, long cords and tight bands can pose safety risks, so design and testing matter.

                                                                                                  Growth. Elastic must be gentle enough to avoid squeezing but strong enough to hold garments on a moving, growing child.

                                                                                                  Softness first

                                                                                                  The ideal baby elastic is soft to touch on both faces and edges. Look for these features.

                                                                                                  • Soft covering yarn. Organic cotton is a favourite because it is gentle and breathable. Fine nylon or soft polyester can also be soft if well finished.
                                                                                                  • Smooth edges. Knitted elastics with soft edges are often more comfortable than stiff woven edges.
                                                                                                  • Low stiffness. A low-modulus elastic gives gentle pressure rather than squeezing.
                                                                                                  • Brushed or napped surfaces. Some elastics have a brushed back for extra softness against the skin.
                                                                                                  • Adequate width. Wider soft bands distribute pressure better than narrow cords.

                                                                                                  Organic cotton covers

                                                                                                  Organic cotton is grown without synthetic pesticides and fertilisers and is often processed under standards that restrict harmful chemicals. For parents, this appeals as a reassuring choice. In elastic, organic cotton yarn is used as the covering or in the body of knitted bands. It feels natural and breathes well. It is also less likely to trap heat and moisture than some synthetic covers.

                                                                                                  Remember that organic is a claim that should be verified through certification. If a supplier says an elastic is organic cotton, ask for evidence and be clear about which parts of the product are certified.

                                                                                                  The rubber or spandex core

                                                                                                  The core provides stretch. In baby clothing, both natural rubber and spandex are used.

                                                                                                  Natural rubber core provides soft, resilient stretch and a natural origin. But it contains latex proteins, and a small number of babies and children develop latex allergy, especially those with certain medical conditions or repeated exposure. If a family has a known latex allergy, avoid natural rubber elastic and choose latex-free options. Even without allergy, ensure the rubber is fully covered so that the child's skin does not contact it directly.

                                                                                                  Spandex core is latex-free, fine and highly stretchy. Many modern baby garments use knitted elastic with a spandex core and cotton or nylon covering. It tends to be lightweight and durable.

                                                                                                  If the allergy risk is unknown, a latex-free spandex core is generally the more cautious choice for items worn against the skin for long periods. Always follow local regulations and labelling rules.

                                                                                                  Safe dyes and finishes

                                                                                                  Chemicals matter. Look for elastic that complies with recognised safety standards for textiles in children's products. Typical restrictions include limits on harmful azo dyes, heavy metals, formaldehyde, phthalates and other substances of concern. Certifications such as GOTS for organic textiles or OEKO-TEX product labels show that the product has been tested for harmful substances.

                                                                                                  Ask suppliers for test reports. For white or light shades, check that no optical brighteners or harsh bleaching were used. For coloured elastic, check colour fastness to washing, rubbing and perspiration, particularly to saliva, because babies chew on clothing.

                                                                                                  Colour fastness for babies

                                                                                                  Colour fastness to saliva and perspiration is especially important. Babies chew on cuffs and drool on collars, and sweat can transfer dye. Poor fastness can stain skin and clothes and may expose babies to dye chemicals. Select elastic that has passed tests for colour fastness to washing, rubbing, perspiration and saliva.

                                                                                                  Washing and hygiene

                                                                                                  Baby clothes often need hot washing, up to sixty degrees Celsius, to remove bacteria and stains. Not all elastics tolerate this. Polyester and nylon blends with well-set spandex typically handle hot washing better than natural rubber. If the elastic is intended for hot washing, check technical specifications and ask for wash test results. Always follow the garment's care label.

                                                                                                  Safety design: avoid hazards

                                                                                                  • Avoid long cords or loose elastic loops near the neck, since these can be strangulation hazards. Follow national safety standards for drawstrings and cords in children's clothing.
                                                                                                  • Avoid tight bands around wrists, ankles and thighs. Elastic should be snug but never restrictive.
                                                                                                  • Secure the ends of elastic in casings and seams so they cannot come loose.
                                                                                                  • Check for small parts such as decorative elements that might detach.
                                                                                                  • Test the garment after sewing to ensure the elastic does not leave red marks after a short wear.

                                                                                                  Choosing elastic for specific baby items

                                                                                                  Bodysuit leg openings and necklines: soft knitted elastic, narrow width, light tension.

                                                                                                  Pants and shorts waistbands: soft wide elastic, around fifteen to twenty-five millimetres, with gentle recovery.

                                                                                                  Sleeper cuffs and ankles: soft rib knit with a small amount of spandex, or very soft narrow elastic.

                                                                                                  Hats and headbands: wide soft bands with low modulus to avoid pressure on the head.

                                                                                                  Nappy covers and swim nappies: soft, moisture-tolerant elastic with good recovery and stable under wetting.

                                                                                                  Socks: fine spandex and cotton or nylon, with gentle top bands to avoid leaving marks.

                                                                                                  Tips for sewing baby clothes

                                                                                                  1. Pre-wash fabrics and elastic samples to check for shrinking and colour bleeding.
                                                                                                  2. Use soft thread and ballpoint needles for knit fabrics.
                                                                                                  3. Do not overstretch elastic when attaching it. Keep tension light and even.
                                                                                                  4. Cover edges or use casings so elastic does not rub directly against skin.
                                                                                                  5. Test on a baby-sized form or a sample before making the full garment.
                                                                                                  6. Label the garment honestly, including fibre content and care instructions.

                                                                                                  For brands and manufacturers

                                                                                                  Companies producing baby products carry an extra responsibility. Maintain full documentation of materials, dyes and tests. Use suppliers who can provide batch-level information. Conduct wash and wear trials, including chewing and saliva tests. Offer latex-free options clearly labelled. Following recognised standards and being transparent builds the trust that parents place in baby brands.

                                                                                                  Balancing comfort, safety and sustainability

                                                                                                  Parents increasingly want clothing that is kind to both their babies and the planet. Organic cotton and certified safe processing address both concerns. Durable elastic that keeps its shape through repeated washing also supports sustainability, because garments can be handed down to siblings and friends. In baby clothing, quality and care go hand in hand with environmental responsibility.

                                                                                                  Questions to ask before buying

                                                                                                  • Is the elastic certified or tested for harmful substances?
                                                                                                  • What is the core material and is it latex-free?
                                                                                                  • How soft are the edges and surface?
                                                                                                  • Has it been tested for colour fastness including saliva and perspiration?
                                                                                                  • Can it be washed at the temperature required for baby clothing?
                                                                                                  • Is it free from small parts and loose ends?

                                                                                                  Final thoughts

                                                                                                  Choosing elastic for baby clothing is a matter of gentleness: gentle on the skin, gentle in its pull and gentle in its chemistry. A soft organic cotton cover, a carefully chosen core, safe dyes and honest testing together make elastic that parents and babies can trust. It is a small component, but in a baby's wardrobe it can be the difference between a garment that is loved and one that is left in the drawer.

                                                                                                  Frequently asked questions

                                                                                                  Why choose organic elastic for babies?

                                                                                                  Babies have sensitive skin, so soft, gentle materials with low chemical use are a safer choice.

                                                                                                  Is natural rubber safe for babies?

                                                                                                  It is soft and flexible, but latex sensitivity is possible, so check for allergies and certifications.

                                                                                                  What should I check on baby clothing labels?

                                                                                                  Look for certified organic fibres, safety standards and soft, non-irritating elastic that is not too tight.

                                                                                                  How should baby clothes with elastic be washed?

                                                                                                  Use a mild detergent and cool water, and avoid heat and bleach so the elastic stays soft and stretchy.

                                                                                                    Organic Elastic: What Makes Elastic Truly Organic?

                                                                                                    Organic cotton, certified latex and low-impact dyes: explore what organic elastic really means and how to spot genuine products.

                                                                                                    By SNEH Editorial•16 November 2026•6 min read•1,303 words

                                                                                                    In this article

                                                                                                    1. What does organic mean in textiles?
                                                                                                    2. The ingredients of elastic
                                                                                                    3. Organic cotton as the main fabric
                                                                                                    4. The elastic core: natural rubber and organic latex
                                                                                                    5. What about spandex?
                                                                                                    6. Certification standards to know
                                                                                                    7. Dyes and finishing in organic elastic
                                                                                                    8. Benefits of organic elastic
                                                                                                    9. Limitations and honest caveats
                                                                                                    10. How to spot greenwashing
                                                                                                    11. Questions to ask your supplier
                                                                                                    12. Care of organic elastic
                                                                                                    13. The future of organic elastic
                                                                                                    14. Final thoughts

                                                                                                    Organic has become one of the most popular words in modern shopping, from food to cosmetics to clothing. It is now arriving in the world of elastic, and buyers are asking whether organic elastic really exists and what the word means. The truth is nuanced. Elastic is a composite product made from several materials, so its organic status depends on each ingredient and on how it is processed. This article explains what organic elastic can mean, how it is certified and how to judge claims carefully.

                                                                                                    What does organic mean in textiles?

                                                                                                    In agriculture, organic farming avoids synthetic pesticides, synthetic fertilisers and genetically modified seeds, and it emphasises soil health and biodiversity. In textiles, the word usually applies to fibres grown organically, such as organic cotton, but it can also extend to processing, dyeing and working conditions when an overall standard is used.

                                                                                                    For a product to be truly organic, its organic status should be verified by an independent certification body, not just claimed in advertising. Without certification, the word organic can be misleading.

                                                                                                    The ingredients of elastic

                                                                                                    A typical elastic has three kinds of components.

                                                                                                    1. The elastic core. Natural rubber, synthetic rubber or spandex.
                                                                                                    2. The covering or body yarn. Cotton, polyester, nylon or a blend.
                                                                                                    3. Dyes, finishes and auxiliaries. Colourants, softeners, spinning oils and other processing chemicals.

                                                                                                    Organic elastic tries to improve the sustainability and safety of as many of these components as possible.

                                                                                                    Organic cotton as the main fabric

                                                                                                    The most common organic ingredient in elastic is organic cotton yarn. It is grown without synthetic pesticides and fertilisers, and it is often processed under standards that limit harmful chemicals. Elastic with an organic cotton cover is popular for baby clothing, underwear and products that touch skin for long periods.

                                                                                                    Cotton is soft, breathable and absorbent, so it is a natural fit for comfort-focused elastic bands. The elastic core, however, remains a challenge, because it must be made of materials that provide stretch.

                                                                                                    The elastic core: natural rubber and organic latex

                                                                                                    Natural rubber comes from the rubber tree, so in principle it can be grown according to organic principles. Some plantations hold organic certification for latex, and there are specific standards for organic latex products. When natural rubber thread comes from such certified sources, it can serve as an organic core.

                                                                                                    An important point is that organic does not mean hypoallergenic. Natural rubber latex, organic or not, contains proteins that can cause allergic reactions in sensitised people. Anyone with a latex allergy should avoid natural rubber elastic regardless of its organic status.

                                                                                                    What about spandex?

                                                                                                    Spandex is a synthetic polymer made from petrochemical raw materials, so it cannot be organic in the agricultural sense. Many organic textile standards allow a limited percentage of synthetic fibres, including elastane, in certified products, because stretch is essential for some garments. The permitted percentage differs by standard and product type, so it is best to check the current rules of the standard in question.

                                                                                                    This means an elastic can be partly organic. For example, it may have organic cotton covering with a small elastane core, and the product may still meet an organic textile standard if the synthetic share is within permitted limits.

                                                                                                    Certification standards to know

                                                                                                    Several well-known standards apply to organic textiles.

                                                                                                    • Global Organic Textile Standard (GOTS). One of the best-known standards, covering the entire supply chain from fibre to finished product, including environmental and social criteria. It sets rules for the minimum percentage of organic fibres, restricts hazardous chemicals and requires wastewater treatment in processing.
                                                                                                    • Organic Content Standard (OCS). Verifies the amount of organic material in a product, but does not cover processing chemicals or social aspects in the same way.
                                                                                                    • OEKO-TEX labels. Some labels test finished products for harmful substances. They are not organic certifications but are often used together with organic claims to show product safety.
                                                                                                    • Standards for organic latex. Certain schemes specifically address organic latex raw material and processing.

                                                                                                    When a supplier claims organic elastic, ask which standard applies, which parts of the product are certified and request a copy of the certificate. Check the certificate's scope and validity.

                                                                                                    Dyes and finishing in organic elastic

                                                                                                    Colour is a large environmental factor. Organic standards typically restrict harmful dyes and chemicals, including certain azo dyes, heavy metals and formaldehyde. They may require lower-impact dyeing processes with wastewater treatment. Some manufacturers use natural dyes derived from plants, though these can be more difficult to control and often have lower colour fastness. Many certified organic elastics use low-impact synthetic dyes that meet strict safety requirements.

                                                                                                    Finishes such as softeners and spinning oils should also be selected carefully to avoid substances of concern.

                                                                                                    Benefits of organic elastic

                                                                                                    • Reduced chemical exposure for farmers, workers and consumers.
                                                                                                    • Better soil and water health from organic farming practices.
                                                                                                    • Comfort for skin from soft natural covering yarns and restricted chemicals.
                                                                                                    • Transparency through certification and supply chain traceability.
                                                                                                    • Market appeal for brands serving eco-conscious customers, especially in baby and childrenswear.

                                                                                                    Limitations and honest caveats

                                                                                                    It is important to be realistic. Organic elastic may cost more because certified materials are more expensive and processes are more controlled. Availability may be limited in some colours and widths. Performance may differ slightly from conventional elastics, particularly if natural dyes or certain organic cottons are used. Also, the stretch core may not be fully organic, so the product may be labelled as made with organic material rather than fully organic.

                                                                                                    Another caveat is that organic is not the same as sustainable in every respect. A product can be organic yet still travel long distances, use significant energy or be disposed of poorly. A genuine sustainability approach considers the full life cycle.

                                                                                                    How to spot greenwashing

                                                                                                    Greenwashing is when companies exaggerate or invent environmental claims. Be cautious if you see the following.

                                                                                                    • The word organic with no certification or explanation.
                                                                                                    • Vague phrases such as eco-friendly, natural or green with no evidence.
                                                                                                    • Certificates that do not match the supplier's name or product.
                                                                                                    • Claims that the entire elastic is organic when it contains spandex.
                                                                                                    • Prices that look too good to be true.

                                                                                                    Ask for transaction certificates, lot-level documentation and test reports. Reputable suppliers will provide them.

                                                                                                    Questions to ask your supplier

                                                                                                    1. Which standard certifies your organic elastic?
                                                                                                    2. Which components are organic and what is the percentage?
                                                                                                    3. What is the elastic core made from?
                                                                                                    4. Which dyes and finishes are used and are they restricted-substance compliant?
                                                                                                    5. Can you provide valid certificates and test reports?
                                                                                                    6. How do you ensure traceability and segregation from non-organic material?
                                                                                                    7. Is the elastic suitable for people with latex allergy?

                                                                                                    Care of organic elastic

                                                                                                    Organic elastic benefits from the same gentle care as other elastics: wash in cool water with mild detergent, avoid bleach, dry away from strong heat and sunlight, and store in a cool, dry place. Good care prolongs life, and a long life is itself an environmental benefit.

                                                                                                    The future of organic elastic

                                                                                                    Research is exploring bio-based spandex made partly from plant sources, recycled elastane, and natural rubber with improved traceability. Brands and consumers are also pushing for circular design, where garments can be repaired, reused and recycled. Over time, organic elastics will probably become more common and more varied.

                                                                                                    Final thoughts

                                                                                                    Organic elastic is real, but it is a layered concept. It usually means organic cotton covering, responsibly processed rubber or a limited amount of synthetic stretch material, and safe dyes and finishes, all verified by credible certification. By asking good questions and checking documentation, buyers can separate genuine organic products from marketing noise. Choosing organic elastic is one way to make everyday products kinder to people and the planet, one waistband at a time.

                                                                                                    Frequently asked questions

                                                                                                    What makes elastic organic?

                                                                                                    Organic elastic uses certified organic fibres, such as organic cotton, and natural rubber sourced and processed under recognised standards.

                                                                                                    Is organic elastic fully natural?

                                                                                                    Not always. It depends on the standard and the blend, and some products still include small amounts of synthetic parts.

                                                                                                    Which certifications matter?

                                                                                                    GOTS and similar standards verify fibres, processing and chemical use, so ask for the certificate.

                                                                                                    Is organic elastic more expensive?

                                                                                                    It often costs more because of certified inputs, but many buyers value the lower chemical use and traceability.

                                                                                                      Overlock and Coverstitch Threads for Knit Garments: Choosing the Right Thread

                                                                                                      Learn how overlock and coverstitch seams work on knits, which threads suit needles and loopers, and how to fix skipped stitches, popped seams and uneven tension.

                                                                                                      By SNEH Editorial•16 November 2026•6 min read•1,262 words

                                                                                                      In this article

                                                                                                      1. Why knits need special stitches
                                                                                                      2. What an overlock stitch does
                                                                                                      3. What a coverstitch does
                                                                                                      4. Which thread goes where
                                                                                                      5. Understanding thread types
                                                                                                      6. Choosing thread thickness
                                                                                                      7. Setting tension and stitch length
                                                                                                      8. Troubleshooting common problems
                                                                                                      9. Thread quality and storage
                                                                                                      10. Final thoughts

                                                                                                      Knit garments such as T-shirts, leggings, underwear and sportswear stretch every time they are worn. The seams must stretch with them. If the seam is stiffer than the fabric, it will pop when the garment is pulled on. For this reason, knit garments are usually sewn with overlock and coverstitch machines, and the choice of thread is just as important as the choice of machine. This guide explains what each stitch does, which threads work best in the needles and the loopers, and how to solve the most common problems.

                                                                                                      Why knits need special stitches

                                                                                                      A woven fabric barely stretches along its threads, so a straight lockstitch seam is usually fine. A knit fabric is made of interlocking loops that open and close as the fabric stretches. A straight stitch cannot open in the same way, so the thread snaps. Overlock and coverstitch seams solve this by building the seam from loops of thread, which can extend and return like the fabric around them.

                                                                                                      What an overlock stitch does

                                                                                                      An overlock machine, often called a serger, trims the fabric edge, joins the layers and wraps thread around the raw edge in one pass. The seam is made by needle threads and looper threads working together.

                                                                                                      • Needle threads form the straight line that holds the seam.
                                                                                                      • Upper and lower looper threads form the loops that wrap around the edge and lock it.

                                                                                                      Common types include three-thread, four-thread and five-thread overlock. Four-thread is popular on knits because it is strong and stretchy, and the stitching is neat. Five-thread safety stitches combine a chain stitch and overlock and are used in some garments where strength matters.

                                                                                                      What a coverstitch does

                                                                                                      A coverstitch machine makes parallel lines of straight stitching on the top of the fabric, with a looper thread forming a loose, stretchy weave on the underside. It is used for hems, necklines, waistbands, sleeve ends and attaching elastic. Because the stitch lines are exposed, appearance matters as well as strength.

                                                                                                      Typical versions use two or three needles, with a looper below. The look, with its neat rows on top and the interlaced loops on the back, is a familiar sign of a professionally made knit garment.

                                                                                                      Which thread goes where

                                                                                                      A single garment can use several threads, and each has a different job.

                                                                                                      Needle threads

                                                                                                      Needle threads are usually fine, strong and smooth. Polyester core-spun or spun polyester threads are common, since they are strong and do not shrink much. Needle threads pass through the fabric and are under a lot of friction, so a smooth, even thread helps prevent breaks and skipped stitches.

                                                                                                      Looper threads

                                                                                                      Looper threads travel a long path and do not pass through fabric, so they can be bulkier. Many makers use textured threads here, such as textured polyester or nylon, because the soft, springy loops cover the edge nicely and add stretch. Texturised thread is also gentler against the skin, which is important for underwear and baby clothes.

                                                                                                      Matching fibre content

                                                                                                      Using the same fibre family as the garment is a good starting point. Polyester threads suit polyester sportswear and most general knit fabrics. Cotton or cotton-covered threads may be chosen for natural, matte looks, though they are less stretchy and weaker than synthetics of similar thickness.

                                                                                                      Understanding thread types

                                                                                                      Spun polyester

                                                                                                      Made by twisting short fibres, this thread has a soft, slightly fuzzy surface. It sews smoothly on most machines and gives a matte finish, and it is a common all-round choice for needle threads.

                                                                                                      Continuous filament polyester

                                                                                                      Made from long, smooth strands, it is strong and slightly shiny. It is useful where strength matters, but its shine may be unwanted on some garments.

                                                                                                      Core-spun thread

                                                                                                      A strong filament core is wrapped in spun fibre, combining strength with a soft surface. Many factories choose it for needle threads in high-speed sewing.

                                                                                                      Textured or bulked threads

                                                                                                      These are filament yarns that have been treated to form soft, springy loops. They give excellent coverage and stretch, making them favoured for looper threads, and for the underside of coverstitch seams.

                                                                                                      Elastic and stretch threads

                                                                                                      Some threads contain elastic fibres or have very high stretch. They are used where an extra stretchy seam is needed, such as swimwear and activewear, but they require careful tension settings and usually only in the looper.

                                                                                                      Choosing thread thickness

                                                                                                      Thread thickness is usually shown by a number, and different suppliers use slightly different systems, so always check the label. In general:

                                                                                                      • Finer thread gives a smoother, flatter seam, which suits lightweight and body-hugging garments.
                                                                                                      • Thicker thread gives a stronger, more visible seam and suits heavy fabrics.
                                                                                                      • Using a thread that is too thick for the needle can cause breakage and uneven stitches.

                                                                                                      Match the needle size and thread thickness. A ballpoint or stretch needle designed for knits should be used so it moves between the loops without cutting the yarn.

                                                                                                      Setting tension and stitch length

                                                                                                      Even the right thread fails with the wrong settings.

                                                                                                      1. Start with the machine's recommended settings, then adjust in small steps.
                                                                                                      2. Test on a scrap of the real fabric, folded in the same layers as the seam.
                                                                                                      3. Check that loops lie flat. If the edge curls or the seam puckers, tension is probably too tight.
                                                                                                      4. Stretch the sample. The seam should open and spring back without snapping or leaving ladders.
                                                                                                      5. Adjust differential feed. Overlock machines have a feed setting to prevent wavy or stretched seams. A little extra feed can stop stretching, while less can stop puckering.

                                                                                                      Troubleshooting common problems

                                                                                                      • Skipped stitches. Often caused by a wrong or blunt needle, poor threading or too thick a thread. Change to a fresh ballpoint needle first.
                                                                                                      • Popped seams. The stitch is too tight or too short, or the thread is too stiff for the fabric. Use a stretchier looper thread and loosen the tension.
                                                                                                      • Wavy hems. The fabric is being stretched while sewing. Reduce the pressure or adjust the feed.
                                                                                                      • Thread breaks. Check for rough guides, old thread, burrs on the needle plate and tension that is too high.
                                                                                                      • Tunnelling on coverstitch. The needle threads are pulling the fabric between the rows. Loosen the needle tension or use a lighter thread.
                                                                                                      • Fuzzy lint build-up. Cheap or poor quality thread sheds lint into the machine. Choose even, clean thread and clean the machine often.

                                                                                                      Thread quality and storage

                                                                                                      Good thread is even in thickness, free of slubs and well wound. Poor thread varies along its length, causing tension problems that no adjustment will cure. Buy from a dependable source, test new lots before bulk use, and store thread away from heat, damp and direct sunlight, which can weaken it.

                                                                                                      For production, it is also wise to keep a record of which thread suits which fabric. When a garment style works well, noting the thread type, size, needle and tension saves time later.

                                                                                                      Final thoughts

                                                                                                      Choosing a thread for knit garments is about balance: strength for the seam, softness for the skin, stretch to move with the fabric and a smooth surface so the machine runs well. In most cases, a smooth polyester needle thread combined with a textured looper thread gives a reliable base. From there, small adjustments to needle, tension and feed will tune the seam to the fabric. Always test on a real sample, stretch it and look at it before starting production. A little testing early prevents a great deal of trouble when the garments reach their wearers.

                                                                                                      Frequently asked questions

                                                                                                      Why can't I use a straight stitch on knit fabric?

                                                                                                      Knit fabric is made of loops that open and close when stretched, and a straight stitch cannot open in the same way so the thread snaps. Overlock and coverstitch seams build the seam from loops that can stretch and return.

                                                                                                      What thread should I use in the needles and the loopers?

                                                                                                      Needle threads are usually fine, strong and smooth, such as polyester core-spun or spun polyester. Looper threads can be bulkier and are often textured polyester or nylon for soft, stretchy coverage.

                                                                                                      How do I fix skipped stitches on my overlocker?

                                                                                                      The usual causes are a wrong or blunt needle, poor threading or a thread that is too thick. Change to a fresh ballpoint needle first.

                                                                                                      What causes popped seams on knit garments?

                                                                                                      The stitch may be too tight or too short, or the thread too stiff for the fabric. Use a stretchier looper thread and loosen the tension.

                                                                                                        Colour Matching Systems for Textiles: Shade Cards, Lab Dips and Digital Standards

                                                                                                        How do buyers and makers agree on exactly the same colour? Learn how shade cards, colour codes, lab dips and digital measurement help match textile and elastic colours.

                                                                                                        By SNEH Editorial•16 November 2026•6 min read•1,223 words

                                                                                                        In this article

                                                                                                        1. Why textile colour is tricky
                                                                                                        2. The language of colour: references
                                                                                                        3. Lab dips: the practical step
                                                                                                        4. Judging colour fairly
                                                                                                        5. Instrument measurement
                                                                                                        6. Setting tolerances
                                                                                                        7. Managing lots in production
                                                                                                        8. Digital tools and their limits
                                                                                                        9. Common mistakes
                                                                                                        10. Final thoughts

                                                                                                        Colour is one of the hardest things to communicate. Two people can look at the same red and describe it differently, and a colour on a phone screen rarely looks the same on fabric. In textiles, where dyes, fibres and finishes all change the final shade, matching colours takes a system. This article explains the tools buyers and manufacturers use, from shade cards and colour codes to lab dips and instrument measurement, and how they fit together in everyday production.

                                                                                                        Why textile colour is tricky

                                                                                                        Several reasons make colour matching harder for textiles than for paper or paint:

                                                                                                        • Different fibres take dye differently. The same dye recipe on cotton, polyester, nylon and elastic produces visibly different shades.
                                                                                                        • Texture and gloss change appearance. A shiny filament looks different from a matte yarn, even when the colour measurement is similar.
                                                                                                        • Light changes colour. A shade can match in daylight and differ under shop lighting, a phenomenon called metamerism.
                                                                                                        • Batch variation. Small changes in water, temperature and timing mean that two dye lots rarely match perfectly.
                                                                                                        • Screens are unreliable. Displays differ in brightness and colour settings, so on-screen colour cannot be trusted for approval.

                                                                                                        The language of colour: references

                                                                                                        To communicate colour, people use references that everyone can see or measure.

                                                                                                        Physical shade cards

                                                                                                        A shade card is a card or book with real samples of dyed material for each colour in a range. Suppliers use them to show their available colours, and buyers use them to choose. Because the samples are real textiles, they show how a colour looks on the material, which is more reliable than a printed swatch.

                                                                                                        Standard colour systems

                                                                                                        Standard colour libraries assign codes to colours, so that a buyer in one country and a factory in another can refer to the same reference. Textile-specific libraries provide colour chips on fabric, with codes that identify each shade. Using a code reduces misunderstanding, although the final result must still be checked on the actual material, since dyes and fibres vary.

                                                                                                        Customer-provided samples

                                                                                                        Often the buyer supplies a swatch of fabric or a sample of the item to be matched. The factory then tries to reproduce that colour on elastic or thread. This is the most direct reference, though the sample must be kept clean, flat and out of strong light.

                                                                                                        Lab dips: the practical step

                                                                                                        A lab dip is a small piece of material dyed in the laboratory to match a target colour. It is the standard first step when a new colour is requested.

                                                                                                        The process usually runs like this:

                                                                                                        1. The buyer supplies the target, such as a fabric swatch or a colour reference.
                                                                                                        2. The dye house formulates a recipe, choosing dyes and quantities based on the target and the fibre.
                                                                                                        3. A small sample is dyed and dried.
                                                                                                        4. The lab dip is compared with the target under agreed lighting.
                                                                                                        5. If it is not close enough, the recipe is adjusted and a new lab dip is made.
                                                                                                        6. Once the buyer approves a lab dip, the approved sample becomes the standard for bulk production.

                                                                                                        Several rounds may be necessary, and time must be allowed for them. Approving a lab dip is a formal step, so the approved sample should be signed, dated and stored by both sides.

                                                                                                        Judging colour fairly

                                                                                                        Even when everyone is careful, judging colour by eye depends on conditions. Good practice includes:

                                                                                                        • Use consistent lighting. A standard light booth with defined daylight and other light sources is ideal. Without one, use natural daylight from a north-facing window, avoiding direct sun.
                                                                                                        • Compare side by side. Place the target and the sample next to each other, flat and in the same direction.
                                                                                                        • Check under more than one light source. Look at daylight, warm indoor light and fluorescent light to detect metamerism.
                                                                                                        • Avoid colourful surroundings. Bright walls and clothes reflect coloured light onto samples.
                                                                                                        • Rest your eyes. Looking at one colour for too long tires the eye, so take breaks and look at a neutral grey.

                                                                                                        Instrument measurement

                                                                                                        Colour measuring instruments, such as spectrophotometers, convert colour into numbers. They measure how much light a surface reflects at each wavelength and compute colour coordinates in a standard system. The difference between the target and the sample is expressed as a single number, often called delta E. A smaller number means a closer match.

                                                                                                        Instrument measurement offers several advantages:

                                                                                                        • it removes personal opinion from first-level decisions;
                                                                                                        • it allows tolerances to be written into purchasing agreements;
                                                                                                        • it tracks consistency between lots;
                                                                                                        • it supports digital recipes, speeding up matching.

                                                                                                        However, numbers do not replace the eye entirely. A sample may pass numerically but look different on the finished product, because of texture, gloss or the way colours interact with neighbouring materials. Most professional systems combine instrument readings with visual approval.

                                                                                                        Setting tolerances

                                                                                                        No two dye lots are identical, so buyers and suppliers agree on how much variation is acceptable. A tolerance may be expressed as a maximum delta E, or as a visual grade against the approved standard. Tolerances should be:

                                                                                                        • written in the order or specification;
                                                                                                        • appropriate to the product, with tighter limits where colours sit side by side in the same garment;
                                                                                                        • tested on actual production lots, not only on lab samples.

                                                                                                        For elastic, which often runs next to fabric, even small differences can be visible, so tolerances are important for visible waistbands and trims.

                                                                                                        Managing lots in production

                                                                                                        Several habits help keep colour consistent in production:

                                                                                                        1. Order enough for a full run. Buying all the elastic for an order from one dye lot avoids shade variation within a garment.
                                                                                                        2. Label every roll with its lot number. This allows tracing and prevents mixing.
                                                                                                        3. Check each lot on arrival. Compare against the approved standard before cutting or sewing.
                                                                                                        4. Keep the standard safe. Store the approved sample in a dark, cool place, since light and humidity can alter it.
                                                                                                        5. Do not mix lots in one garment, unless agreed and tested.
                                                                                                        6. Record results. Notes on lots, approvals and rejections build useful history.

                                                                                                        Digital tools and their limits

                                                                                                        Digital colour tools, from phone apps to design software, help share ideas quickly. They are useful for early design discussions, mood boards and trend planning. But because screens vary, digital colour should be treated as a rough guide. The approval step must always be made on a physical sample or an instrument measurement.

                                                                                                        Common mistakes

                                                                                                        • Approving colour from a photo or a screen.
                                                                                                        • Skipping the lab dip to save time, then facing a mismatch in bulk.
                                                                                                        • Judging under poor or mixed lighting.
                                                                                                        • Mixing dye lots inside one product.
                                                                                                        • Forgetting that different fibres in the same garment may need separate matching.
                                                                                                        • Failing to write down tolerances, leaving disagreements to opinion.

                                                                                                        Final thoughts

                                                                                                        Matching textile colour is a team effort between buyer and maker. Real samples, standard references, lab dips, controlled lighting and, where possible, instrument measurement all play a role. No single tool is enough on its own. By agreeing on references, approving physical samples, setting tolerances and keeping control of dye lots, brands and factories can deliver colours that look the same where it matters: on the finished product in the customer's hands.

                                                                                                        Frequently asked questions

                                                                                                        What is a lab dip?

                                                                                                        A small piece of material dyed in the laboratory to match a target colour, which the buyer approves before bulk dyeing.

                                                                                                        Why can't I approve colour from a screen?

                                                                                                        Screens differ in brightness and colour settings, so on-screen colour rarely matches the real textile.

                                                                                                        What is metamerism?

                                                                                                        It is when two colours match under one light source but look different under another, so samples should be checked under more than one light.

                                                                                                        How do I keep colour consistent across production?

                                                                                                        Order enough from one dye lot, label rolls by lot, check each lot against the approved standard and agree written tolerances.
