                                                                                                                                  Spandex Denier and Draft Explained: Understanding the Numbers on a Spandex Yarn

                                                                                                                                  What do 20D, 40D and 70D mean on a spandex yarn, and what is draft? Learn how thickness and stretch settings change the fabric you make.

                                                                                                                                  By SNEH Editorial•16 November 2026•6 min read•1,190 words

                                                                                                                                  In this article

                                                                                                                                  1. What is denier?
                                                                                                                                  2. Denier compared with tex and decitex
                                                                                                                                  3. Why denier matters for spandex
                                                                                                                                  4. What is draft?
                                                                                                                                  5. Typical draft ranges
                                                                                                                                  6. How denier and draft work together
                                                                                                                                  7. Fabric stretch and recovery
                                                                                                                                  8. Core spun and covered spandex
                                                                                                                                  9. Choosing spandex denier for a project
                                                                                                                                  10. Common problems
                                                                                                                                  11. Final thoughts

                                                                                                                                  If you have ever looked at a spandex yarn specification, you will have met strange numbers and abbreviations: 20D, 40D, 70D, draft ratio, elongation and more. These figures decide how a stretch fabric feels, how much it stretches and how well it recovers. They are the language that yarn buyers, knitters and weavers use every day. This article translates the most important numbers into plain words, starting with denier and moving on to draft.

                                                                                                                                  What is denier?

                                                                                                                                  Denier is a unit that describes the thickness of a yarn or fibre. One denier is the weight in grams of nine thousand metres of that yarn. A yarn that weighs twenty grams for nine thousand metres is a twenty denier yarn, written 20D. The higher the number, the thicker and heavier the yarn.

                                                                                                                                  For spandex, common deniers are:

                                                                                                                                  • 10D to 20D for very fine, light products such as sheer hosiery and delicate lingerie;
                                                                                                                                  • 30D to 40D for general knitwear, socks and lightweight stretch fabrics;
                                                                                                                                  • 70D to 140D for swimwear, activewear and shapewear, where stronger support is needed;
                                                                                                                                  • 210D and above for heavy-duty uses such as thick supports, narrow elastic bands and industrial products.

                                                                                                                                  Because denier measures weight per length, it says nothing about colour, softness or how stretchy the yarn is. It simply tells you how thick it is.

                                                                                                                                  Denier compared with tex and decitex

                                                                                                                                  Different regions and industries use different units. Tex is the weight in grams of one thousand metres. Decitex, written dtex, is the weight in grams of ten thousand metres. As a rule of thumb, one denier is about 1.11 decitex, so 40 denier is close to 44 dtex. You will see both in the market, so it is useful to be able to convert between them.

                                                                                                                                  Why denier matters for spandex

                                                                                                                                  The denier of spandex affects several properties of fabric:

                                                                                                                                  1. Holding power. A thicker spandex yarn holds more tension, so fabrics made with it feel firmer and give stronger compression.
                                                                                                                                  2. Fabric weight and feel. Heavy spandex adds weight. Fine yarns keep the fabric light and soft.
                                                                                                                                  3. Transparency. Fine yarns allow sheer fabrics. Thick yarns make denser fabrics.
                                                                                                                                  4. Cost. Thicker yarn uses more material, so it costs more per metre.
                                                                                                                                  5. Appearance. A coarse spandex inside a fine fabric may show through or create ridges.

                                                                                                                                  Designers choose a denier that balances support and comfort. A sports legging needs more holding power than a light summer top, so it will use a thicker spandex yarn or a higher percentage.

                                                                                                                                  What is draft?

                                                                                                                                  Draft is a term from the knitting and weaving world. It describes how much a spandex yarn is stretched while it is being fed into the machine and combined with another yarn. When the tension is released, the spandex springs back, and the fabric shrinks and gathers into a stretch structure.

                                                                                                                                  Draft is usually written as a ratio or a multiple. If a spandex yarn is stretched to three times its relaxed length while it is knitted in, the draft is three times, or 3.0. A higher draft means more stretch is built into the knitted loop and the finished fabric will have higher power, but also more risk of the yarn breaking or becoming too tight.

                                                                                                                                  Typical draft ranges

                                                                                                                                  Draft values depend on the machine, the fabric and the end use. As a rough picture:

                                                                                                                                  • Low draft, around two to three times, creates fabrics with gentle stretch and soft handle.
                                                                                                                                  • Medium draft, around three to four times, is common in general knitwear and many activewear fabrics.
                                                                                                                                  • High draft, above four times, gives high compression and strong recovery, but needs well-controlled equipment and quality yarn.

                                                                                                                                  Manufacturers often adjust draft to get a specific fabric weight and stretch. A small change can alter the feel noticeably.

                                                                                                                                  How denier and draft work together

                                                                                                                                  Denier and draft are partners. Imagine two fabrics that both use 40D spandex. In one, the spandex is knitted at a low draft, and in the other at a high draft. The second fabric will have more built-in tension and a tighter, more compressive feel, although the yarn thickness is the same. Likewise, a thick spandex at a low draft can give about the same holding power as a thinner spandex at a high draft.

                                                                                                                                  This is why fabric specifications always list the spandex denier, the draft, the base yarn and the knitting structure. Changing any one of them affects the others.

                                                                                                                                  Fabric stretch and recovery

                                                                                                                                  Two practical outcomes matter to the user of the fabric: how far it stretches and how well it returns.

                                                                                                                                  Stretch is how much the fabric can extend, measured as a percentage. Fabrics may have two-way stretch, in one direction only, or four-way stretch, in both width and length.

                                                                                                                                  Recovery is how well the fabric returns to its original dimensions. Good draft control and quality yarn help the fabric to bounce back instead of becoming baggy at knees and elbows.

                                                                                                                                  A well-balanced fabric has enough stretch for comfort and movement, with firm recovery so that clothes keep their shape.

                                                                                                                                  Core spun and covered spandex

                                                                                                                                  Spandex is rarely used bare in clothing. It is usually combined with other fibres in one of several ways:

                                                                                                                                  • Bare spandex plating, where bare spandex is knitted together with another yarn;
                                                                                                                                  • Covered spandex, where a spandex core is wrapped with nylon or polyester yarn;
                                                                                                                                  • Core-spun yarn, where staple fibres such as cotton are spun around a spandex core, making a soft yarn for denim and shirts.

                                                                                                                                  In covered and core-spun yarns, the spandex is already stretched at a certain draft during production. This affects the elasticity of the final yarn and, in turn, the fabric.

                                                                                                                                  Choosing spandex denier for a project

                                                                                                                                  Here is a simple guide, though real choices depend on machine and design:

                                                                                                                                  1. Sheer hosiery or fine knit tops: 10D to 20D.
                                                                                                                                  2. T-shirts, socks and light jersey: 20D to 40D.
                                                                                                                                  3. Leggings, activewear and swimwear: 40D to 70D, sometimes more for firm support.
                                                                                                                                  4. Shapewear and compression garments: 70D to 140D or higher.
                                                                                                                                  5. Narrow elastic tapes and industrial products: heavier deniers according to the load.

                                                                                                                                  Always test a sample. Machines, base yarns and finishing all influence the result.

                                                                                                                                  Common problems

                                                                                                                                  When denier or draft is wrong, you may see:

                                                                                                                                  • Baggy fabric from low draft or poor-quality spandex;
                                                                                                                                  • Tight, harsh fabric from high draft or heavy denier;
                                                                                                                                  • Streaks and barre, which are uneven stripes caused by variations in draft or yarn;
                                                                                                                                  • Spandex breaks, leading to holes or ladders in the fabric;
                                                                                                                                  • Shrinkage after washing if the fabric was not properly relaxed and heat-set.

                                                                                                                                  A good manufacturer monitors tension, checks yarn quality and tests the finished fabric.

                                                                                                                                  Final thoughts

                                                                                                                                  Denier tells you how thick a spandex yarn is, and draft tells you how much tension it carries when knitted in. Together with the base yarn and the fabric structure, they decide how a stretch fabric feels, performs and ages. Once you can read these numbers, specifications stop looking like a secret code and become a practical tool for choosing the right fabric for each product.

                                                                                                                                  Frequently asked questions

                                                                                                                                  What does denier mean?

                                                                                                                                  Denier is the weight in grams of 9,000 metres of yarn, so a higher number means a thicker yarn.

                                                                                                                                  What is draft in spandex?

                                                                                                                                  Draft is how much the spandex is stretched when it is combined with another yarn or fabric.

                                                                                                                                  How does draft affect fabric?

                                                                                                                                  Higher draft gives tighter, more compressive fabric, while lower draft gives a looser, softer feel.

                                                                                                                                  How do I choose the denier for my fabric?

                                                                                                                                  Use finer denier for light, sheer fabrics and heavier denier for firm, high-support garments, then test.

                                                                                                                                    Washing, Drying and Ironing Spandex Fabric: A Complete Care Guide

                                                                                                                                    Heat, harsh chemicals and rough handling shorten the life of stretch fabric. This guide shows how to wash, dry, iron and store spandex garments so they keep their shape.

                                                                                                                                    By SNEH Editorial•16 November 2026•6 min read•1,267 words

                                                                                                                                    In this article

                                                                                                                                    1. Why spandex needs special care
                                                                                                                                    2. Washing spandex the right way
                                                                                                                                    3. What to avoid in the wash
                                                                                                                                    4. Drying without damage
                                                                                                                                    5. Ironing and steaming spandex
                                                                                                                                    6. Special cases: swimwear, activewear and shapewear
                                                                                                                                    7. Storing stretch garments
                                                                                                                                    8. Signs your spandex garment is wearing out
                                                                                                                                    9. Final thoughts

                                                                                                                                    Spandex, also sold under brand names such as Lycra and elastane, gives leggings, swimwear, activewear and underwear their stretch and recovery. The fibre is strong and flexible, but it is also sensitive. Heat, strong chemicals and rough handling can slowly damage it, and the result is a garment that bags at the knees, loses its snap or turns thin and shiny. The good news is that a few simple habits keep stretch fabrics comfortable for much longer. This guide covers washing, drying, ironing and storing spandex garments.

                                                                                                                                    Why spandex needs special care

                                                                                                                                    Spandex fibre is a polymer that stretches several times its length and returns. In most garments it is blended with other fibres such as cotton, polyester or nylon, often making up only a small share of the fabric. Even so, it controls the fit.

                                                                                                                                    The fibre is vulnerable to a few things:

                                                                                                                                    • High heat, which can weaken the fibre and change the way it recovers.
                                                                                                                                    • Chlorine bleach and strong oxidising chemicals, which can break down the polymer.
                                                                                                                                    • Friction and snagging, which wear the surface and can cut the fine elastic filaments.
                                                                                                                                    • Long exposure to sunlight, body oils and some lotions, which speed up ageing.

                                                                                                                                    Always read the care label first. It reflects the whole fabric, including the other fibres, and it is the best starting point. The tips below are general guidance and should not replace the label.

                                                                                                                                    Washing spandex the right way

                                                                                                                                    How you wash matters more than how often you wash, though sweaty activewear should not be left damp for long.

                                                                                                                                    1. Turn garments inside out. This protects the outer surface and helps wash away sweat and oils from the skin side.
                                                                                                                                    2. Use cool or lukewarm water. Cold to about thirty degrees Celsius is a common recommendation. Hot water is harsher on elastic fibres.
                                                                                                                                    3. Choose a gentle detergent. A mild liquid detergent rinses out more easily than strong powders and is kinder to the fibre.
                                                                                                                                    4. Use a gentle cycle, or wash by hand for delicate pieces such as lingerie and swimwear.
                                                                                                                                    5. Close zips, hooks and hook-and-loop fastenings so they do not snag the fabric.
                                                                                                                                    6. Use a mesh laundry bag for small or delicate items.
                                                                                                                                    7. Do not overload the machine. Crowded washing increases friction.

                                                                                                                                    Hand washing

                                                                                                                                    For special pieces, fill a basin with cool water, add a small amount of mild detergent, and gently press the garment under the water for a few minutes. Rinse thoroughly in clean cool water. Avoid wringing or twisting, because this stretches the fibres unevenly.

                                                                                                                                    What to avoid in the wash

                                                                                                                                    Some products that are common in laundry can harm stretch fabric.

                                                                                                                                    • Chlorine bleach is best avoided on spandex blends. If whitening is needed, check the label for any permitted alternative.
                                                                                                                                    • Fabric softener can coat the fibres. In sportswear it may reduce moisture-wicking and trap odour. In many stretch fabrics it is best left out.
                                                                                                                                    • Very hot water and hot soaking.
                                                                                                                                    • Washing with rough items such as jeans, towels or items with zips, which cause pilling and snags.

                                                                                                                                    If garments smell even after washing, a rinse with a small amount of white vinegar in cool water is sometimes used, but check that it is suitable for the fabric colours and finishes first.

                                                                                                                                    Drying without damage

                                                                                                                                    Drying is where many stretch garments are quietly ruined.

                                                                                                                                    • Air drying is the safest option. Lay the garment flat on a clean towel or hang it on a rack away from direct sun.
                                                                                                                                    • Avoid hot tumble drying. High heat is one of the main causes of lost stretch, curling edges and a rough feel. If you must use a dryer, choose the lowest heat or an air-only setting and remove the garment while still slightly damp.
                                                                                                                                    • Do not hang heavy wet pieces by narrow straps. Wet fabric is heavy and the weight can stretch the straps or waistband. Lay them flat instead.
                                                                                                                                    • Keep away from radiators, heaters and strong sunlight. Direct heat and ultraviolet light can age the fibres and fade colours.
                                                                                                                                    • Press out water gently. Roll the garment in a towel and press instead of twisting it.

                                                                                                                                    Most stretch garments dry quickly because of their thin construction, so patience is usually not a big cost.

                                                                                                                                    Ironing and steaming spandex

                                                                                                                                    Many stretch garments do not need ironing at all. They are designed to hang smoothly, and wrinkles often fall out once the garment is worn. If you must press one:

                                                                                                                                    1. Check the label. If it says do not iron, follow it.
                                                                                                                                    2. Use the lowest heat setting. Synthetic or delicate settings are typical.
                                                                                                                                    3. Turn the garment inside out or place a thin pressing cloth between the iron and the fabric.
                                                                                                                                    4. Keep the iron moving. Do not leave it resting on the fabric.
                                                                                                                                    5. Avoid steam directly on delicate or printed areas unless the label allows it.

                                                                                                                                    A handheld steamer used at a short distance is often gentler than a hot iron, but it should still be used with caution. Never iron over prints, glitter, rubberised logos or heat-transfer designs, since these can melt or stick.

                                                                                                                                    Special cases: swimwear, activewear and shapewear

                                                                                                                                    Different garments face different challenges.

                                                                                                                                    • Swimwear meets chlorine, salt and sun. Rinse it in cool fresh water soon after use, wash it gently and dry it flat in the shade. Avoid sitting on rough surfaces and avoid long soaks in hot tubs, since heat and chemicals together are tough on elastic.
                                                                                                                                    • Activewear collects sweat and body oil. Wash it soon after exercise and avoid leaving damp items in a gym bag.
                                                                                                                                    • Shapewear and compression garments depend on strong recovery. Gentle hand washing and flat drying help them keep their support. Rotating between several garments gives the fibres time to recover between wears.
                                                                                                                                    • Baby and children's wear with elastic parts should be washed with mild detergent and checked regularly for loose or overstretched elastic.

                                                                                                                                    Storing stretch garments

                                                                                                                                    Good storage prevents damage you do not see until the next wear.

                                                                                                                                    • Fold instead of hanging for heavy or stretchy garments, since hanging can stretch shoulders and straps.
                                                                                                                                    • Store clean and fully dry items only. Trapped moisture can cause odour and mildew.
                                                                                                                                    • Keep away from heat and direct light.
                                                                                                                                    • Avoid sharp hooks and rough surfaces that can snag fine fabric.
                                                                                                                                    • Do not overstretch garments when putting them on. Ease them over the body and avoid pulling with long nails or rings.

                                                                                                                                    Signs your spandex garment is wearing out

                                                                                                                                    Even with good care, elastic fibres age. Watch for these warning signs:

                                                                                                                                    • the waistband no longer holds firmly;
                                                                                                                                    • the fabric stays baggy after wearing;
                                                                                                                                    • thin, shiny or see-through patches appear;
                                                                                                                                    • fibres snap and the edges curl or roll;
                                                                                                                                    • the garment feels stiff, rough or sticky.

                                                                                                                                    When these signs appear, a garment may still be fine for lounging or as a base layer, but it will no longer give the support it was made for. If the issue shows very early, check the care label, since the wrong washing method may be to blame.

                                                                                                                                    Final thoughts

                                                                                                                                    Caring for spandex is mostly about avoiding extremes: not too hot, not too harsh and not too rough. Wash gently in cool water, skip bleach and softener, dry flat away from heat, press only when necessary and store garments clean and dry. These small habits take little time and can noticeably extend the life of leggings, swimwear and activewear, which saves money and reduces waste. Always let the care label on your own garment have the last word.

                                                                                                                                    Frequently asked questions

                                                                                                                                    What temperature should I wash spandex fabric at?

                                                                                                                                    Follow the care label, but a cool or warm gentle wash is generally safest because heat weakens the stretch fibres.

                                                                                                                                    Can I tumble dry spandex garments?

                                                                                                                                    High heat damages spandex, so air drying or a low heat setting is better.

                                                                                                                                    Is it safe to iron spandex fabric?

                                                                                                                                    Use a low temperature with a pressing cloth if the label allows ironing, and avoid direct high heat.

                                                                                                                                    Why should I avoid fabric softener on stretch clothes?

                                                                                                                                    Softener can coat the fibres and reduce stretch recovery and moisture handling over repeated washes.

                                                                                                                                      How Spandex Fibre Is Produced: Dry Spinning Explained

                                                                                                                                      From liquid polymer to filament: a clear, step-by-step explanation of how spandex is made, with a focus on the dry spinning process.

                                                                                                                                      By SNEH Editorial

                                                                                                                                      Spandex in Denim: How Stretch Jeans Are Made and Cared For

                                                                                                                                      Discover how a little spandex turns rigid denim into comfortable stretch jeans, the types of stretch yarn used, fit tips, and care steps that keep jeans shapely.

                                                                                                                                      By SNEH Editorial•16 November 2026•6 min read•1,220 words

                                                                                                                                      In this article

                                                                                                                                      1. What spandex adds to denim
                                                                                                                                      2. How stretch denim is made
                                                                                                                                      3. From yarn to jeans
                                                                                                                                      4. Understanding stretch and recovery
                                                                                                                                      5. Choosing stretch jeans for fit
                                                                                                                                      6. Caring for stretch jeans
                                                                                                                                      7. Common problems and how to handle them
                                                                                                                                      8. Sustainability and repair
                                                                                                                                      9. Final thoughts

                                                                                                                                      Traditional denim is a tough, rigid cotton twill. It was built for work, and it took weeks of wear to soften and shape itself to the body. Stretch jeans changed that. By adding a small amount of spandex, makers produce denim that moves with the wearer, sits comfortably from the first day and keeps close-fitting shapes. This guide explains how spandex is used in denim, what the different constructions mean, and how to care for stretch jeans so that they last.

                                                                                                                                      What spandex adds to denim

                                                                                                                                      Spandex, also known by the brand-neutral name elastane, is a synthetic fibre that can stretch many times its length and then spring back. In denim it is used in small proportions. Most stretch denim contains only a few percent spandex, with the rest being cotton and sometimes polyester or other fibres. Even this small share changes the fabric noticeably.

                                                                                                                                      The benefits include:

                                                                                                                                      • Comfort. The fabric gives when the wearer sits, bends or climbs stairs.
                                                                                                                                      • Shape retention. Knees and seat are less likely to bag out, since the fabric recovers.
                                                                                                                                      • Closer fits. Skinny and slim styles are only practical because the fabric can stretch around the body.
                                                                                                                                      • Wider size range. Stretch makes a pair of jeans forgiving across slightly different body shapes.

                                                                                                                                      How stretch denim is made

                                                                                                                                      Spandex filament is very fine and rarely appears on its own in a fabric. It is usually covered by or combined with cotton so that the yarn looks and feels like ordinary denim yarn.

                                                                                                                                      Core spun yarn

                                                                                                                                      The most common route is core spun yarn. A spandex filament forms the core, and cotton fibres are spun around it. The result looks and feels like a cotton yarn, but with a stretchy heart. This yarn is typically used in the weft, which runs across the width of the fabric, giving stretch around the body.

                                                                                                                                      Weft stretch and bi-stretch

                                                                                                                                      Most stretch denim has stretch in the weft only. This is called weft stretch or comfort stretch. Fabrics that stretch in both directions are described as bi-stretch, and they are used where very high flexibility is needed, such as in some women's and sportswear-inspired styles. Warp stretch needs more careful weaving, since warp yarns are under high tension on the loom.

                                                                                                                                      Dual core and other yarns

                                                                                                                                      Some yarns combine spandex with other stretch or textured fibres to adjust how the fabric feels and recovers. Different makers use different yarn designs to balance stretch, strength and a natural denim look.

                                                                                                                                      From yarn to jeans

                                                                                                                                      After the yarn is made, stretch denim follows the usual denim path with extra care.

                                                                                                                                      1. Dyeing. Warp yarns are traditionally dyed with indigo in rope or sheet dyeing, while weft yarns are often left undyed or dyed separately.
                                                                                                                                      2. Weaving. The dyed warp and the stretch weft are woven into a twill.
                                                                                                                                      3. Finishing. The fabric is washed, set with heat and finished to control shrinkage and to stabilise the stretch.
                                                                                                                                      4. Cutting and sewing. Pattern makers allow for the stretch and recovery of the particular fabric.
                                                                                                                                      5. Garment washing. Jeans are often washed, softened or treated to get a worn look. Gentle treatment is important, since harsh processing can stress the spandex.

                                                                                                                                      Heat setting deserves a special mention. Spandex needs to be set at the right temperature and time. Too little heat leaves the fabric unstable, while too much can damage the filament and reduce its recovery.

                                                                                                                                      Understanding stretch and recovery

                                                                                                                                      Two terms matter when judging stretch denim.

                                                                                                                                      • Stretch is how far the fabric extends under a given pull.
                                                                                                                                      • Recovery is how well it returns to its original size afterwards.

                                                                                                                                      A fabric can stretch easily but recover poorly, and that is the cause of jeans that become baggy at the knees. Good stretch denim balances both, so makers often test growth, which is the amount of permanent lengthening after stretching and resting. High stretch is not always better. For everyday jeans, a moderate stretch with strong recovery usually gives a better, longer-lasting fit than extreme stretch.

                                                                                                                                      Choosing stretch jeans for fit

                                                                                                                                      Buyers can choose well by thinking about how they will use the jeans.

                                                                                                                                      • Rigid or very low stretch gives a classic, structured look and is often preferred for straight and relaxed cuts.
                                                                                                                                      • Comfort stretch suits most people, with enough give for daily movement while keeping the denim feel.
                                                                                                                                      • High stretch or super stretch gives a second skin fit and is popular for skinny and legging-style jeans, though it may relax faster with wear.

                                                                                                                                      Try sitting, bending and squatting in the fitting room. Jeans that feel just snug in the shop may relax slightly with wear, since stretch fabrics often loosen a little. Many people size so the jeans feel close but not tight at first.

                                                                                                                                      Caring for stretch jeans

                                                                                                                                      Care affects how long the spandex lasts. A few simple habits go a long way.

                                                                                                                                      • Wash less often and wash cool. Warm or cool water is gentler than hot. Frequent hot washing shortens the life of spandex.
                                                                                                                                      • Turn jeans inside out. This reduces surface abrasion and helps protect colour.
                                                                                                                                      • Use mild detergent. Avoid chlorine bleach, which can damage spandex and cotton.
                                                                                                                                      • Skip fabric softener when possible. Softener residue can coat fibres, and some advice suggests it may affect stretch performance.
                                                                                                                                      • Avoid high heat drying. Heat is a main enemy of spandex. Air drying, or tumble drying on a low setting, protects recovery.
                                                                                                                                      • Do not iron at very high temperatures. If ironing is needed, use a moderate setting and follow the care label.

                                                                                                                                      Always follow the care label on the particular jeans, since fabrics and finishes differ.

                                                                                                                                      Common problems and how to handle them

                                                                                                                                      Baggy knees and seat. Some bagging is normal after hours of sitting. Often a cool wash and an air dry help the fabric recover. If bagging stays, the stretch may be worn out or the fabric may have been over stretched.

                                                                                                                                      Fading and colour loss. Indigo denim fades naturally. Washing inside out and using cooler water slows it, and some people use colour-catching detergents for dark pairs.

                                                                                                                                      Thin spots on thighs. Friction between thighs wears the fabric. Higher quality fabrics with stronger yarns last longer, and some people mend early with a small patch inside.

                                                                                                                                      Shrinkage. Stretch denim is usually treated to limit shrinkage, but the first few washes may still change fit slightly. Following the label reduces surprises.

                                                                                                                                      Sustainability and repair

                                                                                                                                      Making jeans uses a lot of water, energy and chemicals, so the best environmental choice is often to wear a good pair for as long as possible. Washing less, repairing small tears and choosing well made fabrics all help. Because stretch denim blends cotton with synthetic fibre, recycling is more difficult than for a single fibre fabric, which is another reason to value long life. Research into easier recycling of blended textiles continues.

                                                                                                                                      Final thoughts

                                                                                                                                      Spandex quietly transformed denim. A small share of stretch yarn gives comfort, a closer fit and better shape retention, as long as the fabric is well made, heat set correctly and cared for sensibly. For makers, the key is balancing stretch with recovery and strength. For wearers, cool washes, gentle drying and a little patience are the simple habits that keep stretch jeans looking and feeling right for years.

                                                                                                                                      Frequently asked questions

                                                                                                                                      How much spandex is in stretch jeans?

                                                                                                                                      Most stretch denim contains only a few percent spandex, with the rest cotton and sometimes polyester or other fibres. Even this small share noticeably changes comfort and fit.

                                                                                                                                      What is the difference between weft stretch and bi-stretch denim?

                                                                                                                                      Weft stretch, also called comfort stretch, stretches only across the width of the fabric. Bi-stretch denim stretches in both directions and is used where very high flexibility is needed.

                                                                                                                                      Why do my stretch jeans go baggy at the knees?

                                                                                                                                      The fabric may stretch easily but recover poorly, or the stretch may be worn out or the fabric over stretched. A cool wash and air dry often helps the fabric recover from normal bagging.

                                                                                                                                      How should I wash stretch jeans so the spandex lasts?

                                                                                                                                      Wash less often in cool water, turn them inside out, use mild detergent, avoid chlorine bleach and skip fabric softener where possible. Air dry or tumble dry on low, since heat is the main enemy of spandex.

                                                                                                                                        How Spandex Fibre Is Produced: Dry Spinning Explained

                                                                                                                                        From liquid polymer to filament: a clear, step-by-step explanation of how spandex is made, with a focus on the dry spinning process.

                                                                                                                                        By SNEH Editorial

                                                                                                                                        Spandex in Shapewear and Compression Wear: Fabric, Fit and Care

                                                                                                                                        How spandex makes shapewear and compression garments work, what fabric blends and constructions to look for, how to size them well and how to wash them correctly.

                                                                                                                                        By SNEH Editorial•16 November 2026•6 min read•1,228 words

                                                                                                                                        In this article

                                                                                                                                        1. What spandex actually does
                                                                                                                                        2. How much spandex is in these fabrics
                                                                                                                                        3. Fabric constructions used for shaping and compression
                                                                                                                                        4. Other parts of the garment that depend on stretch
                                                                                                                                        5. Getting the fit right
                                                                                                                                        6. Comfort, breathability and skin feel
                                                                                                                                        7. Washing and care
                                                                                                                                        8. Common problems and what they mean
                                                                                                                                        9. Final thoughts

                                                                                                                                        Shapewear, sports compression tights, support leggings and recovery sleeves all rely on the same quiet hero: spandex. This fine, stretchy fibre can extend several times its own length and then spring back, which is what allows a garment to hold the body firmly yet move with it. But not all shaping or compression garments are alike. The amount of spandex, the way the fabric is knitted and the way the garment is cut decide whether it feels supportive or simply tight. This article explains how these garments work, what to look for when making or buying them, and how to make them last.

                                                                                                                                        What spandex actually does

                                                                                                                                        Spandex, also known by brand names such as Lycra, elastane or elastomeric fibre, is a synthetic fibre made from a long-chain polymer. It is almost never used alone. Instead, a very fine spandex yarn is combined with another fibre such as nylon, polyester or cotton. The partner fibre gives the fabric its surface, feel and strength, while the spandex provides stretch and recovery.

                                                                                                                                        Two qualities matter most.

                                                                                                                                        • Stretch, which lets the garment go on and move with the body.
                                                                                                                                        • Recovery, which is the ability to return to the original size. Good recovery means the garment keeps its shape after wearing and washing.

                                                                                                                                        In shapewear, recovery is what produces the gentle inward pressure. In compression wear, it creates a more graduated, firm hold.

                                                                                                                                        How much spandex is in these fabrics

                                                                                                                                        There is no single correct figure, but in general the firmer the garment, the more spandex it contains. Everyday stretch fabrics may use only a small percentage, while shaping and compression fabrics often use a noticeably higher share. Light control garments sit in the middle, and firm shaping panels often use more.

                                                                                                                                        What matters is not only the percentage but how the spandex is used. A fabric with a moderate amount of spandex in a dense, tight knit can feel firmer than a loose knit with more spandex. This is why you should judge a fabric by testing it, not just reading the label.

                                                                                                                                        Fabric constructions used for shaping and compression

                                                                                                                                        Warp knits and circular knits

                                                                                                                                        Most shaping and compression fabrics are knitted, not woven. Two main families are common.

                                                                                                                                        • Warp knits, which are stable, resist running and are often used for firm panels, power mesh and smooth, flat surfaces.
                                                                                                                                        • Circular and seamless knits, which are made on tubular machines and allow garments with few or no seams, shaped zones and varying tightness in different areas.

                                                                                                                                        Zoned compression

                                                                                                                                        Many modern garments vary the tightness from one part of the body to another. A seamless leg garment, for instance, may be firmer at the ankle and softer at the thigh. This is achieved by changing the stitch density or the amount of spandex in each zone as the garment is knitted.

                                                                                                                                        Power mesh and panels

                                                                                                                                        Power mesh is a lightweight but strong stretch fabric often used in tummy panels and side sections. Layers of different fabrics may be stitched together, with a firmer inner layer and a soft outer layer, so the garment shapes without feeling harsh.

                                                                                                                                        Other parts of the garment that depend on stretch

                                                                                                                                        The main fabric is only part of the story.

                                                                                                                                        • Waistbands and leg bands are often made from knitted or woven elastic, sometimes with silicone grip strips so they do not slide.
                                                                                                                                        • Seams need stretchy stitches and strong, stretchy thread, so they do not snap when the garment is pulled on.
                                                                                                                                        • Hook-and-eye tapes and fastenings must be soft against the skin and strong enough to take repeated stress.
                                                                                                                                        • Bonded or taped edges give a smooth line under clothing, avoiding visible ridges.

                                                                                                                                        Using a good elastic trim and the right thread is as important as choosing the main fabric. The weakest point in a garment is usually the first to fail.

                                                                                                                                        Getting the fit right

                                                                                                                                        Compression and shaping garments should feel firm and supportive, but never painful. Fit is the single biggest factor in comfort.

                                                                                                                                        1. Measure carefully. Use a size chart based on body measurements, such as waist, hips and thighs, not just a usual clothing size.
                                                                                                                                        2. Expect a snug fit. A garment that slides on without any resistance is probably too loose to do its job.
                                                                                                                                        3. Check for numbness, pain or deep marks. These are signs the garment is too tight or the size is wrong. Sizing up or choosing a lighter level is sensible.
                                                                                                                                        4. Look for rolling edges. A band that rolls down or digs in may be too narrow or too tight.
                                                                                                                                        5. Choose the right level for the purpose. A light hold is fine for daily wear, while firmer options are for specific uses such as sports or recovery.

                                                                                                                                        For medical or circulation concerns, a qualified health professional should advise on suitable garments, since they can recommend the correct type and level.

                                                                                                                                        Comfort, breathability and skin feel

                                                                                                                                        A tight garment worn for hours must also feel pleasant.

                                                                                                                                        • Nylon blends are smooth, strong and common in shaping garments.
                                                                                                                                        • Polyester blends are good at moving moisture and are widely used in sports compression.
                                                                                                                                        • Cotton blends feel soft and breathable, though they dry slowly and may stretch out of shape sooner.
                                                                                                                                        • Moisture-wicking finishes and mesh zones help keep the wearer drier.
                                                                                                                                        • Flat seams and tagless labels reduce irritation.

                                                                                                                                        Light colours may show through light clothes, which is why nude shades in several depths are important for inclusive ranges.

                                                                                                                                        Washing and care

                                                                                                                                        Heat, chemicals and rough handling are the enemies of spandex. With good care, a garment can keep its hold for much longer.

                                                                                                                                        • Wash in cool or lukewarm water. Hot water can weaken the fibre and reduce recovery.
                                                                                                                                        • Use mild detergent. Avoid strong bleach, which damages spandex.
                                                                                                                                        • Skip fabric softener. It can coat fibres and reduce moisture movement and grip.
                                                                                                                                        • Use a mesh bag or hand wash. This protects the garment from hooks and agitation.
                                                                                                                                        • Do not wring or twist. Press the water out gently.
                                                                                                                                        • Dry flat or hang in the shade. High dryer heat shortens the life of the elastic.
                                                                                                                                        • Rotate garments. Having more than one lets the fibres rest and recover between wears.

                                                                                                                                        Sun lotions, body oils and perspiration can also degrade spandex over time, so rinse the garment after heavy use.

                                                                                                                                        Common problems and what they mean

                                                                                                                                        • Bagging or loss of shape. The spandex has lost recovery, often from heat, age or chemical damage.
                                                                                                                                        • Rolling at the top. The band is too narrow, too loose or lacks a grip strip.
                                                                                                                                        • Snapped stitches. The thread or stitch type is not stretchy enough for the fabric.
                                                                                                                                        • Pilling or surface wear. Rubbing and rough washing are common causes.
                                                                                                                                        • Yellowing or stiffness. Chlorine, heat or residue from detergent may be the reason.

                                                                                                                                        Final thoughts

                                                                                                                                        Spandex makes modern shapewear and compression wear possible, but the result depends on much more than the fibre itself. The knit structure, the blend, the trims, the stitching and the cut all work together. For makers, careful testing of fabric, elastic and thread on real bodies is worth the time. For wearers, choosing the right size and level, and caring for the garment gently, will keep it comfortable and effective for much longer. Good compression feels like a firm, reassuring hug, never a struggle.

                                                                                                                                        Frequently asked questions

                                                                                                                                        How does spandex make shapewear work?

                                                                                                                                        Spandex gives stretch so the garment goes on and moves with the body, and recovery so it returns to size and produces gentle inward pressure. It is combined with fibres such as nylon, polyester or cotton that provide surface, feel and strength.

                                                                                                                                        How tight should shapewear or compression wear feel?

                                                                                                                                        It should feel firm and supportive but never painful. Numbness, pain or deep marks suggest it is too tight or the wrong size, so size up or choose a lighter level.

                                                                                                                                        How do I wash shapewear so it keeps its hold?

                                                                                                                                        Wash in cool or lukewarm water with mild detergent, avoid bleach and fabric softener, and use a mesh bag or hand wash. Do not wring, and dry flat or hang in the shade.

                                                                                                                                        Why does the top band of my compression garment roll down?

                                                                                                                                        The band may be too narrow, too loose or lack a grip strip. Choosing the right size and a better band design usually fixes it.
