                                                                                                                                          Spandex Recycling and Sustainable Stretch: Where the Industry Is Heading

                                                                                                                                          Spandex makes clothes comfortable but is hard to recycle. Learn why, what the industry is trying, and how makers and buyers can reduce waste today.

                                                                                                                                          By SNEH Editorial•16 November 2026•6 min read•1,180 words

                                                                                                                                          In this article

                                                                                                                                          1. Why spandex is everywhere
                                                                                                                                          2. Why blends are difficult to recycle
                                                                                                                                          3. Approaches being explored
                                                                                                                                          4. What makers can do now
                                                                                                                                          5. What buyers and wearers can do
                                                                                                                                          6. Be careful with green claims
                                                                                                                                          7. The road ahead
                                                                                                                                          8. Final thoughts

                                                                                                                                          Stretch has changed how clothes fit and feel. Leggings, sportswear, socks, underwear and jeans all rely on spandex, also called elastane, to move with the body. Yet the same fibre that makes garments comfortable also makes them difficult to recycle. As the textile industry looks for ways to reduce waste, spandex is at the centre of a practical question: how can we keep the stretch without leaving a problem behind? This article explains why spandex is hard to recycle, what approaches are being explored and what makers and buyers can do now.

                                                                                                                                          Why spandex is everywhere

                                                                                                                                          Spandex is a synthetic fibre known for very high stretch and quick recovery. It is rarely used alone. Instead it is blended in small amounts, often a few percent of the fabric, with cotton, polyester, nylon or other fibres. Even a small share can give fabric comfort, shape retention and freedom of movement.

                                                                                                                                          This small share is also exactly why recycling is hard. A garment that is mostly cotton with a little spandex is not a pure material. It is a mix of two very different fibres twisted together.

                                                                                                                                          Why blends are difficult to recycle

                                                                                                                                          Recycling works best with clean, single-material streams. Blended fabrics create several difficulties.

                                                                                                                                          • Mixed fibres. Cotton, polyester and spandex have different chemistry and melting behaviour, so ordinary mechanical recycling struggles to separate them.
                                                                                                                                          • Elastic damage to machines. In mechanical recycling, fabric is shredded and pulled apart into fibres. Spandex tends to stretch and tangle rather than break cleanly, which can cause problems.
                                                                                                                                          • Shorter, weaker fibres. Mechanical recycling shortens fibres, and elastic content can reduce the quality of the recycled yarn.
                                                                                                                                          • Other additions. Dyes, finishes, prints, zips, buttons and labels add more complexity.
                                                                                                                                          • Collection and sorting. Used clothes are collected in huge, mixed volumes. Sorting by fibre content is slow, and labels are not always accurate or readable.

                                                                                                                                          For these reasons, much stretch clothing ends up in landfill or is incinerated instead of becoming new clothing.

                                                                                                                                          Approaches being explored

                                                                                                                                          Researchers and companies are trying several routes. Some are at commercial scale in certain products, and others remain at development or pilot stage, so it is wise to treat claims with care.

                                                                                                                                          Mechanical recycling

                                                                                                                                          Garments are sorted, shredded and spun again. This works better for fabrics with a very low spandex share, and recycled fibres are often blended with new fibre to keep strength. It is the simplest route but has limits on quality and on how many times a fibre can be recycled.

                                                                                                                                          Chemical recycling

                                                                                                                                          Chemical methods break fibres down into their building blocks or dissolve one fibre so that another can be recovered. For example, some processes aim to dissolve or separate the elastane from polyester or nylon, so that the main fibre can be reused. These methods may handle blends better, but they require energy, solvents and careful handling, and their environmental benefit depends on how they are run and powered.

                                                                                                                                          Recycled input materials

                                                                                                                                          Some elastane producers use recycled raw materials, such as waste from production, as part of the input. This reduces use of fresh raw material, though the finished fibre still needs a plan for the end of its life.

                                                                                                                                          Bio-based spandex

                                                                                                                                          Another direction is making spandex-type polymers partly from plant-based sources instead of fossil raw materials. This may lower reliance on oil, but a bio-based fibre is not automatically recyclable or biodegradable, so the full life cycle still matters.

                                                                                                                                          Mono-material design

                                                                                                                                          A promising idea is to design stretch garments from one type of fibre, for example polyester with a very small share of elastic or a stretchy structure that does not need elastane. A single-material garment is easier to recycle, though it may behave a little differently from traditional blends.

                                                                                                                                          What makers can do now

                                                                                                                                          You do not have to wait for perfect technology to make better choices.

                                                                                                                                          1. Use only as much spandex as needed. Many garments need only a small percentage for comfort. Extra stretch adds cost and recycling difficulty without much benefit.
                                                                                                                                          2. Design for durability. A garment that lasts twice as long halves the waste per wear. Good stitching, strong elastics and colourfast fabrics help.
                                                                                                                                          3. Keep blends simple. Fewer fibre types and fewer trims make later recycling easier.
                                                                                                                                          4. Choose recycled content where it makes sense, and ask suppliers for documentation instead of relying on marketing words.
                                                                                                                                          5. Reduce production waste. Careful pattern layout and use of off-cuts, for example for small accessories, cut waste at the source.
                                                                                                                                          6. Label clearly. Accurate fibre content on labels helps sorters and recyclers.
                                                                                                                                          7. Offer repair and care advice. Replacing worn elastic can extend the life of garments.

                                                                                                                                          What buyers and wearers can do

                                                                                                                                          • Buy fewer, better pieces. Choose garments you expect to wear for years.
                                                                                                                                          • Wash gently. Heat, harsh detergent and tumble drying wear out spandex quickly. Washing in cool or lukewarm water and drying in the open air keeps stretch longer.
                                                                                                                                          • Skip fabric softener on stretch fabrics, since it can coat fibres and reduce performance.
                                                                                                                                          • Repair or reuse. Replace worn elastic, alter fit or turn old garments into cleaning cloths or crafts.
                                                                                                                                          • Donate or resell garments still in good condition.
                                                                                                                                          • Use take-back programmes where available, but check what actually happens to the clothes instead of assuming recycling.

                                                                                                                                          Be careful with green claims

                                                                                                                                          Words like sustainable, eco and recyclable are used loosely. Helpful questions include: what percentage is recycled content, how is it verified, and what happens to the product at the end of its life? Reliable suppliers can answer simply and share certificates or test reports where they exist. Claims that sound too good, with no detail, deserve caution.

                                                                                                                                          It is also worth remembering that the biggest impact of clothing often comes from how many items are made and how long they are worn, not only from the fibre type. Reducing overproduction and extending garment life matter as much as any fibre innovation.

                                                                                                                                          The road ahead

                                                                                                                                          Several trends point to progress. Brands face growing pressure to take responsibility for products at the end of their life, which pushes designers toward recyclable choices. Sorting technology is improving, including methods that identify fibres automatically. Chemical separation of blends is being tested at larger scale. And more designers are exploring stretch built into the structure of the fabric, such as knit design, rather than relying only on elastane.

                                                                                                                                          None of these solutions is complete yet. Most likely the future will combine several approaches: simpler blends, better collection and sorting, a mix of mechanical and chemical recycling and longer-lasting garments.

                                                                                                                                          Final thoughts

                                                                                                                                          Spandex gives clothing comfort and fit that people value, but its thin, tangled presence inside blended fabrics makes recycling hard today. The industry is working on chemical separation, recycled and bio-based inputs and simpler designs, while makers and wearers can already reduce harm by using less elastane, building durable products, washing gently and repairing when possible. Sustainable stretch will come from many small decisions made across the chain, from fibre to finished garment to the care it receives at home.

                                                                                                                                          Frequently asked questions

                                                                                                                                          Why is spandex hard to recycle?

                                                                                                                                          It is usually blended in small amounts with other fibres, and the mixed fabric is hard to separate. Spandex also stretches and tangles in mechanical recycling machines.

                                                                                                                                          Can spandex be recycled chemically?

                                                                                                                                          Some chemical processes aim to separate elastane from other fibres or break fibres into building blocks. Many are still at pilot or early commercial scale, so check claims carefully.

                                                                                                                                          How can makers use spandex more sustainably?

                                                                                                                                          Use only as much as the garment needs, keep blends simple and design for durability. Ask suppliers for documentation of any recycled or bio-based content.

                                                                                                                                          How can I make stretch clothes last longer?

                                                                                                                                          Wash in cool or lukewarm water, avoid fabric softener and tumble drying, and dry in the open air. Replacing worn elastic can also extend garment life.

                                                                                                                                            From liquid polymer to filament: a clear, step-by-step explanation of how spandex is made, with a focus on the dry spinning process.

                                                                                                                                            Spandex in Swimwear: How Chlorine, Sun and Salt Affect Stretch and How to Protect It

                                                                                                                                            Swimwear needs stretch that survives pools and sunshine. Learn why chlorine and UV damage spandex and how fabric choice and care extend swimwear life.

                                                                                                                                            By SNEH Editorial•16 November 2026•6 min read•1,165 words

                                                                                                                                            In this article

                                                                                                                                            1. Why swimwear contains spandex
                                                                                                                                            2. What chlorine does
                                                                                                                                            3. What sunlight does
                                                                                                                                            4. Salt water, sunscreen and body oils
                                                                                                                                            5. Heat and friction
                                                                                                                                            6. How to choose long-lasting swimwear
                                                                                                                                            7. How to care for swimwear
                                                                                                                                            8. Storing swimwear
                                                                                                                                            9. Signs it is time to replace
                                                                                                                                            10. A note on sustainability
                                                                                                                                            11. Final thoughts

                                                                                                                                            A swimsuit has one of the hardest jobs in a wardrobe. It must stretch around the body, stay put in moving water, dry quickly and keep its shape through hot sun, chlorine, salt, sunscreen and sweat. Most swimwear gets its stretch from spandex, and spandex does not like all of those things. Understanding what damages swimwear helps you to choose better fabrics and to look after your swimsuits so that they last more than one season.

                                                                                                                                            Why swimwear contains spandex

                                                                                                                                            Swimwear fabrics are usually a blend of nylon or polyester with a high percentage of spandex, often between fifteen and twenty-five percent or more. Spandex gives the fabric the ability to stretch two or four ways, to hug the body, and to recover its shape. Without it, a swimsuit would sag when wet and restrict movement.

                                                                                                                                            The base fibre also matters:

                                                                                                                                            • Nylon is soft, smooth and has a good feel on the skin, but it can fade and weaken under strong sunlight and some chemicals.
                                                                                                                                            • Polyester resists chlorine and sunlight better and holds colour well, though it can feel a little less soft.
                                                                                                                                            • Special polyester types are made specifically for chlorine resistance and are used in competition and training swimwear.

                                                                                                                                            What chlorine does

                                                                                                                                            Pool water contains chlorine or chlorine compounds to kill germs. These chemicals are oxidising agents. They attack many materials, and spandex is among the more sensitive. Over time, chlorine breaks down the polymer chains in the spandex, which leads to a gradual loss of stretch and recovery. The fabric becomes thinner, saggy and baggy, and the swimsuit can become see-through.

                                                                                                                                            Several things make chlorine damage worse:

                                                                                                                                            • High chlorine concentration. Heavily treated pools and hot tubs are tougher on fabric.
                                                                                                                                            • Heat. Warm water speeds up chemical reactions.
                                                                                                                                            • Long exposure. Wearing a wet swimsuit for hours or leaving it damp after swimming gives chlorine more time to act.
                                                                                                                                            • Repeated use. Damage builds up with every swim.

                                                                                                                                            Fabrics designed for chlorine resistance use special spandex types and polyester bases that resist these chemicals better.

                                                                                                                                            What sunlight does

                                                                                                                                            Ultraviolet light from the sun also degrades fibres. It fades dyes, weakens fibres and makes spandex brittle. Fabrics that spend long hours in strong sun age faster. Nylon is more sensitive to UV than polyester in general, while some modern fabrics include UV protection finishes to protect both the wearer and the fabric. High UPF swimwear is designed to block UV and is commonly used for children and for sun protection.

                                                                                                                                            Salt water, sunscreen and body oils

                                                                                                                                            Sea water is generally gentler on spandex than chlorine, but salt crystals can build up in the fabric and cause stiffness and abrasion as the suit dries. Sunscreens, tanning oils and body lotions contain oils and chemicals that can break down spandex and stain fabric. Sweat and body oils add to the load. This is why swimsuits worn day after day without proper rinsing wear out faster than those that are rinsed and rested.

                                                                                                                                            Heat and friction

                                                                                                                                            Hot water in spas and hot tubs speeds up chemical damage. Rough surfaces such as pool edges, sand, rocks and slides cause abrasion, leading to pilling and thin spots. Washing machines and tumble dryers also introduce heat and friction, which is a common cause of early damage to swimwear.

                                                                                                                                            How to choose long-lasting swimwear

                                                                                                                                            When shopping, look for features that signal durability:

                                                                                                                                            1. Fibre content. Look at the label for polyester-based fabrics if you swim in chlorinated pools often. Some labels mention chlorine-resistant fibres.
                                                                                                                                            2. Spandex quality. A good brand of spandex, whether Lycra or another well-made fibre, usually holds up better.
                                                                                                                                            3. Lining. A well-made lining keeps the swimsuit opaque as the outer fabric ages.
                                                                                                                                            4. Construction. Strong seams, good elastic in the leg openings and straps and neat finishing show careful production.
                                                                                                                                            5. UV protection. If you spend long hours in the sun, UPF-rated fabrics help both skin and fabric.
                                                                                                                                            6. Colour. Dark and strong colours may fade less visibly than pale ones, although this depends on the dye quality.

                                                                                                                                            For frequent swimmers, training swimwear made for chlorine is often a wise investment.

                                                                                                                                            How to care for swimwear

                                                                                                                                            Good care makes a large difference. Follow these habits:

                                                                                                                                            • Rinse straight away. After swimming, rinse the suit in cool, clean fresh water to remove chlorine, salt and sunscreen. Do this as soon as possible and do not leave a wet suit in a bag.
                                                                                                                                            • Wash gently. Hand wash in cool water with a mild detergent made for delicate fabrics, or follow the care label. Avoid bleach, strong detergents and fabric softener, which can coat and damage fibres.
                                                                                                                                            • Do not wring or twist. Squeeze the water out gently, then roll the suit in a towel to remove moisture.
                                                                                                                                            • Dry in the shade. Lay the suit flat or hang it in a shaded, ventilated place. Direct sun and tumble dryers cause damage.
                                                                                                                                            • Rotate your swimsuits. Give each suit a day or two to rest and fully recover between wears. This is one of the simplest ways of extending life.
                                                                                                                                            • Avoid rough surfaces. Sit on a towel instead of rough concrete, and take care with slides and wooden decks.
                                                                                                                                            • Avoid long soaks. Do not sit in a hot tub or leave your suit in the sun while wet for hours.
                                                                                                                                            • Remove it promptly. Do not stay in a wet swimsuit for longer than necessary.

                                                                                                                                            Storing swimwear

                                                                                                                                            Dry swimwear fully before storing. Keep it flat or loosely folded in a cool, dry place, away from sunlight and chemicals. Avoid hanging suits by their straps for long periods, since this can stretch the straps and elastic.

                                                                                                                                            Signs it is time to replace

                                                                                                                                            Even with care, swimwear eventually wears out. Signs include:

                                                                                                                                            1. The fabric looks thin or shiny, or becomes see-through when wet.
                                                                                                                                            2. The suit feels loose and no longer holds its shape.
                                                                                                                                            3. Elastic at the leg and strap edges has gone limp.
                                                                                                                                            4. Fabric has pilled, fuzzed or developed holes.
                                                                                                                                            5. Colours have faded unevenly.

                                                                                                                                            A worn swimsuit may not give the coverage and support you need, so replacing it is sensible.

                                                                                                                                            A note on sustainability

                                                                                                                                            Swimwear made from recycled nylon or polyester is becoming common, often made from fishing nets and plastic waste. These fabrics reduce the use of virgin materials. They are still blends with spandex, so recycling the finished garment remains difficult. Caring for swimwear properly and buying fewer, better pieces is one of the most practical ways to reduce waste.

                                                                                                                                            Final thoughts

                                                                                                                                            Swimwear asks a lot of spandex. Chlorine, sun, heat, salt and oils all slowly break it down, and the damage shows up as loose, thin fabric. Choosing chlorine-resistant, well-made fabrics and giving your swimsuits good care, with fresh water rinsing, gentle washing, shade drying and rest between wears, will keep them fitting and looking good for much longer. A few minutes of care after each swim is a small price for stretch that lasts.

                                                                                                                                            Frequently asked questions

                                                                                                                                            Does chlorine damage spandex?

                                                                                                                                            Yes, repeated exposure weakens spandex, so rinse swimwear in fresh water after each swim.

                                                                                                                                            How should I wash swimwear?

                                                                                                                                            Rinse in cool water, wash gently by hand with mild soap and dry in the shade.

                                                                                                                                            Can sunlight harm swimwear?

                                                                                                                                            Strong UV and heat can fade colours and weaken the stretch fibres, so avoid drying in direct sun.

                                                                                                                                            Why does swimwear lose shape?

                                                                                                                                            Chlorine, heat, sunscreen oils and rough washing all break down the elastic fibres over time.

                                                                                                                                              Spandex vs Lycra: Are They the Same Thing?

                                                                                                                                              Spandex, elastane, Lycra: three names, one family of fibres. Learn what the words actually mean and how to read them on a label.

                                                                                                                                              By SNEH Editorial•16 November 2026•6 min read•1,316 words

                                                                                                                                              In this article

                                                                                                                                              1. The generic name: spandex or elastane
                                                                                                                                              2. The brand name: Lycra
                                                                                                                                              3. Other brand names
                                                                                                                                              4. Are they chemically different?
                                                                                                                                              5. What the label tells you
                                                                                                                                              6. What makes spandex special
                                                                                                                                              7. Spandex compared with natural rubber
                                                                                                                                              8. The role of the blend
                                                                                                                                              9. Common myths
                                                                                                                                              10. How to choose between branded and generic
                                                                                                                                              11. Caring for spandex and Lycra garments
                                                                                                                                              12. A quick vocabulary summary
                                                                                                                                              13. Final thoughts

                                                                                                                                              Walk into a clothing shop in New York and the label might say spandex. Walk into one in London or Paris and it says elastane. Walk into a sports store and you see the word Lycra on swimsuits and leggings. Are these three different materials, or one material with three names? The short answer is that they refer to the same family of stretch fibres, but the words are not interchangeable in every situation. This article untangles the vocabulary and explains what really matters when you read a fabric label.

                                                                                                                                              The generic name: spandex or elastane

                                                                                                                                              Spandex and elastane are generic names for a manufactured fibre in which the fibre-forming substance is a long-chain synthetic polymer made of at least a high percentage of segmented polyurethane. Technically, the fibre is a polyurethane-based elastomer, which means it behaves like rubber but has a different chemical makeup.

                                                                                                                                              The two words are simply regional. In the United States and Canada, the fibre is called spandex. In most of Europe, India, and many other regions, it is called elastane. Some countries use other local words, such as the Spanish term for the fibre, but the international textile labelling standards treat these names as equivalent descriptions of the same fibre type.

                                                                                                                                              An interesting fact is that the word spandex is an anagram of the word expands, which reflects its most famous quality.

                                                                                                                                              The brand name: Lycra

                                                                                                                                              Lycra is a brand name, not a generic term. It was originally created by the chemical company DuPont, and the brand is now owned by a company called The LYCRA Company. Lycra fibre is a type of spandex, produced under strict specifications and often combined with other brand programmes and quality standards. Garments that carry the Lycra name are saying that the stretch fibre inside meets the brand's requirements.

                                                                                                                                              In everyday speech, many people say Lycra for any stretchy fabric, much as people say Hoover for a vacuum cleaner or Sellotape for adhesive tape. This habit is understandable, but strictly speaking, not every spandex product is Lycra, just as not every cola is a particular brand of cola.

                                                                                                                                              Other brand names

                                                                                                                                              Lycra is the best-known brand, but others exist. Different producers market their own spandex or elastane fibres under names such as Creora, Roica and others. Each producer may have its own technologies, such as chlorine-resistant fibres, heat-set friendly fibres or soft-touch fibres. When you see an unfamiliar name on a label, it is usually a brand of spandex.

                                                                                                                                              Are they chemically different?

                                                                                                                                              Chemically, spandex is spandex. Whether a fibre is sold under a brand name or a generic label, it is made from the same family of polymers. The differences lie in the details: the specific raw materials, the molecular design, the spinning process and the finishing treatments. These details can change properties such as stretch, recovery force, heat tolerance, chlorine resistance and softness.

                                                                                                                                              So a premium branded fibre may perform better in demanding uses such as swimwear or high-performance sportswear, while a lower-cost generic fibre may be perfectly adequate for casual garments. The brand name alone does not guarantee quality, but it does indicate that the producer stands behind a defined standard.

                                                                                                                                              What the label tells you

                                                                                                                                              Fibre content labels list the generic names. A legging might say 88 percent polyester and 12 percent elastane. Another might say 90 percent nylon and 10 percent spandex. Both are describing a similar structure of fabric. If a brand name like Lycra appears, it is usually in addition to the generic name, for example elastane (Lycra), or on a separate swing tag.

                                                                                                                                              Labelling rules differ between countries, so brand names may not substitute for the legal fibre name. This is why you will often see the generic name in the care label and the brand on promotional tags.

                                                                                                                                              What makes spandex special

                                                                                                                                              Spandex is remarkable for several reasons.

                                                                                                                                              • Extreme stretch. It can stretch to several times its original length, often more than five times, and return.
                                                                                                                                              • Good recovery. It returns to its original length with consistent force.
                                                                                                                                              • Fineness. It can be spun into very fine filaments that are invisible inside a fabric.
                                                                                                                                              • Lightness. A small amount can transform a fabric without adding bulk.
                                                                                                                                              • Compatibility. It blends easily with cotton, wool, silk, polyester, nylon and many other fibres.
                                                                                                                                              • Resistance to body oils and sweat better than natural rubber.

                                                                                                                                              These qualities explain why spandex entered almost every area of clothing, from socks to evening wear.

                                                                                                                                              Spandex compared with natural rubber

                                                                                                                                              Before spandex, stretch came mainly from natural rubber. Rubber thread is strong and elastic but thicker, heavier and more sensitive to heat, light and body oils. Spandex is finer, lighter and tougher in many conditions. It also does not contain natural latex proteins, so it is a common choice for people with latex sensitivity. Rubber still has advantages in some heavy-duty applications, but spandex dominates fine garments.

                                                                                                                                              The role of the blend

                                                                                                                                              Almost nobody wears 100 percent spandex. It is usually blended in small amounts, typically between two and twenty percent, with other fibres. The other fibres provide appearance, comfort, strength and moisture handling. Spandex provides stretch and shape retention.

                                                                                                                                              For example, a cotton shirt with two percent spandex has a little give that makes it comfortable and helps it keep its shape. A swimsuit with twenty percent spandex has strong stretch and body-hugging fit. An article in this blog explores blend percentages in detail.

                                                                                                                                              Common myths

                                                                                                                                              Myth 1: Spandex and Lycra are completely different fibres. In reality, Lycra is one brand of spandex.

                                                                                                                                              Myth 2: Spandex is rubber. It is not rubber, though it behaves like it. Spandex is a synthetic polyurethane-based polymer.

                                                                                                                                              Myth 3: More spandex is always better. Too much spandex can make fabric feel tight or plastic-like and may wear out sooner. The best percentage depends on the garment.

                                                                                                                                              Myth 4: Branded fibres cannot fail. Even the best fibre can be damaged by heat, chlorine, rough washing or poor garment construction.

                                                                                                                                              Myth 5: Spandex lasts for ever. All spandex ages, especially with heat and chemicals, as another article explains.

                                                                                                                                              How to choose between branded and generic

                                                                                                                                              Consider the following.

                                                                                                                                              1. Application. For demanding uses like swimwear, competition sportswear and shapewear, a high-quality branded or well-specified fibre can be worth the cost.
                                                                                                                                              2. Quality documentation. Ask for technical data, test results and certifications, whether the fibre is branded or generic.
                                                                                                                                              3. Customer expectations. If your customers value known brands, a licensed fibre may support your marketing.
                                                                                                                                              4. Budget. For basic everyday garments, a reliable generic fibre may be more economical.
                                                                                                                                              5. Supplier reliability. Consistency across batches is more important than the name.

                                                                                                                                              Caring for spandex and Lycra garments

                                                                                                                                              Whatever name is on the tag, the care advice is similar. Wash in cool or lukewarm water, avoid bleach and strong detergents, minimise fabric softener, avoid high heat in drying and ironing, and rinse swimwear after use in chlorinated or salt water. These habits protect the fibre and keep garments comfortable.

                                                                                                                                              A quick vocabulary summary

                                                                                                                                              • Spandex: generic name used mainly in North America.
                                                                                                                                              • Elastane: generic name used mainly in Europe and many other regions.
                                                                                                                                              • Lycra: a brand of spandex fibre.
                                                                                                                                              • Stretch fibre: an everyday term that may refer to spandex or other elastic fibres.
                                                                                                                                              • Elastomeric fibre: a technical term for any fibre with rubber-like stretch, including spandex and rubber.

                                                                                                                                              Final thoughts

                                                                                                                                              The next time you see spandex, elastane or Lycra on a label, you will know that you are looking at the same remarkable family of stretch fibres, named differently by geography and branding. What matters most is not the name but the quality, the blend and the care. Understanding the vocabulary lets you shop, design and buy with confidence, and keeps you from being confused by the many words used for a single wonderful idea: a fibre that stretches and comes back.

                                                                                                                                              Frequently asked questions

                                                                                                                                              Are spandex and Lycra the same?

                                                                                                                                              Both are the same type of stretch fibre. Lycra is a brand name for spandex, much like Kleenex is a brand of tissue.

                                                                                                                                              What is elastane?

                                                                                                                                              Elastane is the name used for spandex in Europe and many other regions, so spandex, elastane and Lycra describe the same fibre type.

                                                                                                                                              Is Lycra better than generic spandex?

                                                                                                                                              Lycra is a branded product with controlled quality. Good generic spandex can also perform well, but quality varies by maker.

                                                                                                                                              Why is spandex mixed with other fibres?

                                                                                                                                              Spandex gives stretch and recovery, while fibres such as cotton or polyester give feel, strength and breathability.
