                                                                                                                                                Testing Elastic at Home and in the Lab: Simple Checks and Professional Methods

                                                                                                                                                How do you know if elastic is good? Learn easy home tests and the professional laboratory methods used to measure stretch, recovery, strength and colour fastness.

                                                                                                                                                By SNEH Editorial•16 November 2026•7 min read•1,425 words

                                                                                                                                                In this article

                                                                                                                                                1. Why test elastic at all?
                                                                                                                                                2. Simple tests you can do at home
                                                                                                                                                3. Keeping records
                                                                                                                                                4. Professional laboratory tests
                                                                                                                                                5. Understanding a test report
                                                                                                                                                6. Building a testing routine
                                                                                                                                                7. Common testing mistakes
                                                                                                                                                8. Final thoughts

                                                                                                                                                Looking at a roll of elastic tells you very little about how it will behave after a month of wear. Two rolls can look identical and perform very differently. That is why testing matters. Quality checks reveal whether elastic stretches enough, returns to shape, withstands washing and keeps its colour. This article covers simple tests anyone can do at home or in a small workshop, then explains the professional laboratory methods that factories and buyers rely on.

                                                                                                                                                Why test elastic at all?

                                                                                                                                                Elastic sits inside products that people wear against their skin for many hours. A failure is more than an inconvenience: it can mean returned goods, unhappy customers and wasted material. Testing helps you to:

                                                                                                                                                • compare suppliers fairly, using numbers instead of impressions;
                                                                                                                                                • confirm that every batch matches the approved sample;
                                                                                                                                                • predict how the elastic will perform after washing and long use;
                                                                                                                                                • find problems before a large order is sewn into thousands of garments.

                                                                                                                                                Simple tests you can do at home

                                                                                                                                                You do not need a laboratory to get useful information. These checks use a ruler, a marker, a clock and a washing machine.

                                                                                                                                                1. Width check

                                                                                                                                                Lay the relaxed elastic flat on a table without stretching it. Measure from edge to edge with a ruler or a caliper in several places along a one-metre length. Good elastic is consistent. If the width changes noticeably, the quality control in production may be weak.

                                                                                                                                                2. Stretch test

                                                                                                                                                Mark a length of exactly ten centimetres on the relaxed elastic. Stretch it gently to its comfortable maximum, not to the point of tearing, and measure the new length between the marks. If the marks are now twenty centimetres apart, the elastic has stretched by one hundred percent. Compare this with the supplier's stated stretch.

                                                                                                                                                3. Recovery test

                                                                                                                                                After stretching the marked piece, hold it stretched for about thirty seconds, then release it. Wait a minute and measure between the marks again. Good elastic returns to almost ten centimetres. If it stays at eleven or twelve, it has lost recovery and will sag in use. A stronger version of this test is to stretch and release the piece many times, such as fifty cycles, then measure again. Poor elastic shows a clear permanent stretch.

                                                                                                                                                4. Hand feel and appearance

                                                                                                                                                Run the elastic through your fingers. It should feel even and smooth, not scratchy, and the edges should be clean. Look for loose yarns, knots, holes and uneven colour. For skin contact products, rub the elastic against your inner wrist or cheek, since these areas are sensitive.

                                                                                                                                                5. Wash test

                                                                                                                                                Cut a sample, measure it carefully, and wash it as the finished product would be washed. Hang it to dry, then measure again. Changes in length show shrinkage. Look for colour bleeding into the wash water, fading, fraying or loss of stretch. For a harsher test, repeat the wash several times.

                                                                                                                                                6. Colour rub test

                                                                                                                                                Rub the elastic firmly on a clean white cloth, first dry and then slightly damp. If colour transfers to the cloth, the dye is not well fixed, and it may stain clothes or skin.

                                                                                                                                                7. Heat test

                                                                                                                                                Elastic can be damaged by heat. Check the manufacturer's advice, and if you plan to iron or tumble dry, test a small sample at the temperature you will use. Look for shrinkage, shine, stiffness or loss of stretch afterwards.

                                                                                                                                                8. Sewing test

                                                                                                                                                Sew a sample into the actual product, using the same needle and stitch. Check for puckering, broken yarns, rolling and stitch skipping. A test seam often shows problems that no laboratory number would predict.

                                                                                                                                                Keeping records

                                                                                                                                                Write down your results. Note the date, the batch number, the supplier, the measurements and what you saw. If a later batch behaves differently, your records will show it. Keep a labelled piece of the approved elastic as your reference sample, because comparing by eye or hand against a real piece is the easiest way to spot change.

                                                                                                                                                Professional laboratory tests

                                                                                                                                                Factories, large buyers and independent laboratories use standardised methods and machines. Standardisation matters because it means that results from different places can be compared. Typical tests include the following.

                                                                                                                                                Tensile strength and elongation

                                                                                                                                                A tensile testing machine grips the sample at both ends and pulls it at a fixed speed. It measures the force needed to stretch the elastic and records how far the elastic extends before it breaks. The result shows the breaking strength and the elongation at break. It helps buyers verify that the elastic can hold the load it will carry.

                                                                                                                                                Modulus or load at stretch

                                                                                                                                                Instead of testing to breaking point, many tests measure the force at specific stretch levels, such as fifty or one hundred percent. This shows how firm the elastic feels in use. Two elastics with the same maximum stretch can feel very different if one needs far more force to extend.

                                                                                                                                                Fatigue and cycle testing

                                                                                                                                                Machines stretch and release the elastic thousands of times to simulate months of wear. Afterwards, technicians measure how much length and force have been lost. This test predicts long-term recovery much better than a single stretch.

                                                                                                                                                Dimensional change after washing

                                                                                                                                                Samples are washed in a controlled machine cycle with a known detergent, and their length and width are measured before and after. The result is a percentage of shrinkage or growth. Controlled testing makes sure that the elastic behaves predictably in the factory's finishing processes.

                                                                                                                                                Colour fastness

                                                                                                                                                Laboratories test how colour resists washing, perspiration, rubbing, light and water. Results are usually graded on a scale of one to five, where five is excellent. Different standards define the exact methods, and buyers often specify minimum grades for their products. Colour fastness is especially important for coloured elastic used next to pale fabric.

                                                                                                                                                Heat and ageing resistance

                                                                                                                                                Samples may be placed in ovens, steam chambers or light cabinets to check what happens under heat, humidity or sunlight. These tests give an early warning about materials that will become brittle or lose stretch as they age.

                                                                                                                                                Chemical and safety testing

                                                                                                                                                Textile laboratories can test for restricted substances such as certain dyes or heavy metals, and they check pH, formaldehyde and other items depending on the market's rules. For baby and children's products, safety requirements are stricter. Certificates from recognised standards are a useful signal, but a buyer should always confirm what a certificate actually covers.

                                                                                                                                                Weight and construction analysis

                                                                                                                                                Technicians measure weight per metre, count yarns, check the proportion of rubber or spandex, and identify the cover fibres. This confirms that what the supplier delivered matches the specification.

                                                                                                                                                Understanding a test report

                                                                                                                                                A good test report lists the sample, the method or standard used, the conditions and the result. Look for:

                                                                                                                                                1. The standard named. Without it, results are hard to compare.
                                                                                                                                                2. The number of samples tested. One sample can mislead, because a single piece may be better or worse than the batch average.
                                                                                                                                                3. Conditions such as temperature and humidity. Elastic behaves differently when warm or damp.
                                                                                                                                                4. A pass or fail limit. The report is more useful when it compares results against a requirement.

                                                                                                                                                Building a testing routine

                                                                                                                                                For a small business, a sensible routine could be:

                                                                                                                                                • check width and appearance on every roll as it arrives;
                                                                                                                                                • do stretch, recovery and wash tests on each new batch;
                                                                                                                                                • keep a sealed reference sample from the approved batch;
                                                                                                                                                • send a sample to an independent laboratory when starting with a new supplier or entering a market with strict rules;
                                                                                                                                                • document results so you can discuss problems with suppliers using facts.

                                                                                                                                                Larger manufacturers add statistical checks, sampling every batch and recording results in a quality system.

                                                                                                                                                Common testing mistakes

                                                                                                                                                • Stretching elastic beyond its normal working range and then judging it unfairly.
                                                                                                                                                • Measuring while the elastic is still stretched or damp.
                                                                                                                                                • Testing only one piece from a roll.
                                                                                                                                                • Ignoring the difference between stretch at the start and after many cycles.
                                                                                                                                                • Trusting a certificate without reading what it covers.

                                                                                                                                                Final thoughts

                                                                                                                                                Testing turns opinions into evidence. A ruler, a marker and a washing machine will reveal a surprising amount about width, stretch, recovery and colour fastness. Professional methods go further by measuring force, fatigue, safety and ageing under controlled conditions. Together, these checks protect your products and your customers. Whether you are a hobbyist buying a metre or a manufacturer buying a tonne, a few well-chosen tests will save you from costly surprises.

                                                                                                                                                Frequently asked questions

                                                                                                                                                How can I test elastic quality at home?

                                                                                                                                                Stretch a sample to its limit several times, check it returns to its original length, and wash it to see if it holds up.

                                                                                                                                                What do labs measure in elastic?

                                                                                                                                                Typical tests include elongation, tension, recovery, shrinkage, colour fastness and durability after washing.

                                                                                                                                                What is recovery in elastic testing?

                                                                                                                                                Recovery is how well the elastic returns to its original length after being stretched.

                                                                                                                                                Why test a sample before a bulk order?

                                                                                                                                                A sample test shows whether the elastic suits your product and washing conditions before you commit to large quantities.

                                                                                                                                                  Textured and Bulked Yarns Explained: How Flat Filaments Become Soft and Stretchy

                                                                                                                                                  Plain continuous filaments feel smooth and cold. Texturing adds crimp, bulk and stretch. Learn how textured yarns are made and where they are used.

                                                                                                                                                  By SNEH Editorial•16 November 2026•6 min read•1,283 words

                                                                                                                                                  In this article

                                                                                                                                                  1. What is texturing?
                                                                                                                                                  2. Why texturing matters
                                                                                                                                                  3. False twist texturing
                                                                                                                                                  4. Air-jet texturing
                                                                                                                                                  5. Stuffer box and other crimping methods
                                                                                                                                                  6. Textured yarns in sewing thread
                                                                                                                                                  7. Textured yarn in fabrics
                                                                                                                                                  8. Textured yarn and elastic
                                                                                                                                                  9. Properties of textured yarns
                                                                                                                                                  10. Common defects
                                                                                                                                                  11. Choosing textured yarns
                                                                                                                                                  12. Final thoughts

                                                                                                                                                  A freshly extruded polyester or nylon filament is straight, smooth and shiny. It is strong, but it feels slick and slightly cold, and fabrics made from it can look flat and plastic. Most synthetic clothing does not feel like this, because the yarns have been textured. Texturing is a process that adds curls, crimps or loops to filaments, turning flat strands into soft, bulky yarns with a warmer feel and some natural stretch. This article explains what textured yarns are, the main ways of making them and the places where they are used.

                                                                                                                                                  What is texturing?

                                                                                                                                                  Texturing changes the shape of continuous synthetic filaments. A smooth filament is deformed into a permanent wavy, coiled or looped form. The deformation traps air between the filaments, so the yarn becomes bulkier, softer and more insulating. It also gives the yarn extensibility, meaning that it can stretch a little and recover, which is useful in knitting and sewing.

                                                                                                                                                  This is possible because thermoplastic fibres such as polyester and nylon soften with heat. They can be bent into a new shape when hot, and the shape is locked in when they cool. This is the same principle as heat setting of fabric.

                                                                                                                                                  Why texturing matters

                                                                                                                                                  Texturing solves several problems of plain filament yarn:

                                                                                                                                                  1. Softness. The crimped surface feels gentler against the skin.
                                                                                                                                                  2. Bulk and cover. Textured yarn fills out fabric, so cloth looks fuller and less transparent.
                                                                                                                                                  3. Warmth. Trapped air improves thermal insulation.
                                                                                                                                                  4. Stretch and comfort. Crimp provides extension without elastic fibres, which is valuable in comfort stretch fabrics.
                                                                                                                                                  5. Appearance. Textured yarns reduce the shiny, synthetic look and can imitate the appearance of spun yarns.
                                                                                                                                                  6. Moisture handling. The structure can help move moisture along fibres in sports fabrics, depending on the fibre and finish.

                                                                                                                                                  False twist texturing

                                                                                                                                                  The most widely used method is false twist texturing, done on high-speed machines. The steps are:

                                                                                                                                                  1. Feeding. A partially oriented or fully drawn filament yarn is fed from a package.
                                                                                                                                                  2. Twisting. A spinning device, such as a set of friction discs, inserts a high twist into the moving yarn.
                                                                                                                                                  3. Heating. The twisted yarn passes through a heater, where it is heated to a temperature that softens the polymer.
                                                                                                                                                  4. Cooling. The yarn cools while still twisted, locking the twist into the filaments.
                                                                                                                                                  5. Untwisting. After the twisting device, the twist is removed from the yarn, but the filaments keep their set coil-like shape.
                                                                                                                                                  6. Winding. The textured yarn is wound onto a package, sometimes with a second heater to stabilise it.

                                                                                                                                                  The result is a yarn with a crimped, springy character. The settings, such as temperature, twist level and speed, control the amount of bulk and stretch. Machines can run at very high speeds, which makes the process economical.

                                                                                                                                                  Air-jet texturing

                                                                                                                                                  Air-jet texturing takes a different path. Several filaments are overfed into a jet of compressed air. The turbulence causes the filaments to form small loops and tangles, which are locked together by interlacing. The resulting yarn has a spun-like appearance with a rough, staple-like surface, but without much stretch.

                                                                                                                                                  Air-textured yarns are used where a natural look and feel are needed, for example in upholstery, home textiles, workwear and some casual clothing. They bridge the gap between filament and spun yarns.

                                                                                                                                                  Stuffer box and other crimping methods

                                                                                                                                                  Another method is stuffer box crimping, in which filaments are pushed into a heated box where they fold into a zigzag crimp. This produces bulk and is mainly used for carpet yarns and staple fibres.

                                                                                                                                                  Knit-de-knit methods involve knitting the yarn into a tube, heat setting it, and then unravelling it, which leaves a wavy crimp in the filaments. It is a slower process, used for special effects.

                                                                                                                                                  Edge crimping, gear crimping and other methods exist for niche products.

                                                                                                                                                  Textured yarns in sewing thread

                                                                                                                                                  Textured thread is widely used in overlocking and coverstitch machines. The looper threads in these machines need to be soft, bulky and stretchy, so that they cover the raw edge of fabric comfortably and extend with the seam. Textured nylon or polyester, sometimes called wooly nylon or bulked thread, is the standard choice for these jobs.

                                                                                                                                                  Because of its extensibility, textured thread gives:

                                                                                                                                                  • stretchy seams in knit fabrics, swimwear and activewear;
                                                                                                                                                  • soft edges that do not irritate the skin;
                                                                                                                                                  • good coverage of raw edges, so seams look neat;
                                                                                                                                                  • comfortable hems and cuffs.

                                                                                                                                                  However, textured thread is generally not recommended as the needle thread on a lockstitch machine, because the loops and crimps can snag in the needle eye and tension discs. Smooth, strong thread is better in the needle.

                                                                                                                                                  Textured yarn in fabrics

                                                                                                                                                  Textured polyester is one of the world's most used yarns. It appears in:

                                                                                                                                                  • jersey and knit fabrics for T-shirts, dresses and sportswear;
                                                                                                                                                  • fleece and brushed fabrics, where bulk and softness are essential;
                                                                                                                                                  • linings, curtains and home furnishings;
                                                                                                                                                  • carpets and rugs, where bulked nylon and polyester are used for resilience;
                                                                                                                                                  • socks, tights and underwear, where textured nylon provides stretch and comfort.

                                                                                                                                                  In many of these uses, textured yarn is combined with elastane or spandex to deliver even greater stretch and recovery.

                                                                                                                                                  Textured yarn and elastic

                                                                                                                                                  In narrow elastic fabrics, the covering yarns are often textured. A textured cover gives the elastic a softer feel against the skin and better coverage over the rubber or spandex core. It also helps to hide the core, so that the elastic looks more even and smooth. For products such as baby clothing and underwear, soft textured polyester or nylon covers are popular.

                                                                                                                                                  Properties of textured yarns

                                                                                                                                                  Compared with flat yarns, textured yarns tend to have:

                                                                                                                                                  • Lower tenacity, meaning that they are slightly weaker than plain filament of the same type, although still strong for most uses.
                                                                                                                                                  • Higher bulk, giving a greater volume for the same weight.
                                                                                                                                                  • Greater extensibility, from the crimp structure.
                                                                                                                                                  • Softer handle and better draping.
                                                                                                                                                  • Different dye uptake, which can vary with degree of crimp, so dyeing needs careful control.

                                                                                                                                                  Texturing quality is monitored by measuring crimp contraction, crimp stability and other values that indicate how bulky and stretchy the yarn will be.

                                                                                                                                                  Common defects

                                                                                                                                                  Problems in texturing can show up in the finished fabric. Some typical defects include:

                                                                                                                                                  • Uneven crimp, which causes streaks and uneven dyeing in knitted fabrics.
                                                                                                                                                  • Broken filaments, called fluff or fuzz, which can snag and lead to pilling.
                                                                                                                                                  • Tension variations, which change crimp from package to package and lead to barre in fabrics.
                                                                                                                                                  • Overheating or underheating, which changes bulk and dye affinity.

                                                                                                                                                  Quality control includes checking yarn at several stages and testing knitted samples for dye uniformity.

                                                                                                                                                  Choosing textured yarns

                                                                                                                                                  For manufacturers and buyers, helpful questions when choosing textured yarn include:

                                                                                                                                                  1. Is the yarn made for knitting, weaving or sewing, and on which machine will it run?
                                                                                                                                                  2. What is the linear density, expressed in denier or dtex, and the number of filaments?
                                                                                                                                                  3. What are the crimp characteristics?
                                                                                                                                                  4. Is it for dyeing, and is dye uptake consistent between lots?
                                                                                                                                                  5. Does it need elastane or another yarn to be combined for stretch?

                                                                                                                                                  Final thoughts

                                                                                                                                                  Texturing is what turns a plain, slippery filament into the soft, stretchy yarn of everyday clothing. False twist and air-jet methods create crimp and loops that add bulk, warmth and comfort, and textured threads make flexible seams possible in overlockers and coverstitch machines. Without texturing, synthetic textiles would feel very different from the ones we know. The next time you pull on a soft knit sweater or look at a neat stretchy hem, you can remember that tiny crimps in thousands of filaments are doing quiet work.

                                                                                                                                                  Frequently asked questions

                                                                                                                                                  What is textured yarn?

                                                                                                                                                  It is yarn treated to add crimp or loops, which gives it bulk, softness and stretch.

                                                                                                                                                  What is the difference between textured and bulked yarn?

                                                                                                                                                  Both add volume and softness, but they use different processes, such as air texturing or heat and mechanical crimping.

                                                                                                                                                  Where are textured yarns used?

                                                                                                                                                  They are used in sportswear, socks, knitwear, upholstery and sewing threads for stretch seams.

                                                                                                                                                  Why choose textured thread for stretch seams?

                                                                                                                                                  Its crimped structure lets it stretch with the fabric, so seams are less likely to break.

                                                                                                                                                    Thread Count, Denier and Tex: Measuring Yarn Thickness Without the Confusion

                                                                                                                                                    Denier, decitex, tex, Ne and Nm: a clear guide to the numbers that describe how thick or fine a thread really is.

                                                                                                                                                    By SNEH Editorial

                                                                                                                                                    6 min readRead article →
                                                                                                                                                    ← Threads & Yarns

                                                                                                                                                    Thread Count, Denier and Tex: Measuring Yarn Thickness Without the Confusion

                                                                                                                                                    Denier, decitex, tex, Ne and Nm: a clear guide to the numbers that describe how thick or fine a thread really is.

                                                                                                                                                    By SNEH Editorial•16 November 2026•6 min read•1,300 words

                                                                                                                                                    In this article

                                                                                                                                                    1. Why we need yarn numbering systems
                                                                                                                                                    2. Direct systems: tex, decitex and denier
                                                                                                                                                    3. Indirect systems: English cotton count and metric count
                                                                                                                                                    4. Comparing the systems with an example
                                                                                                                                                    5. Sewing thread sizes
                                                                                                                                                    6. Elastic thread and spandex sizes
                                                                                                                                                    7. What about thread count in fabrics?
                                                                                                                                                    8. Why yarn size affects performance
                                                                                                                                                    9. Measuring yarn yourself
                                                                                                                                                    10. Common mistakes
                                                                                                                                                    11. A handy reference table in words
                                                                                                                                                    12. Final thoughts

                                                                                                                                                    Open a technical sheet for thread or elastic and you meet a bewildering collection of numbers and units: 40 denier, 167 decitex, Ne 30, Nm 50, tex 20. They all describe how thick or fine a yarn is, but they do it in different ways. Understanding these systems is essential for anyone who buys, sells or designs textiles. This article explains the most common yarn measurement systems in simple language, with examples and conversions.

                                                                                                                                                    Why we need yarn numbering systems

                                                                                                                                                    Yarn is too fine to measure with a ruler, and its diameter varies with twist and fibre type. Instead of measuring thickness, the industry measures the relationship between length and weight. If a certain length of yarn weighs more, the yarn is thicker. If it weighs less, the yarn is finer. This approach is accurate, practical and independent of shape.

                                                                                                                                                    There are two families of systems. Direct systems express weight per unit length, so a larger number means a thicker yarn. Indirect systems express length per unit weight, so a larger number means a finer yarn. This difference is the main source of confusion.

                                                                                                                                                    Direct systems: tex, decitex and denier

                                                                                                                                                    Tex

                                                                                                                                                    Tex is the international standard direct system. One tex is the weight in grams of 1,000 metres of yarn. A yarn of 20 tex weighs 20 grams for every 1,000 metres. Higher tex means thicker yarn.

                                                                                                                                                    Decitex

                                                                                                                                                    Decitex, abbreviated dtex, is one tenth of a tex, or the weight in grams of 10,000 metres of yarn. It is useful for fine filaments because the numbers are easier to handle. A yarn of 167 dtex is the same as 16.7 tex.

                                                                                                                                                    Denier

                                                                                                                                                    Denier is an older direct system still widely used for synthetic filaments, hosiery, spandex and many sewing and elastic materials. One denier is the weight in grams of 9,000 metres of yarn. So 40 denier means 40 grams per 9,000 metres.

                                                                                                                                                    Conversions between direct systems:

                                                                                                                                                    • Decitex equals denier multiplied by about 1.11. For example, 100 denier is roughly 111 decitex.
                                                                                                                                                    • Tex equals denier divided by about 9. For example, 90 denier is 10 tex.

                                                                                                                                                    Denier is familiar from stockings. Sheer stockings may be 10 to 20 denier, while opaque tights may be 60 to 100 denier or more.

                                                                                                                                                    Indirect systems: English cotton count and metric count

                                                                                                                                                    English cotton count (Ne)

                                                                                                                                                    The English cotton count, written Ne, is used mainly for cotton and spun yarns. It is defined as the number of hanks of 840 yards that weigh one pound. A higher Ne number means finer yarn. Ne 20 is thicker than Ne 40. Many cotton yarns for t-shirts are around Ne 20 to Ne 40, while very fine yarns reach Ne 60, 80 or more.

                                                                                                                                                    Metric count (Nm)

                                                                                                                                                    Metric count, Nm, indicates the number of kilometres of yarn that weigh one kilogram. Nm 50 means 50 kilometres in one kilogram. Higher Nm means finer yarn. It is common for wool, linen and many European yarn products.

                                                                                                                                                    Approximate conversions:

                                                                                                                                                    • Tex equals 1000 divided by Nm. For example, Nm 50 equals 20 tex.
                                                                                                                                                    • Tex equals 590.5 divided by Ne. For example, Ne 30 is about 19.7 tex.

                                                                                                                                                    Comparing the systems with an example

                                                                                                                                                    Imagine a yarn of 20 tex. In other systems it is:

                                                                                                                                                    • Ne about 29.5.
                                                                                                                                                    • Nm 50.
                                                                                                                                                    • Denier about 180.
                                                                                                                                                    • Decitex 200.

                                                                                                                                                    Seeing the same yarn in several languages helps to build intuition. The important rule is that tex, decitex and denier go up as the yarn gets thicker, while Ne and Nm go up as the yarn gets finer.

                                                                                                                                                    Sewing thread sizes

                                                                                                                                                    Sewing thread has its own labelling traditions. Many threads are described by a tex size, such as Tex 27 or Tex 40, combined with ticket numbers such as Tkt 120 or Tkt 50. Another system uses weights, such as 30 weight or 50 weight, common in quilting and embroidery, where a larger number means a finer thread. Different brands use slightly different conventions, so always read the packaging and check the equivalent tex or metric count when comparing.

                                                                                                                                                    Thicker sewing thread gives stronger and more visible stitches. Finer thread gives delicate stitches but lower strength. Choose a size that matches the fabric weight and the needle.

                                                                                                                                                    Elastic thread and spandex sizes

                                                                                                                                                    Spandex is typically labelled in denier or decitex, such as 20 denier, 40 denier, 70 denier or 140 denier. Fine spandex is used for delicate knits, while heavier sizes are used for firmer fabrics and bands. Rubber thread is commonly given by gauge, diameter, or thickness with a unit such as millimetres or inches, though tex and denier are also used in technical contexts.

                                                                                                                                                    For covered yarn, two numbers are provided: one for the core and one for the cover. For example, 40 denier spandex covered with 70 denier nylon describes a fine spandex core wrapped with a thicker nylon yarn. The ratio between core and cover is important to the final stretch.

                                                                                                                                                    What about thread count in fabrics?

                                                                                                                                                    Thread count is a different idea, used mainly for woven fabrics such as bed sheets. It is the number of threads per square inch, counting both warp and weft. A fabric with 100 threads per inch lengthwise and 100 per inch crosswise has a thread count of 200. People often assume that a higher thread count automatically means better quality, but this is not always true. Very high counts can result from using multi-ply yarns, which are counted as separate threads. Fabric quality depends on fibre type, yarn quality, weave structure and finishing as well as count.

                                                                                                                                                    Why yarn size affects performance

                                                                                                                                                    Yarn size has many consequences.

                                                                                                                                                    • Strength. Thicker yarns generally have higher breaking strength.
                                                                                                                                                    • Fabric weight and thickness. Coarse yarns make heavier, bulkier fabrics.
                                                                                                                                                    • Softness and drape. Fine yarns give smoother, more flexible fabrics.
                                                                                                                                                    • Stitch appearance. Thread thickness determines how visible stitches are.
                                                                                                                                                    • Elastic force. Thicker elastic threads exert higher pulling force.
                                                                                                                                                    • Machine compatibility. Needles, guides and tension systems are chosen according to yarn size.

                                                                                                                                                    Measuring yarn yourself

                                                                                                                                                    If you need to estimate yarn size, you can use a simple method. Measure a known length of yarn, for example one metre, weigh it on a precise scale and calculate weight per length. For instance, if one metre weighs 0.02 grams, then 1,000 metres weigh 20 grams, which is 20 tex. For very fine yarns, longer lengths give more reliable results. Condition the yarn at standard temperature and humidity before weighing, because moisture changes weight.

                                                                                                                                                    Common mistakes

                                                                                                                                                    1. Mixing up direct and indirect systems. Remember that a higher Ne is finer, while a higher denier is thicker.
                                                                                                                                                    2. Comparing across different units without converting. Always convert to a common unit first.
                                                                                                                                                    3. Ignoring tolerances. Real yarns have variation, typically a few percent either way.
                                                                                                                                                    4. Trusting thread count alone. Fabric quality depends on much more than a single number.
                                                                                                                                                    5. Forgetting yarn type. A 100 denier elastic behaves very differently from 100 denier polyester.

                                                                                                                                                    A handy reference table in words

                                                                                                                                                    • 10 to 20 denier: very fine, sheer hosiery and delicate stretch.
                                                                                                                                                    • 40 to 70 denier: medium fine, common for spandex in garments.
                                                                                                                                                    • 100 to 150 denier: medium, used for heavier stretch knits.
                                                                                                                                                    • 300 denier and above: coarse, used for bags, upholstery and technical items.

                                                                                                                                                    Final thoughts

                                                                                                                                                    Yarn numbering systems may seem confusing at first, but they follow simple logic: weight against length. Once you understand the difference between direct systems like tex and denier and indirect systems like Ne and Nm, specification sheets become readable. This knowledge helps you compare offers, specify materials correctly and avoid expensive mistakes. The next time you read 40 denier or Ne 30, you will know exactly what the number tells you about the thread.

                                                                                                                                                    Frequently asked questions

                                                                                                                                                    What is denier?

                                                                                                                                                    Denier is the weight in grams of 9,000 metres of yarn. A higher denier means a thicker yarn.

                                                                                                                                                    What is tex?

                                                                                                                                                    Tex is the weight in grams of 1,000 metres of yarn, and it is a simple international unit.

                                                                                                                                                    How do denier and tex relate?

                                                                                                                                                    One tex is about 9 deniers, so 90 denier is roughly 10 tex.

                                                                                                                                                    Is thread count the same as denier?

                                                                                                                                                    No. Thread count usually refers to threads per inch in a fabric, while denier describes the thickness of a single yarn.
