                                                                                                                                                      Choosing Sewing Thread for Stretch Fabrics

                                                                                                                                                      Popped seams and puckered hems are usually thread problems. Learn which threads, needles and stitches keep stretch garments strong.

                                                                                                                                                      By SNEH Editorial

                                                                                                                                                      7 min readRead article →
                                                                                                                                                      ← Threads & Yarns

                                                                                                                                                      Thread Lubrication and Sewing Machine Speed: Preventing Heat, Breaks and Skipped Stitches

                                                                                                                                                      Fast sewing creates friction and heat that can weaken thread. Learn how lubrication, needle choice and speed settings work together to prevent breaks and skipped stitches.

                                                                                                                                                      By SNEH Editorial•16 November 2026•6 min read•1,228 words

                                                                                                                                                      In this article

                                                                                                                                                      1. Where friction and heat come from
                                                                                                                                                      2. What thread lubrication is
                                                                                                                                                      3. Types of lubrication approaches
                                                                                                                                                      4. Needle choice and its effect
                                                                                                                                                      5. Speed and its limits
                                                                                                                                                      6. Tension and thread path
                                                                                                                                                      7. Stretch fabrics and skipped stitches
                                                                                                                                                      8. Choosing thread for high-speed sewing
                                                                                                                                                      9. Maintenance habits that save thread
                                                                                                                                                      10. Final thoughts

                                                                                                                                                      Industrial sewing machines run fast. A busy machine can make thousands of stitches per minute, and each stitch pulls thread through a needle eye, a tension disc, a take-up lever and the fabric. At that speed, friction generates heat. If the thread is not suited to the speed, the result is breaks, fluffy deposits, skipped stitches and weak seams. Lubrication, needle selection and sensible machine settings work together to keep the thread running smoothly. This article explains how.

                                                                                                                                                      Where friction and heat come from

                                                                                                                                                      Thread travels a long path through the machine, and every contact point adds drag:

                                                                                                                                                      • thread guides and tension discs;
                                                                                                                                                      • the take-up lever;
                                                                                                                                                      • the needle eye, where the thread is squeezed and flexed;
                                                                                                                                                      • the fabric, which pulls on the thread at each stitch;
                                                                                                                                                      • the bobbin or looper area.

                                                                                                                                                      The needle is usually the hottest part. At high speed, the needle can reach temperatures well above room temperature because of friction with the fabric, especially with dense or synthetic materials. Thread passing through the needle eye picks up this heat. Many synthetic threads, such as polyester and nylon, can soften or melt if they get too hot, which leads to weak spots and snapped threads.

                                                                                                                                                      What thread lubrication is

                                                                                                                                                      Most industrial sewing thread carries a thin layer of lubricant applied during finishing. This coating reduces the friction between the thread and machine parts. Common finishes are based on waxes, silicones or other specialised compounds, and the right type depends on the fibre and the end use.

                                                                                                                                                      A good finish does several jobs:

                                                                                                                                                      1. Reduces friction at the needle eye and guides.
                                                                                                                                                      2. Reduces heat build-up, protecting the thread and needle.
                                                                                                                                                      3. Smooths the surface, reducing fuzz and lint.
                                                                                                                                                      4. Helps stitch formation, so loops open predictably for the hook or looper.
                                                                                                                                                      5. Protects against abrasion in the thread path.

                                                                                                                                                      The amount of lubricant matters. Too little leaves the thread rough and hot. Too much can transfer to the machine and fabric, attract lint and cause staining, especially on light-coloured fabrics.

                                                                                                                                                      Types of lubrication approaches

                                                                                                                                                      • Factory-applied finish. The thread maker applies a lubricant during winding or finishing. This is the primary system, and thread should be chosen with a finish suitable for the machine speed.
                                                                                                                                                      • Silicone finishes are widely used on synthetic threads for high-speed sewing, because they reduce friction effectively. They can leave residue, so some manufacturers avoid them near sensitive fabrics or where later printing or bonding is needed.
                                                                                                                                                      • Wax finishes suit cotton and certain threads and are typical for hand sewing or heavy stitching. They add stiffness and smoothness.
                                                                                                                                                      • Machine-side lubrication devices. Some factories use small applicators or lubricating pads that apply a controlled amount of lubricant to the thread as it feeds. These are used in demanding operations.

                                                                                                                                                      Always follow the thread manufacturer's advice. Mixing lubricants carelessly can cause build-up and staining.

                                                                                                                                                      Needle choice and its effect

                                                                                                                                                      The needle is the partner of the thread, and it needs the right size, point and eye.

                                                                                                                                                      • Size. The needle must be large enough that thread can pass through the eye freely, yet small enough not to damage the fabric. A needle that is too small squeezes the thread, creating friction and heat. A needle that is too large may leave visible holes and cause loose stitches.
                                                                                                                                                      • Eye shape. Some needles have larger or specially shaped eyes to reduce thread wear, which helps with thick or textured threads.
                                                                                                                                                      • Point type. Ballpoint needles are used on knits to push fibres aside instead of cutting them. Sharp points suit wovens. Using the wrong point on stretch fabric causes skipped stitches or fabric damage.
                                                                                                                                                      • Coating. Coated needles, such as titanium or other hard coatings, reduce friction and heat, so they can run faster and last longer.
                                                                                                                                                      • Condition. A burred or blunt needle shreds thread and damages fabric. Regular needle changes are cheap compared with the cost of defects.

                                                                                                                                                      Speed and its limits

                                                                                                                                                      Machine speed is the main driver of heat. Running at the maximum rated speed on every job is a common mistake. A few principles help:

                                                                                                                                                      1. Match speed to the thread. Some threads tolerate high speed. Others, such as certain bulked or specialty threads, run better more slowly.
                                                                                                                                                      2. Match speed to the fabric. Dense, thick or heavily finished fabrics create more friction. Stretch fabrics may need adjusted settings.
                                                                                                                                                      3. Reduce speed for tricky operations. Sewing across thick seams, corners or multiple layers benefits from lower speed.
                                                                                                                                                      4. Watch for warning signs. Hot needles, melted thread, frequent breaks and fuzzy thread deposits are signs that speed or setup needs changing.
                                                                                                                                                      5. Test before production. Sew trial seams at working speed and check them under a magnifier.

                                                                                                                                                      Tension and thread path

                                                                                                                                                      Friction is also influenced by tension settings. Too much tension drags the thread, increases heat and can pucker seams. Too little produces loose, looping stitches. Tension should be set with the correct thread in place, and both needle and bobbin threads should be balanced. Thread guides should be smooth and free of burrs, since a small nick can fray thread. Clean the machine regularly, since lint and old lubricant collect in the thread path and increase drag.

                                                                                                                                                      Stretch fabrics and skipped stitches

                                                                                                                                                      Skipped stitches are a typical problem on stretch fabrics. They occur when the hook or looper fails to catch the thread loop. Causes include:

                                                                                                                                                      • wrong needle type or size, so the thread loop does not form correctly;
                                                                                                                                                      • fabric flagging, meaning the fabric bounces with the needle, preventing a clean loop;
                                                                                                                                                      • poorly lubricated thread that twists or snarls;
                                                                                                                                                      • worn or damaged needle;
                                                                                                                                                      • incorrect timing between needle and hook;
                                                                                                                                                      • excessive speed.

                                                                                                                                                      Solutions include using the correct ballpoint or stretch needle, choosing a thread with the right finish, adjusting presser foot pressure and slowing down.

                                                                                                                                                      Choosing thread for high-speed sewing

                                                                                                                                                      When buying thread for fast production, check:

                                                                                                                                                      • fibre and construction, such as continuous filament polyester or core-spun thread, which are strong and consistent;
                                                                                                                                                      • finish suited to the speed and fabric;
                                                                                                                                                      • evenness, meaning consistent thickness along the length;
                                                                                                                                                      • strength and elongation;
                                                                                                                                                      • winding quality, since poorly wound cones cause tangles and uneven feeding;
                                                                                                                                                      • colour fastness and shrinkage, which affect the final garment.

                                                                                                                                                      Run trials on your own machines and track breakages per thousand metres. This simple measure often reveals large differences between threads that look the same.

                                                                                                                                                      Maintenance habits that save thread

                                                                                                                                                      • Clean lint from the thread path, bobbin area and feed dogs regularly.
                                                                                                                                                      • Replace needles on a schedule, not only when they fail.
                                                                                                                                                      • Store thread away from heat, dust and humidity to protect finish and strength.
                                                                                                                                                      • Avoid unwinding thread from the wrong end of a cone, which can cause twisting.
                                                                                                                                                      • Keep an eye on thread tension discs and replace worn parts.
                                                                                                                                                      • Record settings that work well for each fabric and thread.

                                                                                                                                                      Final thoughts

                                                                                                                                                      Fast stitching is a balance. Thread, needle, lubricant, tension and speed all influence friction and heat. When one element is wrong, the others cannot fully compensate. By choosing a thread with a suitable finish, using the right needle, setting sensible speeds and keeping machines clean, factories reduce breaks, avoid skipped stitches and produce stronger seams. A few trial seams and careful observation often solve problems that more speed or more tension only make worse.

                                                                                                                                                      Frequently asked questions

                                                                                                                                                      Why does thread break at high sewing speed?

                                                                                                                                                      Friction at the needle eye and guides creates heat that can weaken or melt synthetic thread, especially if the needle or finish is wrong.

                                                                                                                                                      What does thread lubricant do?

                                                                                                                                                      It reduces friction and heat, smooths the surface and helps stitches form, protecting both thread and needle.

                                                                                                                                                      How can I prevent skipped stitches on stretch fabric?

                                                                                                                                                      Use a ballpoint or stretch needle, a suitable thread finish, correct presser foot pressure and a lower speed if needed.

                                                                                                                                                      How often should needles be changed?

                                                                                                                                                      On a regular schedule rather than only after failure, because a blunt or burred needle shreds thread and damages fabric.

                                                                                                                                                        Thread Tension and Stitch Problems on Stretch Seams: Causes and Cures

                                                                                                                                                        Skipped stitches, popped seams and wavy fabric are common when sewing stretch. Learn how needles, thread, tension and stitch choice solve these problems.

                                                                                                                                                        By SNEH Editorial•16 November 2026•7 min read•1,434 words

                                                                                                                                                        In this article

                                                                                                                                                        1. Start with the basics: needle, thread and stitch
                                                                                                                                                        2. Understanding thread tension
                                                                                                                                                        3. Problem 1: Skipped stitches
                                                                                                                                                        4. Problem 2: Popped or broken seams
                                                                                                                                                        5. Problem 3: Wavy or stretched-out seams
                                                                                                                                                        6. Problem 4: Tunnelling and puckering
                                                                                                                                                        7. Problem 5: Thread breakage
                                                                                                                                                        8. Problem 6: Seams that look loose or loopy
                                                                                                                                                        9. Working with elastic
                                                                                                                                                        10. Machines and settings
                                                                                                                                                        11. Build a test routine
                                                                                                                                                        12. Final thoughts

                                                                                                                                                        Sewing stretch fabric can feel like a different craft from sewing ordinary cloth. The fabric moves under the needle, the seams must stretch without snapping, and small adjustments to thread tension can change the result completely. Many sewers and factory operators have met the same set of frustrations: skipped stitches, popped seams, wavy edges and tunnelling. The good news is that almost all of them have clear causes and practical cures. This guide explains what goes wrong and how to put it right.

                                                                                                                                                        Start with the basics: needle, thread and stitch

                                                                                                                                                        Before adjusting tension, make sure the three basic choices are right. Many stretch-seam problems come from a mismatch here.

                                                                                                                                                        The needle. For knit and stretch fabrics, a ballpoint or stretch needle is usually best. Its slightly rounded tip pushes between the yarns instead of piercing them, which prevents cut fibres and runs. A sharp needle can cut elastic yarns and cause holes. Needle size should match the fabric weight: fine for light jersey, medium for heavier knits. Change the needle often, since a blunt or damaged needle causes skipped stitches, snags and fabric damage.

                                                                                                                                                        The thread. Use a good quality polyester or nylon thread with some flexibility. Old, brittle or cheap thread breaks easily. In overlockers, textured or wooly thread in the loopers gives stretch and softness.

                                                                                                                                                        The stitch. A straight stitch has no give. When a seam in stretch fabric is pulled, the thread snaps. Use stitches designed to stretch: a narrow zigzag, a stretch stitch, a triple stretch stitch, an overlock or a coverstitch. Setting the right stitch length and width matters too.

                                                                                                                                                        Understanding thread tension

                                                                                                                                                        Tension is the balance of pull between the upper thread and the bobbin thread. In a balanced stitch, the two threads lock in the middle of the fabric layers, and the stitches look the same from both sides. If the balance is wrong, the stitches look loose or tight, and the seam may pucker or break.

                                                                                                                                                        • Top tension too tight: The bobbin thread shows on the top as small dots or loops, and the fabric puckers.
                                                                                                                                                        • Top tension too loose: The top thread forms loops on the underside of the fabric, and the seam looks untidy and may pull apart.

                                                                                                                                                        Remember that tension dials differ between machines, so always test on a scrap of the real fabric, using the same number of layers as your seam. Change one thing at a time, and write down your settings.

                                                                                                                                                        Problem 1: Skipped stitches

                                                                                                                                                        What you see. The machine misses stitches, leaving gaps in the seam.

                                                                                                                                                        Common causes. Wrong or blunt needle, a needle that is bent or incorrectly inserted, thread unsuited to the needle, poor timing of the machine or the fabric flagging, which means it bounces up and down with the needle.

                                                                                                                                                        Cures.

                                                                                                                                                        1. Fit a new ballpoint or stretch needle in the right size, pushed fully into the clamp, with the flat side the right way round.
                                                                                                                                                        2. Check that thread and needle are compatible, with the thread passing smoothly through the eye.
                                                                                                                                                        3. Use a walking foot or reduce presser foot pressure so fabric does not bounce.
                                                                                                                                                        4. Try a different needle type if the problem continues, such as a specific one for highly elastic fabrics, which has a special scarf.
                                                                                                                                                        5. If these steps fail, the machine's timing may need servicing.

                                                                                                                                                        Problem 2: Popped or broken seams

                                                                                                                                                        What you see. Stitches snap when the garment is pulled or worn.

                                                                                                                                                        Common causes. Straight stitch in a stretch seam, thread with too little elasticity, stitches too long or too tight, or fabric stretched too far for the seam.

                                                                                                                                                        Cures. Switch to a stretch stitch or a narrow zigzag. Reduce the stitch length slightly, so that there are more stitches per centimetre to share the load. Choose thread with some stretch, such as textured polyester or nylon. Where a seam needs strength and stretch, such as a crotch seam, sew twice or use a coverstitch or overlock finish.

                                                                                                                                                        Problem 3: Wavy or stretched-out seams

                                                                                                                                                        What you see. The fabric stretches while sewing and the seam ripples after it relaxes. Hems and necklines look wavy.

                                                                                                                                                        Common causes. Pulling the fabric through the machine, too much presser foot pressure, a heavy hand or a fabric that is cut off grain. The feed dogs push the lower layer more than the top layer, so one layer stretches.

                                                                                                                                                        Cures.

                                                                                                                                                        • Let the machine feed the fabric without pulling or pushing it.
                                                                                                                                                        • Use a walking foot or a differential feed to even out the feeding of the layers.
                                                                                                                                                        • Reduce presser foot pressure.
                                                                                                                                                        • Support the weight of the fabric so it does not drag.
                                                                                                                                                        • Stabilise areas such as necklines and shoulder seams with clear elastic or a strip of fusible stay tape.
                                                                                                                                                        • Pin or clip the fabric carefully, and avoid stretching it when pinning.

                                                                                                                                                        Problem 4: Tunnelling and puckering

                                                                                                                                                        What you see. The fabric between two lines of stitches rises into a ridge, or the stitching draws the fabric into small gathers.

                                                                                                                                                        Common causes. Excessive top tension, stitches too close together, thread too thick for the fabric or a lack of stabiliser on very light fabrics.

                                                                                                                                                        Cures. Loosen the top tension a little, increase the stitch length slightly, and switch to a finer thread and needle. Place tissue paper or a stabiliser under the fabric when sewing delicate stretch fabrics and tear it away after sewing. Press the seam gently after sewing, with an appropriate heat for the fabric.

                                                                                                                                                        Problem 5: Thread breakage

                                                                                                                                                        What you see. The needle thread or bobbin thread snaps repeatedly.

                                                                                                                                                        Common causes. Poor quality or old thread, tension too tight, thread caught on the spool, burrs or rough spots on the needle plate or needle, or a damaged needle.

                                                                                                                                                        Cures. Rethread the machine completely, with the presser foot up so the tension discs open. Replace the needle. Check the thread path for catches. Use a good brand of thread and avoid old spools that have become dry. Make sure the thread unwinds freely from the spool.

                                                                                                                                                        Problem 6: Seams that look loose or loopy

                                                                                                                                                        What you see. Loops on the underside of the seam, or a seam that gapes open when stretched.

                                                                                                                                                        Common causes. Top tension too low, wrong threading, lint in the tension discs or a bobbin that is wound unevenly.

                                                                                                                                                        Cures. Clean the machine, especially around the bobbin case and tension discs. Rethread the machine. Increase the top tension a little, test again, and adjust in small steps.

                                                                                                                                                        Working with elastic

                                                                                                                                                        Many projects include elastic directly sewn onto fabric, in waistbands, cuffs and leg openings. A few tips:

                                                                                                                                                        1. Divide both the elastic and the fabric into equal sections with pins or marks, and match them as you sew so the stretch is even.
                                                                                                                                                        2. Stretch the elastic as you sew, only as much as needed, and keep the tension consistent. Over-stretching creates a tight gather that may cause puckering.
                                                                                                                                                        3. Use a zigzag or stretch stitch, and sew near the edge of the elastic without stitching directly through the stretch yarns where possible.
                                                                                                                                                        4. Use a ballpoint needle and test a sample for stretch and recovery.

                                                                                                                                                        Machines and settings

                                                                                                                                                        Different machines need different settings. On an overlocker, the differential feed can be adjusted to prevent stretching or gathering. Coverstitch machines produce a double line of stitches on top and a looper thread underneath, giving a stretchy and neat hem. On industrial machines, operators adjust tension, presser foot pressure and feed to match each fabric. Whatever the machine, the principle is the same: test, observe, adjust one thing at a time.

                                                                                                                                                        Build a test routine

                                                                                                                                                        For any new stretch fabric:

                                                                                                                                                        • Cut two scraps with the same grain and layers as the actual seam.
                                                                                                                                                        • Sew a test seam with your chosen needle, thread and stitch.
                                                                                                                                                        • Stretch the seam firmly along its length. It should extend with the fabric and return without rippling.
                                                                                                                                                        • Wash and dry the sample, then check again.
                                                                                                                                                        • Keep a record of the settings that worked.

                                                                                                                                                        Spending ten minutes on testing is better than discovering a problem after cutting an entire project.

                                                                                                                                                        Final thoughts

                                                                                                                                                        Most problems on stretch seams come down to four things: the wrong needle, the wrong thread, a stitch with no give, and tension or feeding that is out of balance. When you choose a ballpoint needle, flexible thread and a stretch stitch, then adjust tension and feeding with care, stretch fabric becomes much easier to sew. With a little practice, seams will stretch, recover and last, and the frustrations of skipped stitches and wavy edges will fade.

                                                                                                                                                        Frequently asked questions

                                                                                                                                                        Why do stitches pucker on stretch fabric?

                                                                                                                                                        Usually the tension is too tight or the fabric is being pulled. Reduce tension and let the machine feed the fabric.

                                                                                                                                                        Why do stretch seams break?

                                                                                                                                                        A straight stitch has no give, so use a stretch or zigzag stitch and a stretch-friendly thread.

                                                                                                                                                        Which needle is best for stretch fabric?

                                                                                                                                                        A ballpoint or stretch needle helps avoid skipped stitches and damage to the fibres.

                                                                                                                                                        How do I fix skipped stitches?

                                                                                                                                                        Change to a fresh stretch needle, check threading and adjust tension.

                                                                                                                                                          Denier, decitex, tex, Ne and Nm: a clear guide to the numbers that describe how thick or fine a thread really is.

                                                                                                                                                          By SNEH Editorial

                                                                                                                                                          ← Threads & Yarns

                                                                                                                                                          Types of Threads in the Textile Industry: Cotton, Polyester, Nylon and More

                                                                                                                                                          Sewing and industrial threads explained: what they are made of, how they differ and how to choose the right one for every fabric.

                                                                                                                                                          By SNEH Editorial•16 November 2026•6 min read•1,310 words

                                                                                                                                                          In this article

                                                                                                                                                          1. Thread, yarn and fibre: clearing up the terms
                                                                                                                                                          2. Natural fibre threads
                                                                                                                                                          3. Synthetic threads
                                                                                                                                                          4. Blended and specialty threads
                                                                                                                                                          5. Thread constructions
                                                                                                                                                          6. Choosing thread for fabric
                                                                                                                                                          7. Thread size and needles
                                                                                                                                                          8. Colour and fastness
                                                                                                                                                          9. Storage and care of thread
                                                                                                                                                          10. Environmental trends
                                                                                                                                                          11. Final thoughts

                                                                                                                                                          Threads are the quiet connectors of the textile world. They hold seams together, shape garments, embroider designs and carry the strength of everything we wear. Yet most people never think about thread until a seam bursts. In reality, thread is a technical product with many varieties, each made from different fibres and constructed in different ways. This article introduces the main types of thread used in the textile industry and offers practical advice on choosing between them.

                                                                                                                                                          Thread, yarn and fibre: clearing up the terms

                                                                                                                                                          A fibre is the basic unit of a textile, such as a cotton hair or a polyester filament. A yarn is a continuous strand made by twisting or combining fibres. A thread, in the sewing sense, is a specially engineered yarn designed to be fed through a needle and form stitches. Sewing thread is usually made from several plies of yarn twisted together and then treated with finishes to improve strength, smoothness and sewability.

                                                                                                                                                          Natural fibre threads

                                                                                                                                                          Cotton thread

                                                                                                                                                          Cotton thread is made from spun cotton fibres. It is soft, breathable and easy to sew. It does not melt under a hot iron, which makes it good for pressing and for traditional quilting and heirloom work. Mercerised cotton thread has been treated with an alkali solution that increases strength, lustre and dye affinity.

                                                                                                                                                          Advantages: pleasant natural feel, good heat tolerance, easy to dye, takes well to natural fabrics.

                                                                                                                                                          Limitations: lower strength than synthetic threads, little stretch, can shrink in washing and may rot if left damp for long periods.

                                                                                                                                                          Common uses: quilting, light garments in natural fabrics, embroidery, hand sewing and some home textiles.

                                                                                                                                                          Silk thread

                                                                                                                                                          Silk thread is made from natural silk filaments. It is smooth, strong for its thickness and has a beautiful sheen. Silk thread is traditionally used for fine tailoring, buttonholes, embroidery and basting, because it glides through fabric without leaving marks.

                                                                                                                                                          Advantages: luxurious lustre, fine and strong, excellent drape.

                                                                                                                                                          Limitations: costly, can be damaged by sunlight and strong chemicals, and may be less durable than synthetics under heavy use.

                                                                                                                                                          Linen thread

                                                                                                                                                          Linen thread, made from flax, is very strong and often used for leatherwork, bookbinding, shoes and heavy-duty hand sewing. It is usually waxed to improve smoothness and durability.

                                                                                                                                                          Synthetic threads

                                                                                                                                                          Polyester thread

                                                                                                                                                          Polyester is the most widely used sewing thread in the modern industry. It is strong, resists abrasion, holds colour well, does not shrink significantly and resists many chemicals. Polyester thread comes in several forms.

                                                                                                                                                          • Spun polyester. Made from short staple fibres twisted together, it looks like cotton thread but is stronger.
                                                                                                                                                          • Core-spun polyester. Has a continuous polyester filament in the centre wrapped by spun polyester or cotton fibres, giving high strength with good heat resistance.
                                                                                                                                                          • Continuous filament polyester. Smooth, strong and often used for heavy-duty applications and decorative stitching.
                                                                                                                                                          • Textured polyester. Bulky and soft, widely used for overlocking and stretch seams because it covers the edge well.

                                                                                                                                                          Advantages: durable, economical, colourfast, versatile.

                                                                                                                                                          Limitations: can melt under extreme heat, and very strong thread in light fabrics may cut the cloth if the stitch is too tight.

                                                                                                                                                          Nylon thread

                                                                                                                                                          Nylon thread is very strong, smooth and elastic. It is commonly used for upholstery, leather goods, outdoor gear and bag making. It has good abrasion resistance but is more sensitive to ultraviolet light than polyester, which means it may weaken in strong sunlight over time.

                                                                                                                                                          Advantages: high strength, flexibility, good elasticity.

                                                                                                                                                          Limitations: lower UV resistance, can stretch under load.

                                                                                                                                                          Polypropylene and other synthetic threads

                                                                                                                                                          Polypropylene threads are used in some industrial and technical applications because they are lightweight and resist moisture and chemicals. Other special threads include aramid threads for high-temperature and flame-resistant uses, and PTFE threads for chemical resistance. These are specialist products chosen for performance rather than ordinary garments.

                                                                                                                                                          Blended and specialty threads

                                                                                                                                                          Cotton-wrapped polyester

                                                                                                                                                          Also called core-spun thread, this construction wraps cotton around a polyester filament core. It combines the heat tolerance of cotton on the surface with the strength of polyester inside, making it a favourite for industrial garment sewing.

                                                                                                                                                          Rayon and viscose threads

                                                                                                                                                          Rayon thread has a bright, silky lustre and is used mainly for decorative embroidery. It is less strong than polyester and can be damaged by harsh washing, so it is best for items that do not face hard wear.

                                                                                                                                                          Metallic threads

                                                                                                                                                          Metallic threads, made of a core wrapped with metallised film, give sparkle to embroidery and decorative stitching. They can be fragile, so special needles and slower sewing speeds are recommended.

                                                                                                                                                          Water-soluble thread

                                                                                                                                                          This specialty thread dissolves in water, which allows temporary stitching or stabilising for embroidery and lace. It is a useful tool in craft and in specialised machine embroidery.

                                                                                                                                                          Elastic and stretch threads

                                                                                                                                                          Some threads are designed for stretch, including textured nylon and polyester threads and elastic threads used in shirring. Rubber or spandex covered threads are used on bobbins to gather fabrics. The next articles in this blog explore covered and core-spun yarns in detail.

                                                                                                                                                          Thread constructions

                                                                                                                                                          Spun thread is made from staple fibres, short lengths twisted together. It has a slightly fuzzy surface and a natural feel.

                                                                                                                                                          Filament thread uses continuous strands, which makes it smoother and stronger.

                                                                                                                                                          Textured thread has filaments that have been crimped or bulked, giving elasticity and softness.

                                                                                                                                                          Core-spun thread uses a filament core wrapped with staple fibres.

                                                                                                                                                          Plied thread is made by twisting two or more single yarns together to improve strength and balance. Three-ply thread is typical for general sewing.

                                                                                                                                                          Choosing thread for fabric

                                                                                                                                                          A general rule is to match the thread to the fabric in fibre type and weight. Natural fabrics sew well with cotton or polyester thread, while synthetics often pair with polyester or nylon. A thread that is far stronger than the fabric can cut or pucker light cloth, while a thread weaker than the fabric will break in the seam.

                                                                                                                                                          • Light cotton or silk: fine cotton, silk or fine polyester.
                                                                                                                                                          • Everyday garments: polyester or core-spun polyester.
                                                                                                                                                          • Denim and heavy fabrics: strong polyester, often thicker thread.
                                                                                                                                                          • Stretch fabrics: textured polyester or nylon, or thread with stretch.
                                                                                                                                                          • Leather and upholstery: strong nylon or polyester, thicker sizes.
                                                                                                                                                          • Embroidery: rayon, polyester or silk for lustre.
                                                                                                                                                          • Outdoor items: UV-resistant polyester.

                                                                                                                                                          Thread size and needles

                                                                                                                                                          Thread size is expressed in several systems, which the next articles examine. In practice, the thread must pass smoothly through the needle eye and the fabric. Too thick a thread in a small needle causes breakage, and too thin a thread in a large needle gives weak stitches. Check needle and thread charts when sewing special fabrics.

                                                                                                                                                          Colour and fastness

                                                                                                                                                          Colour matching is essential in garment production. Thread should be tested for colour fastness to washing, rubbing, light and perspiration. A poorly dyed thread can bleed or fade, leaving unsightly seams. Dye lots may vary, so buy enough thread from one lot for a whole project or production run.

                                                                                                                                                          Storage and care of thread

                                                                                                                                                          Keep thread in a cool, dry place away from direct sunlight. Old thread, especially cotton, can become brittle and weak, so test by pulling a length to see if it snaps easily. Store spools in closed boxes to protect from dust.

                                                                                                                                                          Environmental trends

                                                                                                                                                          Sustainable options are growing. Recycled polyester thread made from plastic bottles, organic cotton thread and biodegradable threads are increasingly available. These can help brands reduce environmental impact, though buyers should verify claims through certifications.

                                                                                                                                                          Final thoughts

                                                                                                                                                          Choosing thread is not an afterthought. The right thread produces strong, neat, durable seams and a professional finish, while the wrong one causes puckering, breakage and early failure. Knowing the main types, cotton, silk, polyester, nylon and their blends, equips you to make intelligent choices. Whether you are sewing a single dress or planning a factory run, the humble thread deserves careful attention.

                                                                                                                                                          Frequently asked questions

                                                                                                                                                          What are the most common sewing threads?

                                                                                                                                                          Polyester, cotton and nylon are among the most common, along with blends and specialist threads.

                                                                                                                                                          Which thread is strongest?

                                                                                                                                                          Nylon and polyester threads are generally stronger than cotton, with nylon offering high stretch and polyester offering good strength and colour stability.

                                                                                                                                                          What is core-spun thread?

                                                                                                                                                          It is a thread with a strong filament core wrapped in another fibre, so it combines strength with a good feel.

                                                                                                                                                          How do I choose a thread?

                                                                                                                                                          Match the thread to the fabric type, the seam strength needed and how the item will be washed and worn.
