                                                                                                                                                                  Woven vs Knitted vs Braided Elastic: Which One Do You Need?

                                                                                                                                                                  Three constructions, three personalities. Compare woven, knitted and braided elastic and pick the right one for your project.

                                                                                                                                                                  By SNEH Editorial•16 November 2026•6 min read•1,244 words

                                                                                                                                                                  In this article

                                                                                                                                                                  1. Why construction matters
                                                                                                                                                                  2. Woven elastic
                                                                                                                                                                  3. Knitted elastic
                                                                                                                                                                  4. Braided elastic
                                                                                                                                                                  5. A quick comparison
                                                                                                                                                                  6. How the garment decides the choice
                                                                                                                                                                  7. Sewing considerations
                                                                                                                                                                  8. Common mistakes to avoid
                                                                                                                                                                  9. Choosing for manufacturers
                                                                                                                                                                  10. A simple decision path
                                                                                                                                                                  11. Final thoughts

                                                                                                                                                                  Anyone who has stood in front of a wall of elastic knows the confusion. Some bands look flat and dense, some look soft and stretchy, and some look like tiny ropes. They all stretch, so why are there so many types? The answer lies in how they are made. The three main constructions are woven, knitted and braided, and each is built for different jobs. This guide explains the differences in plain language and helps you choose the right one.

                                                                                                                                                                  Why construction matters

                                                                                                                                                                  Two elastics can be made from exactly the same rubber and polyester and still behave in opposite ways because of how the yarns are arranged. Construction affects how much the band stretches, how it recovers, how it feels against skin, how it looks, whether it curls or rolls, how it behaves when sewn and how long it lasts. Choosing a construction is therefore the first and most important decision when picking elastic.

                                                                                                                                                                  Woven elastic

                                                                                                                                                                  Woven elastic is produced on a narrow-fabric loom. Lengthwise warp yarns, including the elastic core, are interlaced with crosswise weft yarns. The result is a tight, firm structure similar to a tiny strip of woven cloth.

                                                                                                                                                                  Strengths of woven elastic

                                                                                                                                                                  • It is strong and stable. It holds its width even when stretched.
                                                                                                                                                                  • It has high tension, so it gives firm support.
                                                                                                                                                                  • It does not roll or twist easily, so it lies flat inside waistbands.
                                                                                                                                                                  • It tolerates repeated washing well.
                                                                                                                                                                  • It can be made in wide widths with a uniform surface.

                                                                                                                                                                  Weaknesses of woven elastic

                                                                                                                                                                  • It is less soft than knitted elastic and can feel stiff against sensitive skin.
                                                                                                                                                                  • It usually has a moderate stretch range compared with braided types.
                                                                                                                                                                  • It is more expensive to produce than braided elastic.

                                                                                                                                                                  Best uses. Waistbands for trousers and skirts, sportswear, uniforms, bag straps, orthopaedic supports and any application where firmness and stability are essential.

                                                                                                                                                                  Knitted elastic

                                                                                                                                                                  Knitted elastic is made on warp-knitting machines. Instead of crossing at right angles like woven threads, the yarns form interlocking loops. Elastic threads are laid into this loop structure.

                                                                                                                                                                  Strengths of knitted elastic

                                                                                                                                                                  • It is soft and flexible, which makes it comfortable next to skin.
                                                                                                                                                                  • It drapes well and follows the body.
                                                                                                                                                                  • It can be made with decorative edges, patterns and picots.
                                                                                                                                                                  • It is lightweight and breathable.
                                                                                                                                                                  • It handles frequent movement comfortably.

                                                                                                                                                                  Weaknesses of knitted elastic

                                                                                                                                                                  • It can be less strong than woven elastic of the same width.
                                                                                                                                                                  • It may have lower stability and can stretch in width as well as length if poorly designed.
                                                                                                                                                                  • Cutting can sometimes cause the ends to fray if the yarns are not locked correctly.

                                                                                                                                                                  Best uses. Lingerie, underwear, baby clothing, cuffs, necklines, nightwear and any garment where softness matters more than firmness.

                                                                                                                                                                  Braided elastic

                                                                                                                                                                  Braided elastic is made by interlacing yarns diagonally around the elastic core on a braiding machine. It usually looks like a flat or round cord with a small diamond pattern along the surface.

                                                                                                                                                                  Strengths of braided elastic

                                                                                                                                                                  • It stretches a lot, often more than woven or knitted types.
                                                                                                                                                                  • It is inexpensive and quick to make.
                                                                                                                                                                  • It is easy to sew through and works well for general sewing.
                                                                                                                                                                  • It is available in many colours and widths.

                                                                                                                                                                  Weaknesses of braided elastic

                                                                                                                                                                  • It narrows noticeably when stretched, which can cause it to dig into the skin.
                                                                                                                                                                  • It can lose recovery more quickly than woven elastic under heavy use.
                                                                                                                                                                  • It tends to curl and twist inside casings, especially in wide widths.

                                                                                                                                                                  Best uses. Masks, drawcords, crafts, children's clothes, lightweight waistbands in casings, hair accessories and general household sewing.

                                                                                                                                                                  A quick comparison

                                                                                                                                                                  Imagine you are comparing the three on a scale of softness, strength and stretch.

                                                                                                                                                                  • Softness: knitted is generally softest, braided is middle, woven is firmest.
                                                                                                                                                                  • Strength and stability: woven is strongest, knitted is moderate, braided is lowest in wide widths.
                                                                                                                                                                  • Stretch range: braided often has the greatest stretch, knitted is flexible, woven is controlled.
                                                                                                                                                                  • Cost: braided is usually cheapest, knitted is middle, woven is often more costly.
                                                                                                                                                                  • Narrowing when stretched: braided narrows the most, woven the least.

                                                                                                                                                                  These are tendencies, not strict rules. A well-made knitted elastic can be very strong and a poorly made woven one can feel harsh, so always test samples for your actual product.

                                                                                                                                                                  How the garment decides the choice

                                                                                                                                                                  Rather than starting with the elastic, start with the garment and ask what the elastic must do.

                                                                                                                                                                  For a waistband that needs to hold the garment up all day, choose woven elastic or a high-quality knitted elastic with strong recovery. Woven bands resist twisting and give consistent support.

                                                                                                                                                                  For underwear or baby clothes, choose soft knitted elastic. It stays comfortable against delicate skin and can include finished edges that do not scratch.

                                                                                                                                                                  For a drawstring or simple casing, braided elastic is simple, cheap and flexible, but use a narrow width and avoid very wide braided bands because they twist.

                                                                                                                                                                  For a face mask or hair accessory, a narrow braided or knitted cord works well, but pay attention to softness around the ears or scalp.

                                                                                                                                                                  For heavy items such as bags and luggage straps, woven elastic with strong polyester yarns gives durability and resists abrasion.

                                                                                                                                                                  Sewing considerations

                                                                                                                                                                  Construction also affects how you sew. Woven elastic is firm and holds stitches well, so it is easy to attach with straight or zigzag stitches. Knitted elastic needs a stitch that stretches, such as zigzag or a stretch stitch, otherwise the thread may break when the garment is worn. Braided elastic can be sewn through directly but the stitching should not pinch the cords too tightly. In every case, test on a scrap of the same fabric before sewing the final garment.

                                                                                                                                                                  Common mistakes to avoid

                                                                                                                                                                  1. Choosing by width alone. Two elastics of equal width can feel completely different. Always ask about construction and composition.
                                                                                                                                                                  2. Using braided elastic wide in a casing. It twists and ruins the look of the garment.
                                                                                                                                                                  3. Ignoring skin comfort. Stiff edges cause irritation, especially for children and people with sensitive skin.
                                                                                                                                                                  4. Overstretching during sewing. Pulling too hard while sewing leaves the elastic partially extended in the finished garment.
                                                                                                                                                                  5. Skipping the wash test. Elastic that looks great new may shrink, bleed or lose stretch after washing. Test before bulk use.

                                                                                                                                                                  Choosing for manufacturers

                                                                                                                                                                  If you are producing garments in volume, the choice has bigger consequences. Woven elastic costs more but gives consistent results with fewer returns for waistband failure. Knitted elastic gives a premium feel for intimate apparel. Braided elastic can lower costs for basic items. Ask suppliers for technical sheets that show stretch, recovery and shrinkage, and compare actual results from sample batches before committing.

                                                                                                                                                                  A simple decision path

                                                                                                                                                                  If you want the shortest rule of thumb, use this. Need firm and stable support? Choose woven. Need soft and comfortable against the skin? Choose knitted. Need cheap, flexible and general-purpose? Choose braided. Then refine the choice by width, colour, composition and testing.

                                                                                                                                                                  Final thoughts

                                                                                                                                                                  Woven, knitted and braided elastics are not competitors so much as specialists. Each solves a particular set of problems, and a skilled designer or sewist uses all three. Learning their differences saves money, improves comfort and gives your finished products a more professional performance. Next time you pick up a roll of elastic, check how it is made, and let the construction guide your decision.

                                                                                                                                                                  Frequently asked questions

                                                                                                                                                                  What is the main difference between woven, knitted and braided elastic?

                                                                                                                                                                  Woven elastic is firm and narrow with strong holding power. Knitted elastic is soft and flexible. Braided elastic is stretchy and lightweight, and its width narrows when stretched.

                                                                                                                                                                  Which type is best for a waistband?

                                                                                                                                                                  Woven or knitted elastic is usually preferred for waistbands because it holds its shape. Braided elastic is better for lighter uses like casings.

                                                                                                                                                                  Which elastic can be sewn directly onto fabric?

                                                                                                                                                                  Knitted and woven elastic are both commonly sewn on. Braided elastic is usually used inside a casing because it narrows when stretched.

                                                                                                                                                                  Which type is softest against skin?

                                                                                                                                                                  Knitted elastic is generally the softest, which is why it is common in undergarments and baby wear.

                                                                                                                                                                    Yarn Twist Explained: S-Twist, Z-Twist, Twist Level and Why It Matters

                                                                                                                                                                    Twist holds fibres together and shapes how yarn looks, feels and performs. Learn the difference between S and Z twist, how twist level is measured and how it affects results.

                                                                                                                                                                    By SNEH Editorial•16 November 2026•6 min read•1,313 words

                                                                                                                                                                    In this article

                                                                                                                                                                    1. What twist does
                                                                                                                                                                    2. S-twist and Z-twist
                                                                                                                                                                    3. Singles, plied and cabled yarns
                                                                                                                                                                    4. Twist level and how it is measured
                                                                                                                                                                    5. How twist changes yarn performance
                                                                                                                                                                    6. Twist liveliness and balance
                                                                                                                                                                    7. Twist in sewing thread and elastic
                                                                                                                                                                    8. Choosing the right twist
                                                                                                                                                                    9. Final thoughts

                                                                                                                                                                    Take a short length of ordinary sewing thread and look closely. You will see that it is not a straight bundle of fibres. The fibres spiral around each other like a tiny rope. That spiral is called twist, and it is one of the most important features of any yarn. Twist holds short fibres together, adds strength, and changes how a yarn looks and feels. It also decides how a yarn behaves in sewing, weaving and knitting. This article explains what twist is, how S and Z twist differ, how twist level is described and why it matters in real work.

                                                                                                                                                                    What twist does

                                                                                                                                                                    Most natural fibres, such as cotton and wool, are short. On their own they would simply pull apart. When the fibres are drawn out into a strand and twisted, the spiral forces them to grip each other through friction, and the strand becomes strong enough to use.

                                                                                                                                                                    Twist gives a yarn several things:

                                                                                                                                                                    • Strength. More twist generally brings fibres closer and increases grip, up to a point.
                                                                                                                                                                    • Compactness. A highly twisted yarn is thinner, firmer and smoother.
                                                                                                                                                                    • Surface and feel. Low twist gives a soft, fuzzy, bulky yarn. High twist gives a harder, crisper one.
                                                                                                                                                                    • Appearance. The direction and amount of twist affect how light reflects and how a fabric looks.

                                                                                                                                                                    Continuous filament yarns, such as polyester and nylon, do not need twist for strength in the same way, but they are often given a small amount to keep the filaments together and make them easier to handle.

                                                                                                                                                                    S-twist and Z-twist

                                                                                                                                                                    Twist can run in two directions. The names come from the letters themselves.

                                                                                                                                                                    • S-twist: when the yarn is held upright, the visible spirals slope in the same direction as the centre part of the letter S, rising from lower left to upper right is not the pattern; instead the spirals run from upper left down to lower right.
                                                                                                                                                                    • Z-twist: the spirals slope as the centre stroke of the letter Z does, running from lower left up to upper right.

                                                                                                                                                                    A simple way to remember is to hold the yarn vertically and compare the slope of the spirals with the middle stroke of the letter. Neither direction is better in itself. Single yarns are very often spun with Z-twist, and plied yarns are commonly made by twisting singles together in the opposite direction, which is S-twist. The two directions are used in combination to balance the yarn.

                                                                                                                                                                    Singles, plied and cabled yarns

                                                                                                                                                                    Twist also works at several levels.

                                                                                                                                                                    1. Single yarn. Fibres are twisted together into one strand, usually in one direction.
                                                                                                                                                                    2. Plied yarn. Two or more singles are twisted together, usually in the opposite direction to the twist of each single. Plying makes yarn stronger, rounder and more even.
                                                                                                                                                                    3. Cabled yarn. Plied yarns are twisted together again, often in the original direction, for thick, strong cords and ropes.

                                                                                                                                                                    The opposite-direction rule is important. When ply twist runs against the single twist, it partly untwists the singles, which helps the finished yarn become balanced. A balanced yarn lies flat and does not twist on itself.

                                                                                                                                                                    Twist level and how it is measured

                                                                                                                                                                    Twist level is the number of turns in a given length. It is usually written as turns per metre or turns per inch. A low-twist yarn might have only a few hundred turns per metre. Hard-twisted yarns used for special crepe fabrics can be far higher. The exact figures depend on the fibre and yarn thickness, so they are best compared only within the same type of yarn.

                                                                                                                                                                    Another useful idea is the twist multiplier. Because thicker yarns need fewer turns to reach the same tightness, twist is often scaled to yarn thickness so that different yarns can be compared fairly. You do not need the formula to understand the point: the right twist depends on the fibre, thickness and purpose.

                                                                                                                                                                    Common descriptions include:

                                                                                                                                                                    • Soft or low twist, for bulky, soft and warm yarns, often used in knitting or for fabric faces that should feel gentle.
                                                                                                                                                                    • Medium twist, the all-round choice for general weaving and knitting.
                                                                                                                                                                    • High or hard twist, for strength, smooth surface and resistance to pilling.
                                                                                                                                                                    • Crepe twist, a very high twist that makes a yarn spring and curl, giving fabrics a pebbly, textured look.

                                                                                                                                                                    How twist changes yarn performance

                                                                                                                                                                    Changing the twist changes nearly everything.

                                                                                                                                                                    • Strength increases with twist, then falls. As twist rises, fibres grip more strongly. After an optimum point, the fibres are pulled into such a steep angle that strength drops again.
                                                                                                                                                                    • Softness falls as twist rises. Highly twisted yarns feel firmer and harder.
                                                                                                                                                                    • Elasticity changes. A twisted yarn can stretch a little as the spirals open, which is part of why crepe fabrics have a natural give.
                                                                                                                                                                    • Lustre decreases with high twist in some yarns, because the fibres do not lie parallel to the surface.
                                                                                                                                                                    • Pilling tendency often reduces because loose fibre ends are held down.
                                                                                                                                                                    • Thickness and density change. Extra twist pulls the yarn thinner and tighter.

                                                                                                                                                                    Twist liveliness and balance

                                                                                                                                                                    A yarn with a lot of twist stored in it is described as lively. If you hold a length loosely, it kinks and curls into snarls. This stored energy can cause problems in weaving and knitting, such as skewed fabric, loops and spirality, where knitted rows slant instead of running straight.

                                                                                                                                                                    Balanced yarns avoid this. Their twist is arranged so that the yarn hangs straight when relaxed. To calm a lively yarn, mills often use twist setting, applying steam or heat and moisture so that the fibres settle into position. Setting is common for hard-twisted and synthetic yarns.

                                                                                                                                                                    Twist in sewing thread and elastic

                                                                                                                                                                    For sewing thread, twist is critical. A thread must pass through a needle's eye at high speed, form stitches evenly and resist abrasion. Typical sewing threads are made from several plies, and the twist directions are chosen so that the thread does not unravel during stitching. Z-twist is common in sewing thread because many machines are designed for it. Using thread with the wrong twist direction on a machine, or on a sewing method that spins the thread in the other direction, can lead to loosening and breakage.

                                                                                                                                                                    For elastic products, covered yarns provide a good example. In covered elastic, a rubber or spandex core is wrapped with a spiral of another yarn. The wrapping direction and number of turns per metre affect how well the core is covered, how smooth the product feels and how stable it is. Double-covered yarns are often wrapped in opposite directions so that the twist forces balance each other, which gives a straight, calm yarn.

                                                                                                                                                                    Choosing the right twist

                                                                                                                                                                    A few practical rules help in selecting twist for a project.

                                                                                                                                                                    • For softness and warmth, choose lower twist, and accept that it may pill more and be less strong.
                                                                                                                                                                    • For strength and smoothness, choose medium to high twist.
                                                                                                                                                                    • For crinkled or crepe effects, choose very high twist and expect a springy yarn that needs careful handling.
                                                                                                                                                                    • For stable fabric, choose balanced yarn and consider setting.
                                                                                                                                                                    • For sewing, follow the thread maker's recommendation on twist direction and machine type.

                                                                                                                                                                    When working with a supplier, specify twist direction and level clearly, or ask for samples, so that results are repeatable.

                                                                                                                                                                    Final thoughts

                                                                                                                                                                    Twist is easy to overlook because it is built into the yarn, but it quietly shapes strength, feel, appearance and behaviour. S and Z are simply the two directions of the spiral, and the real skill lies in balancing direction, level and ply structure for the job. Whether you are choosing a thread for sewing, a yarn for knitting or a covered yarn for elastic, understanding twist will help you read specifications, avoid faults such as snarling and skewing, and get the result you are looking for.

                                                                                                                                                                    Frequently asked questions

                                                                                                                                                                    What are S-twist and Z-twist?

                                                                                                                                                                    They describe the direction of the twist in a yarn, where the spirals slope like the middle of the letter S or the letter Z.

                                                                                                                                                                    Why does twist level matter?

                                                                                                                                                                    Higher twist gives a stronger, firmer, smoother yarn, while lower twist gives a softer, bulkier yarn that is weaker.

                                                                                                                                                                    Why are plied yarns twisted in the opposite direction?

                                                                                                                                                                    Plying in the opposite direction balances the twist so the yarn does not curl or spiral on itself.

                                                                                                                                                                    Does twist direction affect sewing thread?

                                                                                                                                                                    Yes, the thread twist should suit the machine, as the wrong direction can untwist and cause breaks or loops.
